article_content: UK intelligence agencies are seeking to install 'black box' surveillance devices across national communications networks to monitor citizens' internet usage, according to a report released today. An influential parliamentary committee’s document reveals that these agencies aim to introduce a nationwide monitoring system designed to log nearly all Britons’ activities and communications online. The technology underpinning this surveillance—Deep Packet Inspection (DPI)—would collect data spanning various online services, including social platforms like Facebook and Twitter, Skype calls, and visits to different websites. Civil liberties and privacy advocates have strongly opposed the proposal, warning that it would grant the government unprecedented surveillance powers. The Intelligence and Security Committee’s report, published on Tuesday, outlines the agencies’ perspective on the draft Communications Data Bill, which seeks to update surveillance laws. Government officials insist that quick access to communications data is essential to fighting terrorism and other major crimes. However, the legislation has stalled after the Liberal Democrats withdrew their support. MI5 Director General Jonathan Evans told the committee that access to communications data is critical for investigations, as it reveals key details about suspects’ activities. Authorities emphasize they are not seeking unrestricted access to email content or phone call recordings. Instead, they seek so-called ‘envelope’ data—such as sender, recipient, location, and time—which would still require a court order to access message or call content. For example, agencies could see the email addresses involved in communication or the location and duration of phone calls but would need court approval to access the content. The Government Communications Headquarters (GCHQ) argues that rapid data access is vital in counter-terrorism and other high-level crime efforts. Opponents, however, contend that it is nearly impossible to separate communications data from content and that expanded data access could lead to broader privacy intrusions. Some campaigners also question how the UK can criticize foreign regimes for similar surveillance practices while pursuing this policy. Emma Carr of Big Brother Watch argued that using such intrusive technology undermines civil society and poses significant privacy risks. She expressed concern that content could be collected and stored, potentially setting a troubling example for other countries. Ms. Carr also warned that a lack of court oversight in data collection poses serious risks to privacy rights. Jim Killock, executive director of the Open Rights Group, highlighted the danger of introducing a ‘filter’ system that could cross-reference individuals’ data across services, making near-instant surveillance possible. A major challenge for the UK is obtaining information from overseas companies that may not comply with British requests. While the government states it will not access citizens’ message content without a court order, concerns remain that DPI could enable such access. Various encryption tools, like iSafeguard Freeware, HushMail, and GnuPG, are available to help users protect their privacy. The committee’s report said that surveillance devices would be critical in accessing data from uncooperative overseas providers, relying on DPI to examine data packets. Popular services potentially affected include Facebook, Twitter, Hotmail, and Google Chat. Although the surveillance proposals remain in draft form and some criticisms are noted, the report suggests that improvements in surveillance powers are necessary to keep up with technological change. It also indicates skepticism that encryption would be a sufficient obstacle for intelligence agencies, though some paragraphs remain redacted. Jim Killock argued it is unlikely the government can break advanced encryption.

article_content: Harry Burkhart, who faces accusations of setting several fires in California, was previously diagnosed with a range of mental health issues by a Vancouver doctor. She provided a letter for his court proceedings explaining these health issues. For confidentiality reasons, she did not disclose further case details or the other doctor's identity. Burkhart, a 24-year-old German national, has since been charged with 37 counts of arson tied to 52 separate fires across Los Angeles neighborhoods like Hollywood, West Hollywood, and Sherman Oaks. Both Burkhart and his mother's refugee applications were rejected, and Stancheva has not seen him since March 2010. Dr. Stancheva expressed her shock and disappointment about the events in Los Angeles, noting that it seemed Burkhart was not being treated for his depression at the time.

article_content: A 14-year-old Pakistani Christian girl, Rimsha Masih, who once faced life imprisonment for allegedly burning the Quran, will now have her case heard in juvenile court, her lawyer told CNN. The transfer came after a local court order on Monday, according to Rimsha's attorney Tahir Naveed Choudhry. Pakistani police concluded their investigation and determined that Rimsha is innocent, having been framed by an imam. 'There was no legal evidence against Rimsha,' police officer Munir Jafri said. These recent developments may signal the end of the ordeal for the teenager, who has faced blasphemy accusations since August. 'This is a precursor to the case ending, and it is quite unprecedented in the 25-year history of Pakistan's blasphemy laws,' said Ali Dayan Hasan, Human Rights Watch's Pakistan director. The police submitted their findings to the court, which typically follows police recommendations. There is substantial evidence implicating imam Khalid Jadoon Chishti in framing Rimsha and tearing pages from the holy book himself, Jafri said. Hasan noted this is significant because 'never before has a false accuser been held accountable.' Rimsha's case sparked international outcry against the Pakistani government, with critics arguing that the blasphemy laws are often abused to settle personal scores and to persecute religious minorities. The blasphemy laws, in effect for 25 years, were initially intended to maintain interreligious harmony, according to Hasan. However, military leader amendments in the 1980s turned blasphemy into a capital offense with vague wording, making the laws a tool for coercion and persecution, disproportionately affecting minorities, women, children, and the poor. Since 1986, there have been about 1,400 blasphemy cases in Pakistan, Hasan said. Over 15 people are currently on death row for blasphemy, and 52 have been killed while facing such charges. Rimsha was arrested on August 16. She and her family went into hiding after her release on bail, a move seen as a response to global condemnation. In an interview with CNN, she expressed happiness about reuniting with her family but admitted fearing for their safety. Individuals accused of blasphemy in Pakistan are frequently targeted by vigilantes. During her interview, Rimsha denied burning Quran pages and would not elaborate on the events of August 16. Investigators said her neighbor accused her of using burned Quran pages as cooking fuel, which gathered an angry crowd. There are conflicting reports about whether Rimsha was beaten or fled home when police arrived. Her lawyers claim the neighbor accused her due to a personal dispute, possibly based on unrequited interest. Although recent case developments are promising, Rimsha's ordeal continues. Her next hearing in juvenile court is set for October 1. Most blasphemy law victims come from minority Muslim sects, such as the Ahmadis, often regarded as nonbelievers by the Sunni majority. Her father, Mizrak Masih, a Christian house painter, insists that his family respects both the Quran and the Bible and cannot imagine committing blasphemy. Aid organizations from the United States, Italy, and Canada have offered relocation assistance, but Rimsha has expressed a desire to remain in Pakistan. Ali Dayan Hasan emphasized that, regardless of official findings, people may still believe the accusations, putting Rimsha's safety at risk. 'It's the accusation that endangers your life, and it can endure,' he said.

article_content: Tamika Thomas of Las Vegas, unable to conceive naturally after having her fallopian tubes removed due to two ectopic pregnancies, was using IVF to try for another child. Her efforts were cut short when a CVS pharmacy mistakenly gave her the abortion pill misoprostol instead of the prescribed IVF medication. After taking the pills, Thomas experienced unusually severe cramping—much worse than she expected from IVF treatments. Sensing something was wrong, she reported it to authorities. The Nevada State Board of Pharmacy determined that a technician entered the wrong prescription, and pharmacists failed to notice the error. The pharmacists faced fines and probation, while CVS was fined $10,000. One pharmacist apologized, calling it a human error. However, Thomas described her lasting pain, saying no remedy could fully heal the loss. This happened amid CVS and Walgreens announcing they would sell mifepristone, an abortion pill, over the counter where state law allows. This landscape follows the 2022 Supreme Court overturning Roe v. Wade, leaving abortion laws up to individual states. Attempts to get comment from CVS were unsuccessful at the time of publication.

Benson Henderson will make his UFC welterweight debut as a late replacement for Stephen Thompson on Saturday night, facing fellow Colorado native Brandon Thatch. Henderson steps up after suffering two consecutive losses at lightweight, moving up a division for this five-round main event in his hometown.

"We had been considering a move to 170 pounds for a while," Henderson told Sportsmail. "It's tough to lose the weight, so not having to cut will definitely help."

Henderson, a former lightweight champion, intends to return to lightweight in the future but saw this as an opportunity worth seizing. "I'll be giving up some size and strength, but I've trained with many top 170-pound fighters at my gym. I expect to be faster, quicker, and more athletic than many of the guys in this division."

For the first time, Henderson—usually the bigger fighter at 155 pounds—will face a size disadvantage when he meets Thatch at the 1st Bank Center. Still, he insists the move is only temporary: "This isn't permanent. I'll be back at 155. I stepped up because the opportunity arose. There are other interesting matchups at 170, but I don't plan to stay."

Thatch, standing 6'2", is aware of his physical advantages. "I'm a bigger, longer fighter," he said. "If I keep Henderson at the end of my jab and maintain distance, I'll succeed."

Since joining the UFC, Thatch has finished both Paulo Thiago and Justin Edwards in the first round, and has a record of stopping all 11 of his professional opponents early. As he aims for his third straight UFC win, Thatch embraces the pressures of headlining in Colorado: "Being the main event here is pressure, but it's good. I've done it before. If I keep impressing and winning, my career will continue to progress."

Kimi Raikkonen remains confident that Ferrari can help him become a Grand Prix winner once again—just not this season. His return to Maranello has not met expectations, as many believed he would challenge his teammate, Fernando Alonso. However, changes in regulations and the introduction of a new power unit have left Ferrari trailing its rivals, and Raikkonen has struggled to enjoy his car.

Most recently, Raikkonen achieved his best finish of the season by coming in sixth at the Hungarian Grand Prix. Despite this positive result, he sits at only 27 points in the championship out of Ferrari's total of 142—eight of which he earned in Hungary after starting from 16th on the grid, a poor position caused by a qualifying error from the team.

The 2007 world champion acknowledges that significant changes are required within the team and the car for notable improvement. "It's been a hard first part of the year," Raikkonen said. "I know I haven't lost speed from last year, so it's disappointing to deal with these issues. I hope the second half of the season improves, but one better result doesn't change everything."

Even with a sixth-place finish, Raikkonen was behind Alonso, who finished second in Hungary, as Daniel Ricciardo claimed victory and Lewis Hamilton placed third. Raikkonen rejoined Ferrari this year after last racing for them in 2009, having won the world championship with the team in 2007.

"We have made mistakes and have areas to improve to work better as a team," Raikkonen continued. "There are many things we need to address to achieve our potential. Still, I believe we are on the right path, even if progress has been slow. That's why I'm looking ahead not just to the remaining eight races but also to next season. I believe in the people and the team; we've seen some positive changes, with the right people in the right areas, and I am sure this will pay off."

"We understand where we are and what we need to do, but there's work to be done to reach our goals as Ferrari. We must make significant progress for next year by tackling current issues step by step. With good plans in place, I’m hopeful we can consistently improve, allowing both the team and myself to achieve our ambitions and start winning races again."

article_content: Global conversations about artificial intelligence (AI) rose by 70% from December 2022 to September 2023. Meanwhile, applications to AI and AI-related job postings increased by 11% worldwide and by 5.6% in India. This data comes from LinkedIn’s ‘Future of Work: State of AI @ Work’ report. Experts say the rising importance of AI has led to wider adoption in the workplace and a greater demand for AI talent. In India, Professional Services, Technology, Information and Media, and Financial Services are the sectors most in need of people with AI skills. There has also been an almost 80% rise in the number of LinkedIn members in India watching AI-related courses on LinkedIn Learning this quarter. Skill preferences among Indian learners vary by generation. Gen Z is focusing on digital skills such as programming languages, cloud computing, and data analysis. On the other hand, millennials and Gen X are dedicating more effort to soft skills like leadership, management, personal effectiveness, and personal development. Gen Z professionals in India are 1.3 times more likely than Gen X, and 2.4 times more likely than Baby Boomers, to pursue AI skills. Gen Z also spends 73% more time learning on LinkedIn compared to other generations. The report highlights that advances in generative AI can help remove barriers between cultures, regions, and industries. This could broaden the scope for hybrid work arrangements, which most workers expect today. Organizations in India are responding to demands for flexibility, as hybrid job postings increased from 13.2% in August 2022 to 20.1% in August 2023.

article_content: The expression 'coffee badging,' which has become popular with Gen Z employees, refers to workers briefly visiting the office mainly to connect with colleagues over a cup of coffee or tea before leaving for home. Seema Rekha, Managing Director at Antarmanh Consulting, views this behavior as counterproductive, arguing that it interrupts productivity and slows down service delivery since employees leave during working hours. She also points out that commuting stress and costs often discourage people from spending more time at work, potentially affecting their reputation. However, Rekha mentions that these social interactions can boost employee engagement and foster a sense of belonging, even though leaders have to spend more time in the office to accommodate hybrid schedules. Navneet Singh, CEO of AVSAR, sees coffee badging as more than a short-lived trend—he believes it reflects workers pushing back against rigid return-to-office rules. This, he says, highlights the growing importance of autonomy and intentional face-to-face connections in today’s hybrid work culture. Singh and Rekha agree that while working at the office can help complete tasks efficiently if teams are synchronized, it also demands more effort, involves extended commutes, and can be frustrating when in-person presence still requires digital meetings. Rekha adds that some disengaged employees check in just to feel purposeful—especially if unsure about their personal growth—while high-performing employees tend to focus on finishing tasks efficiently, whether at home or in the office. Overall, coffee badging brings both positives—like improved social well-being and networking—and negatives, such as lower productivity and unfinished work. Rekha notes that distractions from time pressures can lead to incomplete tasks, and she suggests managers develop careful plans considering employee strengths, project priorities, and engagement when organizing hybrid teams. For improvement, Singh advocates for outcome-focused performance reviews, adaptable work policies, good collaboration technology, frequent team engagement, acknowledgment of meaningful contributions regardless of location, and open conversations about workplace preferences.

article_content: As Manchester United prepare to formally introduce Louis van Gaal at Old Trafford, anticipation is high for insights from the famously forthright Dutch manager. Van Gaal is set to outline his vision for United’s future, drawing on core principles established across a celebrated career that includes successful tenures at Ajax, Barcelona, Bayern Munich, and the Dutch national team. Just weeks before the World Cup, Van Gaal addressed an audience of business experts at ‘De Week van de ondernemer’ (The Week of the Businessman) in the Netherlands. Speaking at FC Twente’s stadium in Enschede, he delivered a charismatic talk detailing the philosophy and preparation that underpin his success. Van Gaal spoke candidly about his leadership style, addressing accusations of arrogance. ‘The national coach sees opportunities because he believes in vision and structure,’ he said. ‘When I say that, I mean my vision, and my structure. Yes, that can be seen as arrogant, but I believe in my approach, which provides clarity for those in my organization. That’s important to me.’ Emphasizing the value of preparation, Van Gaal credited his mother for teaching him the importance of readiness and daily training. ‘You don’t achieve results without preparation—training, analysis, and evaluation. I do that every day. In football, that’s normal, but it should be the same in business. I ensure my staff is ready and involved in every process.’ He highlighted the significance of teamwork and expertise, noting, ‘I can’t achieve everything alone. I surround myself with specialists and listen to their advice. My organization includes 12 staff members—assistants, physiologists, analysts—working together to prepare, train, and evaluate. In total, I lead about 37 staff, and with the players, I’m responsible for around 60 people.’ Van Gaal explained that before selecting players, he prioritizes assembling a strong support staff. ‘First, I choose my staff, then we can provide players with the best environment for success. Regardless of the field, experts in each department help me make better decisions, though ultimately I am the one who takes responsibility.’ Discussing tactics, Van Gaal described his preference for a triangle-shaped midfield with a defensive point, referencing Barcelona’s style and Lionel Messi’s unique role as a forward. He emphasized that adaptability is key, showing his players examples from top teams and stressing transparency and clear communication from the outset. As Van Gaal prepares to start at Manchester United, his leadership centers on vision, preparation, and empowering staff and players to achieve collective success.

article_content: Owning a professional sports franchise is a dream for many, but such an ambition requires immense wealth. Curious about how team owners earned their fortunes? Here are nine billionaire owners and the origins of their wealth: 1. Rich DeVos (Orlando Magic, NBA): In 1959, DeVos and his friend Jay Van Andel launched Amway, now part of Alticor and generating $6 billion annually. DeVos's wealth is estimated at $3.5 billion. He bought the Magic for $85 million in 1991. 2. Robert L. Johnson (Charlotte Bobcats, NBA): Johnson founded BET and sold it to Viacom for $3 billion in 2001. Despite financial setbacks, his net worth is $1.1 billion. He was the first African-American billionaire in the U.S. and the first African-American majority owner of a major professional sports team. 3. Robert Kraft (New England Patriots, NFL): After Harvard Business School, Kraft began in the paper industry, founded International Forest Products, and now leads the Kraft Group. He kept the Patriots from relocating and led them to three Super Bowl wins. In 2005, Russian President Vladimir Putin reportedly took one of Kraft’s Super Bowl rings. 4. Hiroshi Yamauchi (Seattle Mariners, MLB): Yamauchi, who changed Nintendo from a playing card company to a video game leader over 55 years, became majority owner of the Mariners in 1992, despite not being a baseball fan and initial U.S. skepticism. 5. Jerry Jones (Dallas Cowboys, NFL): Jones built his wealth in the oil industry, supported by his father's business. A former Arkansas Razorbacks football player, Jones bought the Cowboys in 1989 for approximately $140 million, made significant changes, and helped them win three Super Bowls in the 1990s. 6. Malcolm Glazer (Tampa Bay Buccaneers, NFL; Manchester United, EPL): Glazer expanded his father's jewelry business into real estate and various holdings through First Allied Corporation. Known for his persistence, he acquired the Buccaneers in 1995 and later bought Manchester United. 7. Stanley Kroenke (Denver Nuggets, NBA; Colorado Avalanche, NHL; St. Louis Rams, NFL – partial): Kroenke made his fortune in real estate development and is married to Ann Walton of the Walmart family. He owns several U.S. sports teams and a share in Arsenal F.C. 8. Daniel Gilbert (Cleveland Cavaliers, NBA): Gilbert founded Rock Financial (now Quicken Loans) with $5,000 in 1985. He sold and later bought back the company, then purchased the Cavaliers for $375 million in 2005. Gilbert also owns businesses like Fathead. 9. Stephen Bisciotti (Baltimore Ravens, NFL): Bisciotti co-founded Aerotek, now Allegis Group, a leading staffing company. He bought a 49% stake in the Ravens in 2000 and acquired full ownership in 2004.

article_content: Cocaine use has become so common in rural communities that it is now considered 'normalized.' According to Aidan Ormsby, a drugs and alcohol support manager in Irvinestown, the drug is easily accessed in towns and villages across rural Northern Ireland. 'It's not just cities or urban areas anymore,' he said. 'We're seeing cocaine use in all areas of society, including rural communities.' Mr. Ormsby, who works at the ARC Healthy Living Centre, which supports people throughout Fermanagh and parts of Tyrone, noted: 'Anecdotally, we hear stories from all over Fermanagh and Tyrone that cocaine is available almost everywhere.' He expressed concern about the growing acceptance of this Class A drug. 'People, especially young people, are starting to see it as normal—even for an ordinary night out,' he added. He also believes many people are unaware of how widespread cocaine use and availability now is in rural areas. 'We cover Fermanagh, which is the most rural part of Northern Ireland, and I don't think there's anywhere in Fermanagh or Omagh, or the areas around Omagh, where you couldn't get cocaine. That's become normal, really,' he said. In the past, cocaine was often seen as a drug used mainly by some middle-class people who could afford it. However, increases in supply and demand, along with falling prices, have made it more available and affordable across all socioeconomic groups in recent years. A leading academic researcher on substance use, Professor Anne Campbell of the Drug and Alcohol Research Network at Queen's University Belfast, has told BBC News NI that a public health campaign focused on harm reduction is needed to address the widespread and growing use of cocaine. 'If we don’t inform people of the risks, they can’t make informed choices about what they put in their bodies,' Professor Campbell said. 'We do this for alcohol and smoking, making people aware of potential dangers.' She explained that educating the public about cocaine is challenging because it is an illegal Class A drug, so public health campaigns are less likely. Professor Campbell believes this approach is no longer sustainable. 'Society, and organizations in power, have a responsibility to educate people about cocaine, just as we do with alcohol. We should be able to talk openly about it,' she said. Despite challenges, she emphasized the need for greater public awareness. 'Some people might say talking about these issues condones drug use. I’m not condoning it—cocaine is illegal. But increasingly more people are using it. Do we just stand by and let them suffer without information?' Professor Campbell asked. She warned that ignoring cocaine’s prevalence and the health risks involved is not acceptable. 'We wouldn’t take this approach with any other substance. People should have the information to make their own decisions,' she concluded. According to the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI), drug seizures have shown a mostly upward trend since 2006. Support with addiction is available via BBC Action Line.

article_content: Several of Wednesday's newspapers center their coverage on the measures announced in the King's Speech and the public response. The Times reports that senior Conservatives believe these measures are not a 'game changer' and may fall short of reviving the party's election prospects. They urge the chancellor to bring forward tax cuts in this month's Autumn Statement. An editorial in the Daily Telegraph acknowledges some 'eye-catching' proposals but questions whether the package forms a coherent platform for re-election. The Daily Mail says the speech set the stage for the upcoming election but notes a lack of excitement regarding the economy. The Guardian accuses Prime Minister Rishi Sunak of rehashing old ideas at a time when new policies are needed. While it welcomes positive changes like the introduction of a football regulator, it argues these are overshadowed by 'uglier' measures such as new North Sea oil and gas licenses that undermine green efforts. The Daily Mirror labels the speech as 'vapid, shallow, and tired,' accusing it of offering only political gimmicks and electioneering. Though it praises the policy requiring serious criminals to attend sentencing hearings, it ultimately finds the overall direction lacking. The Daily Telegraph also features a report from Gaza, describing a 'last stand' by Hamas fighters at a hospital, with Israeli troops reportedly cornering the remaining members of a 1,000-strong battalion. Lt Col Blich is quoted saying that Hamas forces have been less formidable than anticipated. The Guardian provides details on Metropolitan Police Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley's refusal to ban the pro-Palestinian march set for Armistice Day, Saturday. The paper describes Sir Mark as defiant in the face of cabinet ministers' calls for a ban, emphasizing the independence of the police force. article_content: Recent storms have caused significant damage at Pompeii, the renowned Roman archaeological site in Italy. Over the past weekend, severe rainfall led to the collapse of a tomb wall in the Porta Nocera necropolis and a section of the Temple of Venus archway. Authorities have responded by limiting access to affected parts of the site, with the Temple of Venus already off-limits and entry to the necropolis now sealed. Despite these incidents, the main area of Pompeii remains open for tourists. Italian cultural leaders expressed alarm at the fragility of the ancient site, with Culture Minister Dario Franceschini calling for an urgent meeting to discuss the recent deterioration. Officials are expected to file detailed reports regarding the causes of the collapses and ongoing maintenance measures. This event marks another in a series of structural failures that have plagued Pompeii in recent years, drawing both national and international criticism concerning site upkeep and resource allocation. The Italian government, alongside EU support, previously assigned resources toward restoration, and oversight measures have recently intensified under current leadership. The damage is especially troubling as Pompeii is not only a UNESCO World Heritage Site but also one of Italy’s top tourist destinations, attracting millions each year. Comparisons have been drawn with the carefully managed Pompeii exhibition at London’s British Museum, which garnered widespread praise and record attendance. Originally buried in the catastrophic eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 A.D.—an event described as powerful as dozens of atomic bombs—the city’s preservation has historically relied on layers of volcanic ash. About two-thirds of Pompeii’s ancient urban landscape has been excavated since its rediscovery in the 18th century.

article_content: Coralyn Hobbs, a 35-year-old mother from Cambridgeshire, publicly criticized the NHS after her 11-year-old son William was labeled overweight in a letter sent home from Ely St Mary’s Junior School. This letter was the result of his participation in the National Child Measurement Programme (NCMP), which checks the height and weight of students. Hobbs argued that this kind of categorization is misleading and potentially damaging, expressing concern that it could contribute to negative body image or even eating disorders in children. She described William as active, sporty, and eating a well-balanced, nutritious diet. According to the NCMP measures, William stands 4ft 9in and weighs six-and-a-half stone, placing him in the ‘overweight’ category per NHS criteria. Hobbs believes such labeling does not accurately reflect her son’s health. The NCMP, which collects data from certain age groups in schools, uses age, height, and sex to assign weight categories, and advises parents on potential lifestyle changes, though these are voluntary. Mandy Mayes, lead nurse for NCMP in Cambridgeshire, acknowledged these issues are sensitive and assured that national standards are used. She encouraged any concerned parents to discuss the findings. School representatives confirmed the program is mandatory nationwide. Tam Fry from the National Obesity Forum emphasized that the NCMP’s purpose is for statistics, not for individual health diagnoses, and warned that the BMI system can sometimes misclassify children when used this way. While the BMI index is adjusted for children, it does have limitations. Official UK statistics show about one in three children are categorized as overweight. Experts recommend parents interpret these letters with care, focusing on healthy lifestyle habits and ensuring children’s self-esteem and well-being remain a priority.

article_content: Steve Davies' second-half goal gave Blackpool just their second Sky Bet Championship win of the season with a 1-0 victory over Birmingham at Bloomfield Road. Davies scored the decisive goal in the second half, earning bottom-of-the-table Blackpool all three points and narrowing the gap to safety to eight points. This defeat was Birmingham's first in their last six games and their first since Gary Rowett became manager. Meanwhile, the Seasiders are now unbeaten in three games. Steve Davies celebrated his winning strike, saluting the crowd as Blackpool secured their second win of the campaign. David Cotterill nearly gave Birmingham an early lead after eight minutes, but his low free-kick from 25 yards was pushed away by Blackpool goalkeeper Joe Lewis. The hosts thought they had scored after 13 minutes when Davies finished Chris Eagles' cross, but the goal was disallowed for offside. In the 20th minute, Stephen Gleeson forced Lewis into another save with a right-footed volley from 25 yards. Blackpool threatened in the 24th minute as Eagles’ free kick found Davies, whose header was deflected onto the roof of the net. Blackpool manager Lee Clark secured victory against his former club. The best chance of the first half fell to Birmingham in the 33rd minute, when Lee Novak’s effort from 12 yards was cleared off the line by Kevin Foley. Just one minute later, Gleeson’s cross was met by Michael Morrison, but his header went across the face of goal. Eagles had the first chance of the second half with a shot from 25 yards that sailed over Darren Randolph’s goal. In the 55th minute, Davies put Blackpool ahead, latching onto a long ball forward from Lewis, maneuvering past Paul Robinson, and scoring past Randolph from 18 yards. Jonathan Grounds almost drew Birmingham level, but Nyron Nosworthy blocked his header. Blackpool threatened again in the 63rd minute as Jacob Murphy broke down the right and forced a save from Randolph with a shot from 18 yards. Murphy then forced Randolph to push a 40-yard attempt over the bar in the 65th minute. Murphy tested Randolph once more in the 79th minute, cutting in from the left and forcing him to save low. Substitute Mark Duffy missed a late chance with a 25-yard free kick, but Blackpool held on for the vital win.

article_content: President Obama's comments Thursday on Michael Brown's death echoed his powerful 2013 speech following Trayvon Martin's shooting. However, he notably avoided directly addressing the topic of race. A year prior, nationwide protests erupted after the acquittal of Trayvon Martin's shooter. Martin, 17, was carrying only Skittles when he was killed. Many protestors believed that Florida's self-defense law enabled George Zimmerman, a civilian, to racially profile Martin and then claim self-defense. Research has shown that in 'stand your ground' states, white individuals who kill black individuals are more likely to be found justified. Now, the fatal police shooting of Michael Brown, an 18-year-old African-American in Ferguson, Missouri, has reignited the national conversation about racial injustice. Brown, who had planned to start college that week, was reportedly shot multiple times after refusing an officer's command to leave the street, according to witnesses. The officer's identity has not been officially released, but a witness told CNN the officer is white. Ferguson is a predominantly black city, yet only three of its police officers are African-American. Social media platforms like Facebook and Twitter are seeing widespread use of the hashtag #iftheygunnedmedown, where young people post contrasting photos to highlight how the media can stereotype minorities. Officer involved in the Ferguson shooting reportedly had no prior disciplinary record. Responding to growing debate and protests—including incidents of looting and unrest—President Obama called for healing and constructive dialogue, not actions that would cause more harm. Some unrest has been interpreted as a plea for attention to persistent problems of racial injustice within the criminal justice system. There is a notable difference between Obama's approach to race in his speech after Trayvon Martin's case and his recent comments on Michael Brown's. This reflects a wider gap between the administration's promises to address racial injustice and the community's growing sense of disappointment. During Obama's 2008 campaign and after naming the first black U.S. attorney general, many expected his presidency to deliver significant change. His 2013 remarks after Trayvon Martin's death showed renewed focus on racial profiling legislation and improving conditions for young black men. He referenced his success passing relevant legislation as an Illinois state senator. However, federal action has faced challenges; roughly two dozen states maintain self-defense laws similar to Florida's, and none have repealed them. Further, federal investigations and hearings have not led to changes in these laws or practices like racial profiling. Efforts to pass the End Racial Profiling Act in Congress, sponsored by Senator Ben Cardin and Representative John Conyers, have so far failed. Ongoing allegations of police bias, such as New York's stop-and-frisk policy and high-profile use of force cases, continue to spark concern. Activists and social media have brought greater attention to stories like that of Darren Rainey, a mentally ill Florida prisoner who died in custody, prompting petitions for federal investigation. While President Obama has condemned police harassment of peaceful protesters and engaged state government officials, many believe more decisive action is needed specifically regarding Michael Brown's case and broader racial injustice. The FBI and Justice Department investigations into Brown's death should be transparent and accessible to the public. Eliminating racial injustice in the U.S. is a complex challenge, as systemwide biases are deeply rooted. Yet, racial profiling legislation is seen as a critical starting point. By preventing law enforcement from unfairly targeting minorities and implementing training to reduce bias, the justice system can move toward positive reform. As an Illinois state senator in 2003, Obama successfully passed a bill mandating the collection of racial data during traffic stops and training to address bias. While Congress has been less receptive, the administration is urged to show the same commitment that was evident in previous reforms. President Obama is seen as having the potential to deliver the 'more perfect union' promised during his 2008 campaign. By prioritizing action against racial profiling, his administration could honor the memory of Michael Brown and others impacted by systemic injustice.

article_content:
Union Home Minister and Minister of Cooperation Amit Shah officially launched the 'Bharat Organics' brand under the newly established National Cooperative Organics Limited (NCOL) during a symposium in New Delhi focused on promoting organic products via cooperatives. At the event, Shah also presented NCOL’s logo, website, and brochure, along with awarding membership certificates to five cooperative societies. 

Shah emphasized NCOL’s role as a dedicated platform for organic farmers, highlighting the launch of six organic products: tur dal, chana dal, sugar, rajma, basmati rice, and Sonamasoori rice. These products are available immediately through Mother Dairy’s Safal outlets and online platforms, with plans to sell a total of 20 organic items by year-end and to expand retail networks nationwide and internationally. 

Half of the profits from NCOL’s sales will be distributed directly to the member farmers to support their income. Headquartered in Gujarat and promoted by the National Dairy Development Board under the Multi State Cooperative Societies Act, 2002, NCOL will manage every step of the organic supply chain—including aggregation, certification, testing, processing, marketing, and export—for the benefit of farmers. 

India ranks fourth globally in organic agricultural land and is the world’s top country in terms of organic producers, with 2.7 million hectares under organic certification. In 2022-23, India produced 2.9 million tonnes and exported 312,000 tonnes of certified organic products worth Rs 5,525 crore, mainly to the US, EU, and Canada. Madhya Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Goa, Maharashtra, Gujarat, and North Eastern states lead in certified organic land. 

NCOL is one of three recently established government cooperatives—the others focus on certified seeds and exports. Across India, cooperative societies number 7.89 crore, with a total of 29 crore members.

article_content: Li Shangfu, seen in Singapore on June 1, served as China's defense minister earlier this year. Chinese leaders officially removed him from his position on Tuesday, according to Chinese state media. Li's dismissal follows about two months out of the public eye. The decision was made by the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress, China's top legislature, during meetings in Beijing. In the same decree, Qin Gang, the former foreign minister who also disappeared from public view in June, was stripped of his state councilor title. Beijing had already replaced Qin with Wang Yi as foreign minister in July. Chinese authorities did not provide an explanation for these dismissals. Analysts consider the changes a sign of turbulence among the Communist Party’s top leadership, with Li being the second minister removed in recent months. There is considerable speculation that Li is under investigation, as he stopped attending official meetings in late August and has not appeared publicly since. However, this remains unconfirmed. Joseph Torigian, a research fellow at Stanford University's Hoover Institution, noted that holding a high military position in China has inherent risks, given the military's importance to the regime’s security. Examples from history include Peng Dehuai, a former defense chief who died in prison after Mao Zedong purged him, and Marshall Lin Biao, who died in a plane crash after allegedly trying to defect. Unlike those figures, Li Shangfu was an outward-facing official, liaising with international delegations. Still, Torigian suggests that did not eliminate him as a potential threat to Xi Jinping. "For Xi Jinping to remove someone like Li Shangfu sends a strong message, but it is not destabilizing," Torigian said. The Financial Times has reported that American officials believe Li is under investigation for corruption, while The Wall Street Journal has reported that Qin faces a national security investigation, possibly linked to an affair. Deng Yuwen, an independent Chinese political commentator in the United States, said that while these removals could damage Xi Jinping’s image, they are unlikely to affect his hold on power. Deng stated the rapid removal of two officials once seen as close to Xi reflects both on Xi’s choices and the concentration of power under his leadership. Recent weeks have also seen a leadership shake-up at the top of China’s military rocket force, responsible for managing the country’s nuclear and missile arsenal. Willy Wo-Lap Lam, a senior fellow at the Jamestown Foundation, noted that the procurement of military equipment is potentially lucrative for corrupt officials, as it involves handling significant monetary transactions. Before becoming defense minister, Li headed the military's principal weapons procurement and development branch. In 2018, the United States sanctioned Li for allegedly purchasing Russian weapons—sanctions that proved diplomatically problematic when he was named defense minister earlier this year.

Chinese officials have reportedly warned that Premier Li Keqiang would cancel his planned visit to the UK unless a meeting with Queen Elizabeth II was guaranteed. The negotiation process was marked by China's insistence on certain diplomatic protocols, including requests for details like the attire Samantha Cameron would choose during their encounter. Both Buckingham Palace and the Prime Minister’s office declined to comment on the reports. Government insiders indicated, however, that meetings between the Queen and foreign leaders who are not heads of state—such as Angela Merkel—have occurred in the past.

Prime Minister David Cameron must carefully navigate the UK’s growing economic partnership with China while considering ongoing concerns about human rights abuses. In 2013, bilateral UK-China trade hit a record high, and Chinese investment in the UK surged, totaling nearly £8 billion over two years. Ambassador Liu Xiaoming expressed optimism about the future of UK-China relations.

Nevertheless, rights groups like Amnesty International maintain that human rights violations are rampant in China. They report widespread detentions without trial, intensified surveillance, and tighter censorship, with thousands executed each year according to estimates. The Chinese government keeps execution numbers secret. There has also been a crackdown on activists and independent voices, particularly leading up to the Tiananmen Square massacre anniversary, an event still officially unacknowledged and censored by Chinese authorities.

article_content:
Construction has commenced on the world’s largest solar bridge in central London. According to developers, the new solar roof atop Blackfriars Railway Bridge over the River Thames will span more than 6,000 square meters upon completion. The installation will feature over 4,400 individual photovoltaic panels designed to generate approximately 900,000 kilowatt hours of electricity each year, providing up to half of Blackfriars station’s annual energy requirements. Solar Century, the UK-based company responsible for the project, estimates that annual CO2 emissions will be cut by more than 500 tons.

“It’s fantastic to see this project finally come to fruition. Blackfriars Bridge is an ideal location for solar,” said Derry Newman, Chief Executive of Solar Century. “Seeing solar power in action is a crucial step towards securing a clean energy future,” he added.

Built in 1886, Blackfriars Railway Bridge is undergoing a major transformation as part of Network Rail’s upgrade to the existing station. Lindsay Vamplew, the project director at Network Rail, stated, “The Victorian rail bridge at Blackfriars is part of our railway history. Constructed in the age of steam, we’re now modernizing it with 21st-century solar technology to create an iconic station for London.”

Along with solar panels manufactured by SANYO Electric Co. Ltd, the renovated station will incorporate rainwater-harvesting systems and sun pipes for natural lighting. The solar roof and revamped station are expected to be completed by summer 2012.

article_content: Machiko Oyama, a 56-year-old Japanese former teacher, has been denied re-entry to the United Kingdom after exceeding the permitted two-year absence allowed under UK immigration rules. Ms. Oyama has been married to 70-year-old British author William Judge for 18 years, and the couple previously lived together in a £1 million London flat. Ms. Oyama originally left the UK in 2005 to return to Japan and care for her terminally ill mother, who had been diagnosed with a brain tumour. During that year, her mother and two aunts passed away. Ms. Oyama applied to return to the UK in February, but her application was refused on the grounds that she had been outside the country for more than two years. The couple believed that an exception in UK immigration law, intended for people with strong connections to Britain, would apply to Ms. Oyama because of their marriage and ongoing ties. Mr. Judge is now preparing to appear before an immigration tribunal to appeal for his wife's return, describing the situation as 'ludicrous' and the rules as 'draconian,' and arguing they may violate their human rights. Evidence cited by Mr. Judge includes his regular visits to see his wife in Japan, their daily phone calls, and the fact that Ms. Oyama owns property in London and pays council tax. According to Ms. Oyama, Mr. Judge stayed with her in Japan for two to three months during each visit. A spokesperson for the UK Border Agency stated that the agency does not comment on individual cases but that each application is evaluated individually.

The driver, 40-year-old Gegham Mkhitaryan, overtook stationary vehicles before hitting the pedestrians: a 23-year-old woman, a 23-year-old man, and a 51-year-old woman. After momentarily slowing, Mkhitaryan sped away from the scene. After the crash, the young woman managed to get up and move to safety, while the other two victims remained on the ground. Bystanders witnessed the event as the driver fled. Police identified the Ssangyong SUV and tracked Mkhitaryan using dashcam footage. He admitted to being intoxicated and said he fled due to fear of punishment for drunk driving. The 51-year-old woman is in intensive care. The other two victims received hospital treatment and have since been released.

During the second half of England’s opening World Cup match against Italy, Raheem Sterling caught the spotlight with his fearless and dynamic play. Notably, he dispossessed Italian veteran Andrea Pirlo on the edge of the penalty area—a display of confidence that showed Sterling is undaunted by reputation.

While Pirlo conducted play with skilled passing and clever movement, Sterling imposed his own stamp with direct runs at defenders, exploiting gaps and showcasing the kind of attacking intent that makes him thrilling to watch. The 19-year-old, trusted by coach Roy Hodgson in the pivotal No. 10 role, did not deserve to be on the losing side in this tightly contested 2-1 defeat.

Early in the match, Sterling darted past Gabriel Paletta and unleashed a powerful shot into the side netting, fooling many into thinking England had scored. His creativity shone when he threaded a superb pass to Wayne Rooney on the left, catalyzing England’s equalizer finished by Daniel Sturridge.

Throughout, Sterling drew defensive attention—Daniele De Rossi was assigned to track him—yet he still managed to create chances, demand possession, and unsettle Italy’s defense. Even when moved to the right wing later in the second half, Sterling remained a constant threat, winning corners and pressing the opposition. He capped his performance by earning a yellow card in stoppage time, stopping an Italian counter-attack.

Though England ultimately fell to Mario Balotelli’s decisive goal for Italy, pundits and supporters alike hailed Sterling as the breakout star. His flair, fearlessness, and high energy suggested a bright future, reaffirming Roy Hodgson’s decision to start him. As England looked ahead to their next game against Uruguay, there was hope that Sterling’s impactful presence could help revive their tournament prospects.

article_content: While Superman discovered his superpowers as a teenager, many people take much longer to find their own—or may never identify them at all. However, understanding your own 'superpower'—the core strength that sets you apart at work, such as creativity, vision, or analytical skills—can be key to advancing your career. Sheryl G. Feinstein, co-author of 'The Brain and Strengths Based School Leadership,' says, 'I believe the first step in a leadership role is to identify your strengths and use them strategically.' Feinstein adds, 'Leaders often try to be everything to everyone, which can lead to a patchwork approach that isn’t effective. They spend time overcompensating for weaknesses instead of focusing on their strengths.' Feinstein points out that leaders who know and use their strengths tend to be more satisfied with their jobs and earn higher salaries, according to research. Corinne Mills, Managing Director of Personal Career Management and author of 'Career Coach,' explains that a personal superpower is like a 'Unique Selling Proposition' that gives you value in the workplace. Recognizing it can help you promote yourself within your organization or to potential employers. But how do you identify your superpower? Mills notes it's hard to be objective about your own abilities, as people often overlook what comes naturally to them. 'Usually, people enjoy using their strongest skills, so they assume everyone can do it, but that’s rarely true.' Mills suggests asking former colleagues or managers whose opinions you trust for honest feedback. 'They can provide objective insights, pointing out strengths you may take for granted.' Executive coach and management consultant Guy Longshaw recommends strengths assessments rooted in positive psychology, a movement aimed at helping people recognize and develop their talents. He says that successful individuals continually challenge themselves in areas where they excel, which keeps them engaged in their careers. Feinstein also believes that self-reflection can help. 'After leading a meeting, think about what went well and what could be improved. Modern assessment tools often confirm what we already sense about ourselves.' Sean McPheat, Managing Director of MTD Training, notes that old advice to 'develop your weaknesses' is outdated. 'Forget about trying to turn weaknesses into strengths. Improving your strengths by 2% is more valuable than a 2% improvement in your weaknesses.' Longshaw agrees: 'Recognize your weaknesses, but don’t waste too much effort trying to fix them.' Instead of focusing on your own shortcomings, building a team with complementary strengths can be far more effective. Feinstein concludes, 'If you’re strong in organization but weaker in vision or relationship-building, a well-balanced team allows everyone to play to their strengths.'

article_content: A set of ancient stone tablets, kept for decades in the Museum of Bologna’s archives, may carry a chilling curse directed at a man named Porcellus. Estimated to be around 1,600 years old, the tablets were misplaced around the start of World War I and were only rediscovered in 2009. Translation and study by Celia Sanchez Natalias of the University of Zaragoza revealed that the tablets call upon a supernatural figure—perhaps the goddess Hekate, though this remains uncertain—to bind and torment Porcellus. The carvings on the tablets show a barefoot, crowned figure with snakes emerging from its head, hands either tied or crossed at the abdomen, a magical sign over the chest, and an eight-pointed star near the groin. Underneath, a bound figure identified as Porcellus is shown with his name inscribed on his arms. Such curse tablets, known as 'defixiones,' were a common feature of ancient rituals, involving inscribed stone or lead to invoke otherworldly powers. Although some characteristics point to Hekate’s involvement, the absence of her distinct features means the deity’s identity is unclear. The curse is designed to bind both the supernatural figure depicted and Porcellus, illustrating ancient beliefs in linking the fates of deity and victim.

article_content: Rowaida Abdelaziz, a 17-year-old high school student in New Jersey, stands by her choice to wear the hijab, a headscarf worn by many Muslim women. She dismisses pity and rejects the assumption that her decision is forced. For Abdelaziz, the hijab symbolizes beauty and faith, guided by the belief that precious things should be protected, as her Egyptian mother taught her. Many young Muslim women in the United States face similar challenges when wearing the hijab. These can include suspicion from strangers, unusual questions such as whether they are nuns or avoiding the sun, and criticism from within their own communities—especially from those who emigrated to escape strict dress codes. Randa Abdel-Fattah, an Australian author of Palestinian and Egyptian heritage, describes the experience of wearing the hijab in Western countries as being under constant scrutiny. She notes wide diversity in how women interpret and practice hijab, influenced by personal, religious, and cultural backgrounds. Historically, the practice of veiling predates Islam, with origins in ancient Assyria and use in Roman and Byzantine societies as a sign of status. Scholar Faegheh Shirazi observes that Islamic texts like the Quran are open to interpretation regarding veiling’s necessity. Teenagers like Sarah Hekmati, who began wearing the hijab at 15 in Detroit, find it helps define their identity. For Sarah, the hijab offered clarity during the turbulent teen years. Her mother, Behnaz—who grew up in Iran without wearing the hijab—worried about American perceptions and was puzzled by her daughter’s choice. Sarah also faced criticism from fellow Iranian-Americans, some of whom viewed the hijab as a symbol of the oppression they left behind. In her social life, Sarah noticed fewer boys saw her as a romantic interest, leading to feelings of invisibility. Abdelaziz and others have dealt with misunderstanding, pity, and even hostility from strangers, but they emphasize that their choices reflect self-respect and a desire to express their faith. While fitting in can be challenging, Abdelaziz says that wearing the hijab has brought her a sense of fulfillment and a stronger sense of who she is. Debates over the hijab continue worldwide, with controversies, legal restrictions, and family disagreements shaping each woman’s experience. Ultimately, the choice to wear the hijab—or not—is deeply personal, mixing faith, empowerment, and the search for identity.

People look dem funny, ask dem weird question like if dem a nun or cyaan tek sun, an even dem own people, especially dem weh run lef place weh hijab did force, criticize dem. Randa Abdel-Fattah, author from Australia weh have Palestinian an Egyptian roots, say when yuh wear hijab inna di West, is like yuh always under microscope. article_content: The Adamawa/Taraba Area Command of the Nigeria Customs Service has confiscated several items, including 15,449 litres of Premium Motor Spirit (PMS), valued at a Duty Paid Value of N13 million. This announcement was made via the NCS's official X handle on Tuesday. Area Controller Salisu Abdullahi provided details of the seizure during a press briefing held on November 17, 2023, at the Area Command headquarters in Yola. Other confiscated items include 19 cartons of foreign insecticide and 26 bags of 50kg foreign parboiled rice. Due to the flammable nature of the PMS, most of the seized fuel has already been disposed of in compliance with existing laws, with the proceeds transferred to the Federation Account. The remaining quantity of PMS will be auctioned after the briefing. Abdullahi noted that no smugglers were apprehended during the operation as they fled the scene, but he pledged to intensify efforts against smuggling, emphasizing that saboteurs should not be allowed to undermine the country's economy. He urged Nigerians, stakeholders, and relevant security agencies operating at the Command’s frontiers to continue cooperating with Customs in the fight against smuggling.

article_content: Despite delays in AI regulation, scammers in India are increasingly using artificial intelligence to target millions of people online. According to a study by McAfee, Indians now spend up to 105 minutes each week reviewing, verifying, or deciding whether digital messages—received through text, email, or social media—are real or fake. The report shows that 82% of Indians have clicked on or fallen for fake messages, especially fake job offers (64%) and fraudulent bank alert messages (52%). McAfee highlights that AI has become a key tool for scammers, helping cybercriminals spread and refine their messages. Phishing and text scams are rising rapidly, with a new phishing website created every 11 seconds. "This highlights the urgent need for solutions that can fight AI-driven scams," McAfee stated in its report. With about 900 million internet users across India, protecting oneself online has never been more important. The study notes that Indians receive nearly 12 scam messages a day through email, text, or social media. On average, each person spends around 1.8 hours weekly checking these messages. Nearly half (49%) say scam messages are harder to spot since they no longer have obvious mistakes. For many, dealing with scam texts all year feels more distressing than undergoing a root canal, according to Roma Majumder, SVP of Product at McAfee. It's not just the speed and frequency—scam messages are also more sophisticated. AI makes it increasingly tough to decide whether a delivery notice or bank alert is genuine. Around 73% of Indians believe they've got a better shot at solving a Rubik's cube than identifying a scam message. "This influx of scams drains people's time, energy, and money. We need AI to fight AI," Majumder added. "Seeing is no longer believing, so people must be equipped with advanced AI tools to block scam messages in real time." McAfee's research outlines four key insights on online scams, underlining growing stress from AI-driven messages and pushing for robust defense solutions. Scam detection now takes over two full work weeks each year for many users. Overall, 90% of Indians report receiving scam messages daily by email or text, and 84% experience them on social media.

article_content: Bitcoin (BTC) and other major cryptocurrencies, including Ethereum and XRP, have seen significant price increases this week, despite concerns that BlackRock and the U.S. government could impact bitcoin negatively. The price of bitcoin rose above $36,000, approaching $40,000 for the first time since May 2022, contributing to a $600 billion boost in the crypto market’s total value since January. Amid concerns of sudden volatility, a window has opened that could allow Wall Street firms managing $17.7 trillion to enter the bitcoin and crypto market. The anticipated bitcoin halving, often associated with price changes, is approaching. Bitcoin’s price surge is fueled by expectations that the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) could soon approve spot bitcoin exchange-traded funds (ETFs), which may also affect Ethereum and XRP prices. From November 9 to November 17, there is a period during which any of the 12 bitcoin spot ETF applications with the SEC could be approved, according to Bloomberg analysts James Seyffart and Eric Balchunas. BlackRock’s ETF application in June started a competition among major asset managers such as Bitwise, VanEck, WisdomTree, Invesco, Fidelity, and Valkyrie, all of whom have had their proposals delayed by the SEC. Analysts suggest there is a strong possibility of ETF approvals by January 10, and approvals could occur during this current window. Separately, Grayscale achieved a legal victory, as a court ordered the SEC to review its application to convert its bitcoin trust to a spot ETF. Bitcoin and the broader crypto market have rebounded from the significant declines seen in 2022. Technical analysis, as noted by FxPro analyst Alex Kuptsikevich, indicates bitcoin could rise to between $41,000 and $45,000 if current trends continue.

article_content: Congresswoman Rashida Tlaib has criticized the Biden administration for not calling for de-escalation amid Israel’s ongoing war in Gaza. On Monday, progressive lawmakers in the United States introduced a congressional resolution demanding an immediate ceasefire and de-escalation in Israel and the occupied Palestinian territories. The resolution is supported by over a dozen Democratic House members, including Cori Bush, Rashida Tlaib, Summer Lee, Ayanna Pressley, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, and Ilhan Omar, reflecting a rising call for a ceasefire in Washington. The resolution states, 'All human life is precious, and targeting civilians, regardless of faith or ethnicity, is a violation of international humanitarian law.' Despite broad Congressional support for Israel, Bush described the resolution as an urgent initiative for Americans to support, urging constituents to encourage lawmakers to back it. Bush added, 'Leaders lead from the front, and we move with the call of the people.' The war began on October 7 when the Palestinian group Hamas launched a coordinated attack against Israel from Gaza, resulting in the deaths of hundreds and the capture of dozens, according to initial reports. Israel responded with extensive airstrikes, which have killed over 2,800 Palestinians, including many children, based on estimates from health authorities. The World Health Organization has documented multiple attacks on medical facilities, causing at least 12 health worker deaths. Israel declared a total blockade on Gaza, restricting fuel and essential supplies from entering the territory. Over a million residents, including hospital patients, were instructed by Israeli authorities to evacuate northern Gaza—a demand the United Nations has called 'impossible.' Advocates argue that the US is in a position to help end the conflict, with a ground invasion of Gaza imminent and the lives of hundreds of thousands at risk. Bush and other lawmakers claim the conflict is occurring with US government support, labeling it 'shameful.' Despite escalating violence, the Biden administration has not endorsed calls for calm in Gaza. Reports suggest the State Department has told diplomats to avoid terms like 'de-escalation' or 'ceasefire.' Secretary of State Antony Blinken reiterated strong US support for Israel during a recent visit. President Biden stated that Israel has a right and obligation to defend itself and has voiced opposition to Hamas, but avoided directly supporting a ceasefire. Rep. Tlaib, the only Palestinian-American in Congress, described the devastation in Gaza, criticizing President Biden, Secretary Blinken, and most of Congress for failing to push for de-escalation. Tlaib labeled the collective punishment of Palestinians as a war crime and called for recognition of Palestinian humanity. The resolution marks a rare break in near-unified Congressional support for Israel’s current military campaign. Congressman Jamaal Bowman, another co-sponsor, called for an end to violence and an urgent ceasefire to protect civilians. Maya Berry from the Arab American Institute emphasized the US role in the conflict through military aid to Israel and its actions at the UN. Washington’s military support—a minimum of $3.8 billion annually to Israel—is likely to increase, with US officials pledging further aid. Beth Miller of Jewish Voice for Peace Action said the resolution gives advocates a concrete demand to present to lawmakers, contrasting with previous resolutions focused solely on Israeli lives.

John Galliano, the former Dior creative director dismissed after a 2011 scandal, has taken a new position with Russian beauty retailer L'Etoile. According to Russian newspaper Kommersant, Galliano will assume his role at L'Etoile on May 22. The announcement appeared on L'Etoile's website with the headline 'John is Back!', sparking rumors of his appointment as creative director. However, Galliano's spokesperson clarified that while more information is forthcoming, he has been consulting for L'Etoile for several months.

Galliano, aged 52, lost his posts at Dior and his namesake brand following a highly publicized incident involving racist and anti-Semitic remarks, actions he attributes to struggles with alcoholism. He has since undergone rehabilitation and sought to rebuild his reputation. L'Etoile, commonly compared to Sephora in the US, is Russia’s largest perfumery chain, operating 750 stores that offer cosmetics and fragrances—including Dior products.

After a period away from the public eye, Galliano returned to fashion in 2013, taking a residency at Oscar de la Renta's studio in New York. The collaboration received acclaim, highlighting Galliano's creative talent, though a permanent role did not materialize due to financial disagreements.

In addition, Galliano has designed costumes for Stephen Fry's stage adaptation of 'The Importance of Being Earnest' and served as guest fashion editor for British Vogue, appearing in the magazine alongside close friend Kate Moss, whose wedding dress he famously designed. In public comments, Galliano has expressed remorse for his past actions and credited the opportunity to design Moss’s wedding gown as a turning point for his recovery.

While at Dior, Galliano played a significant role in fragrance campaigns, such as Dior Addict and J'adore with Charlize Theron. His new role with L'Etoile marks another phase in his ongoing, complex career.

article_content: Across Europe, grape harvest season is underway—from the UK down to Sicily—kicking off the process of collecting and pressing grapes to produce wine. The juices are then fermented in various barrels, setting the stage for blending and bottling next spring. Each vintage is shaped by weather patterns, with temperature and rainfall playing crucial roles. Our recent study examines how these factors determine wine quality. In spring, French winemakers conduct 'en primeur' evaluations, where unfinished wine is presented in a futures market—a tradition born in Bordeaux in the 1950s to help chateaus raise funds, now adopted across Europe. During en primeur, critics and merchants provide tasting notes and numeric quality scores, comparing each new vintage to previous years and other wines. Scoring is swayed by regional weather, soil, and winemaking practices—even for the same grape varieties. Bordeaux is pivotal for this research because its vast en primeur landscape sees thousands of chateaus reviewed by a select group of renowned critics. We've found that top-tier Bordeaux wines are made in years featuring warm temperatures, wetter winters, drier summers, and shorter growing periods. These conditions are expected to become more common with climate change—potentially leading to more robust and higher quality Bordeaux vintages, though risks exist. Take St-Émillion for example, a celebrated Bordeaux appellation. Château-Figeac’s best recent years—2016, 2019, and 2022—correlated with hot, dry summers and wet winters. Alexa Boulton, Château-Figeac's commercial director, acknowledges climate change is increasing the frequency of these optimal years. Still, climate change introduces volatility, with extreme weather events like frosts, hail, drought, and heavy rain becoming more regular, sometimes destroying entire harvests. In 2020, for instance, an April hailstorm wiped out all the grapes on some Bordeaux vines. This pattern isn’t unique to France. The UK’s emerging red wine scene faces similar challenges. English winemaker Natasha Rompante recounted an excellent 2020 vintage due to heat, but in 2021, elevated temperatures and humidity triggered widespread disease and up to 90% crop losses in some vineyards. As global climate conditions evolve, so too does wine. Understanding how temperature and rainfall interact with grapevines is essential for adapting and ensuring the resilience of winemaking worldwide.

article_content: Senegal’s Supreme Court has effectively blocked opposition leader Ousmane Sonko from competing in the upcoming presidential election by overturning a judicial order that had temporarily restored his right to vote. This legal setback for Sonko coincided with a separate decision by the West African regional ECOWAS court, which also rejected his plea for reinstatement on the voter rolls. Sonko, who serves as mayor of Ziguinchor, was returned to a Dakar jail after spending several weeks in hospital due to a hunger strike he staged while detained. Earlier this year, the government dissolved his political party and canceled his voter registration following his conviction on a charge of ‘corrupting youth’. Supporters of Sonko argue that these legal actions are politically driven to prevent him from taking part in February’s presidential election. Initially, a Ziguinchor court had restored his voting rights, but the Supreme Court reversed this decision and handed the case to the Dakar high court, according to his lawyer, Cire Cledor Ly. Senegalese authorities have yet to grant Sonko the necessary sponsorship papers needed for formal presidential candidacy. Sonko, who placed third in the previous presidential contest, has been a leading opposition figure against President Macky Sall’s administration. President Sall has opted not to seek a third term, following months of sometimes violent protests by Sonko’s supporters. In June, Sonko was acquitted of rape and issuing death threats but was convicted of corrupting youth, resulting in a two-year prison sentence that triggered unrest. The government dissolved his party and detained him following these events; he now faces further accusations, including inciting insurrection and conspiracy against the state. Sonko also challenged the dissolution of his party and his removal from the voter roll in the ECOWAS regional court, but according to his legal representatives, the court found no violation of his rights and dismissed his case.

Dakar, Senegal is quickly emerging as an important player in the fashion world—even if it doesn’t yet match the status of places like Paris or New York. The city just hosted its 10th annual Dakar Fashion Week, drawing an international crowd eager to experience innovative African design. Founded ten years ago by Adama Ndiaye, the event has been vital to Dakar gaining attention as a center for Franco-African fashion.

Fashion expert Helen Jennings, editor at the UK’s Arise magazine, noted that this year’s event attracted big names including Alphadi, often called the godfather of African fashion. Jennings emphasized how styles from English-speaking Africa are typically more Western and receive more global attention, while French-speaking regions—including Senegal—feature modern takes on traditional attire like the boubou and kaftan.

Still, Jennings explained, Dakar is not yet at the top: Nigeria and South Africa remain the major African fashion capitals, thanks to notable events like Arise Magazine Fashion Week and Africa Fashion Week. Jennings and others credit the rapid rise of African fashion to strong economic growth and an expanding middle class, resulting in more homegrown designers gaining recognition.

Well-known designers such as Duro Olowu, Xuly Bët, Kofi Ansah, Jewel By Lisa, and Marianne Fassler set examples for new talent, while African fashion weeks, boutiques, online stores, and fashion schools thrive. 

A recent report by McKinsey & Company and TBWA, called 'The Changing Face of the African Consumer,' shows that Africa’s population growth and rising optimism have kept its markets resilient compared to Europe, creating fresh opportunities for businesses on the continent.

Adama Ndiaye hopes that Dakar Fashion Week will one day compete with the likes of Paris and New York—while preserving a uniquely African vibe. This year’s event, held between June 12 and 17, showcased rich colors, distinctive prints, and a blend of classic and modern flair. The runway featured designers from across Africa such as Elien Kuame, who merged western and African aesthetics; Maguette Gueye, who highlighted traditional motifs; and Mamta Lopy, who presented bold, contemporary fashions.

article_content: A fierce supermarket price war is brewing in the UK, with major retailers launching unprecedented, long-term reductions on staple foods. The campaign began after Morrisons pledged to cut prices by £1 billion over three years, a move meant to counter cost-conscious competitors Aldi and Lidl. Asda swiftly fired back, unveiling ads that claimed to offer even lower prices than Morrisons and promising significant savings on top brand items. This escalating competition is pushing Tesco and Sainsbury’s to follow suit, likely leading to substantial cuts—some everyday essentials could drop by as much as 25%. Aldi fueled the rivalry further by promising shoppers savings of up to 35% on their weekly grocery bills. The prospect of a prolonged price war unnerved investors, causing combined share values of Tesco, Sainsbury’s, and Morrisons to tumble by £2 billion. Morrisons' shares alone dropped over 10%. Profits at Asda, backed by parent company Walmart, could also take a hit. Morrisons’ leadership views significant changes in pricing as essential, especially after reporting a £176 million loss. With Aldi and Lidl capturing large slices of the market, ‘the big four’ must stay competitive. Tesco recently cut prices, like reducing a four-pint milk carton from £1.39 to £1, but analysts say much more must be done. Experts liken Morrisons’ bold price-cutting plan to pulling out heavy artillery, as the company expects over £300 million in profit loss annually for three years. Chief Executive Dalton Philips argues the supermarket sector faces its biggest change since the 1950s—shoppers from all backgrounds now flock to discounters, shifting the industry’s standard for low prices. Recent studies indicate that the largest supermarkets have lost £4.4 billion in yearly sales over three years as middle-income shoppers migrate to discounters and largely remain loyal. Sales at Morrisons fell by 3.2% last year, while Aldi and Lidl saw impressive gains of 33.5% and 16.5%, respectively. Philips says permanent price reductions are critical for Morrisons to win back customers and compete effectively. To cushion the blow from smaller profits, Morrisons plans to sell property assets worth an estimated £1 billion. Recent price surveys highlight that Aldi’s prices are significantly lower than Morrisons’ on many basic groceries. Beyond price cuts, Morrisons aims to expand its online offerings and open more convenience stores to catch up with rivals who already thrive in these areas. Morrisons’ total annual loss included substantial one-off charges, and expected profits are predicted to drop by more than half to fund the price war. Market analysts and investors foresee drawn-out discounting battles as necessary for established supermarkets to regain lost sales and protect their market standing. Aldi and Lidl’s reputations are growing, with both winning top honors at recent retail industry awards. Morrisons, one of the UK’s oldest supermarkets, started as a small market stall in Bradford in 1899 and only grew to national prominence after acquiring Safeway in 2004. It now operates over 550 branches but is currently challenged by the rise of budget rivals and a shift toward online shopping.
