article_content: The Chandigarh Transport Undertaking (CTU) launched a shuttle bus service on Saturday at 11 am to help visitors reach Sukhna Lake, Rock Garden, and Bird Park. The service experienced a low response on its first day, with most buses having few passengers. Some users said they were unaware of the shuttle until arriving at Sukhna Lake. According to a CTU conductor, 'Today is the first day. It appears that people are not aware of the shuttle service. The service started at 11 am and will continue until 8 pm. Most people are arriving in their private vehicles.' The fare for the shuttle is set at Rs 10 for a round trip. Shuttle buses pick up and drop off passengers at Rock Garden, Gursagar Sahib Turn, and Sukhna Lake near the ATC light. Director of Chandigarh Transport, Pradhuman Singh, stated, 'Five buses have been deployed to pick up and drop off passengers every five minutes. Today is the service's first day, and the exact passenger count will be known after 8 pm. The shuttle will operate on weekends and public holidays.' Advisory: 1. Visitors can park their private vehicles only in the Municipal Corporation’s paid parking at Sector 5 opposite Sukhna Lake (Parking 1) and the pit parking at Rock Garden (Parking 2) on a first come, first served basis during weekends and holidays. If these lots are full, cars will be directed to Kachhi parking near the High Court (Parking 3) and the rear of offices in Sector 9A (Parking 4), from where the shuttle bus can be used. 2. The CTU shuttle will serve visitors/tourists from Kachhi Parking near Jn No. 3 High Court Chowk (Parking 3) and parking in the rear of offices in Sector 9A (Parking 4), running every five minutes on weekends/holidays. 3. Tourists/visitors traveling via Jan Marg and Vigyan Path should follow the green route to reach Rock Garden, Bird Park, and Sukhna Lake on weekends/public holidays. No vehicles are allowed from Point A to Point B on the Sukhna Lake side, as it is a 'No vehicle zone.' Vehicles exiting Kachhi parking at High Court and Rock Garden pit parking should take a right turn towards Old Barricade Chowk (Jn No. 3) on Jan Marg. 4. No vehicles are permitted towards Sukhna Lake directly from Hira Singh Chowk (roundabout of Sectors 5/6/7/8), the turns of Sector 5 and 8, the roundabout of Sectors 4/5/8/9, or the turn near Sector 4 water tank. Only residents of Sector 4 and 5 have access. 5. All roads around Rock Garden, Bird Park, and Sukhna Lake are ‘Tow Away Zones’ on weekends and public holidays. Parking on these roads is not allowed and violators risk towing or wheel clamping. 6. Drivers coming from Kaimbwala village and Gurdwara Gursahib are not permitted a left turn towards Sukhna Lake to reduce congestion. They should take a right turn to reach their destination. 7. Vehicles from Haryana Raj Bhawan and UT Guest House will be permitted to enter and exit via Hira Singh Chowk.

article_content: Celebrity psychic Psychic Cara, based in Bury, Lancashire and known for working with clients such as Les Dennis and Michelle Collins, says certain foods could help people better connect with the spiritual world. She cautions against eating heavy or processed meals—such as roast dinners, smoked or red meats, pastries, cakes, crisps, sugary drinks, foods high in saturated fats, and too much alcohol—which she says can make meditation more difficult and may block spiritual communication. For easier meditation, Cara suggests light, nutritious meals, for example, a blend of fruits and vegetables or baked white fish with greens and nuts. Cara explains that diet affects brain function, especially by providing nutrients like choline (a B vitamin found in lecithin), which helps produce the neurotransmitter acetylcholine, important for memory and learning. She claims that foods rich in choline can quickly boost memory and improve mood, which she considers helpful for both everyday focus and psychic activities. Cara is currently writing a book, 'Knowing (Before, Now and Then)', where she shares her advice on how dietary choices could support psychic awareness and mental growth.

article_content: Indian equity markets opened flat with a slight positive bias on Wednesday, tracking mixed cues from Asian markets and differing trends among domestic and foreign institutional investors. Comments from US Federal Reserve officials suggested the central bank is nearing the end of its policy tightening cycle, boosting global market sentiment. At around 9:22 am, the BSE Sensex was down by 23 points (0.04%) at 64,918, while the Nifty50 rose by 2 points (0.01%) to 19,408. On the Sensex, ICICI Bank, Bajaj Finance, UltraTech Cement, Infosys, and M&M opened lower. Conversely, Asian Paints, Wipro, HCL Tech, Tata Motors, and Maruti saw gains. Among notable movers, Apollo Tyres gained 5.5% after reporting a consolidated net profit of ₹474.26 crore for the September quarter. Deepak Nitrite shares rose 5.2% following a Q2 net profit of ₹205 crore and revenue of ₹1,778 crore. Sector-wise, the Nifty Pharma index jumped 1%, and Nifty Healthcare gained 0.9%. Nifty indices representing financials, auto, FMCG, and IT also opened higher. In the broader market, Nifty Midcap100 was up 0.75% and Smallcap100 gained 0.9%. In global markets, US equities advanced overnight as Treasury yields fell after several Federal Reserve officials signaled a likely end to the current rate-hiking cycle. The S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite recorded their longest winning streak in two years. Meanwhile, gains in Asian tech stocks were offset by declines in commodity-related shares. Market experts believe the current market environment supports a continued rally, despite ongoing geopolitical uncertainties. V K Vijayakumar, Chief Investment Strategist at Geojit Financial Services, noted the ongoing 'tug of war' between continued FII selling and DII buying, and recommended high-quality large caps for long-term investors. Aditya Gaggar, Director of Progressive Shares, mentioned that technical patterns indicate potential market consolidation with the GIFT Nifty signaling possible attempts to breach resistance at 19,500 and support at 19,315. On Tuesday, foreign institutional investors (FIIs) extended their selling streak to ten sessions, offloading ₹497 crore in equities. In contrast, domestic institutional investors (DIIs) purchased ₹700 crore in shares. Oil prices wavered on Wednesday following a significant slide to three-month lows in the prior session, pressured by concerns over weakening demand in the US and China. Brent crude inched up 4 cents to $81.65 a barrel, while US crude slipped 14 cents to $77.24 a barrel. Both benchmarks touched their lowest levels since July 24 on Tuesday. The Indian rupee edged higher by 2 paise to ₹83.25 per US dollar in early trading as oil prices moderated and US Treasury yields declined. The dollar index, measuring the greenback against six major currencies, rose 0.06% to 105.6. article_content: Buffalo, New York, often called the 'Queen City,' has been ranked as the most affordable city in America by Forbes. Forbes compiled a list of the top 21 most affordable cities using data such as median family income, home prices, and everyday living costs. Housing prices played the biggest role in affordability, and Forbes used information from the National Association of Home Builders and Wells Fargo to assess how far income could stretch for homebuyers. New York City and Honolulu were found to be the least affordable. Forbes highlighted that with a median family income of $63,500 and a median home sales price of $100,000, home ownership is possible for 88.5% of Buffalo residents. The term 'median' means half of households or homes are above and half are below that value. Other cities in the top five most affordable are Memphis, Cincinnati, Dayton, and Knoxville. Only cities with populations greater than 600,000 were considered for the list. Southern cities also performed well, with six making the list, but the Midwest dominated, including five in Ohio: Cincinnati (3), Dayton (4), Akron (6), Toledo (11), and Columbus (20). Notably, no cities from the western United States were included, despite the relative expense of places like California and the expectation that cities in Arizona or New Mexico might have ranked. Top 21 Affordable Cities per Forbes in 2014: 1. Buffalo, NY 2. Memphis, TN 3. Cincinnati, OH 4. Dayton, OH 5. Knoxville, TN 6. Akron, OH 7. Grand Rapids, MI 8. Louisville, KY 9. Oklahoma City, OK 10. Warren, MI 11. Toledo, OH 12. Detroit, MI 13. Birmingham, AL 14. St. Louis, MO 15. Virginia Beach, VA 16. Jacksonville, FL 17. Pittsburgh, PA 18. Tulsa, OK 19. Tampa, FL 20. Syracuse, NY 21. Columbus, OH. Knoxville, Tennessee, ranked fifth, had a Housing Opportunity Index of 77.4.

article_content: AIMIM chief Asaduddin Owaisi stated on Monday that the Uniform Civil Code (UCC) is not needed in India and criticized the BJP for including it in their Telangana election manifesto. Owaisi emphasized the importance of increased freedom of speech and expression, asserting that people should not be targeted based on their clothing or religion. Responding to the BJP’s Telangana election promises—such as implementing the UCC, commemorating September 17 as Hyderabad Liberation Day, and offering free pilgrimages for senior citizens to Ram Mandir in Ayodhya and Kashi—Owaisi accused the BJP of focusing on divisive issues rather than economic development. The BJP, on November 18, announced that it would implement the Uniform Civil Code in Telangana if elected, with Amit Shah stating that a committee would be established to draft the UCC within six months. Owaisi countered that Amit Shah would not present the UCC proposal to Adivasi communities in places like Adilabad, Khammam, or Warangal, as he believes Adivasis—who have constitutional protection for their culture—would reject it. Owaisi argued that India needs more freedom of speech and protection against discrimination by clothing or religion, not the UCC. He further criticized the BJP for being in power at the Centre for nine-and-a-half years, claiming they have weakened the economy, harmed small businesses, failed to provide promised jobs, and preside over high youth unemployment. He alleged that the BJP prefers to focus on issues like the UCC instead of the country's development. Addressing BJP and Congress leaders’ criticisms of the AIMIM during campaign rallies, Owaisi described their comments as displays of political arrogance. He asserted that AIMIM is a strong political force in Telangana and expressed confidence that the people have already made their decision regarding whom to support. Owaisi also accused both the Congress and BJP of promoting politics of hatred. He alleged that Telangana Congress President A Revanth Reddy is influenced by the RSS and that Mohan Bhagwat currently 'controls' the Telangana Congress.

article_content: Best Buy Health and Mass General Brigham (MGB), leaders in their respective fields, have announced a partnership to enhance at-home healthcare services using advanced technology solutions. Their collaboration aims to meet rising demand for accessible care, tackle workforce shortages, and boost patient outcomes. A key objective is to expand MGB’s Home Hospital service, which allows patients with serious conditions like COPD and heart disease to receive hospital-level, short-term care at home. The program delivers daily in-person and virtual visits, offers 24/7 access via phone and video, remote monitoring, and diagnostic services. MGB’s Home Care service, in contrast, delivers long-term care for those managing chronic conditions. Best Buy Health will now support both programs to broaden their effectiveness and reach. A central part of this initiative is Best Buy’s Current Health platform, designed to simplify remote patient monitoring, power telehealth services, and equip care teams with data-driven tools for optimal care. The platform offers logistics management and facilitates training, with Best Buy’s well-known ‘Geek Squad’ assisting patients in preparing their homes and learning about healthcare devices. Additionally, MGB will use the Lively personal emergency response system (PERS) device from Best Buy Health, which enables patients to call for help during emergencies, send alerts to loved ones, and detect falls. This collaboration comes as interest in home-based healthcare increases rapidly. Over the last decade, patient desire for convenience has accelerated this trend, which the COVID-19 pandemic further intensified due to concerns about hospital-acquired infections. Home healthcare can also reduce costs and improve system efficiency. According to research published in the Annals of Internal Medicine, the mean cost of acute care episodes was 38% lower for home patients compared to those in hospitals, with fewer lab tests and imaging orders. The study concluded that home hospitalization reduced costs, readmissions, and resource use while increasing physical activity. Technological leaps, particularly in remote monitoring and virtual care, are making such care models practical. Studies—like one in JAMA Cardiology—show improved chronic disease outcomes when patients use remote monitoring tools for blood pressure and cholesterol. Heather O’Sullivan, President of Healthcare at Home at MGB, believes technology-enabled care is elevating provider capabilities and improving outcomes for communities. Deborah Di Sanzo, President of Best Buy Health, also expresses optimism, while recognizing the complexities of providing high-level care at home. Transitioning away from traditional facility-based care brings unique logistical and operational challenges, and full-scale adoption will take time. Still, collaborations focused on patient safety and outcomes hold great potential to transform healthcare delivery.

article_content: Manila is usually bustling and difficult to manage, but when Pope Francis visited for a Mass attended by six million people despite the rain, what unfolded was remarkable. The event revealed the strength and spirit of Filipinos. Before the Mass, crowds packed the main boulevard since dawn, hoping to glimpse the Pope on his way to Rizal Park. 'The Pope is a human saint—when we see him, our problems disappear,' said 35-year-old Evangeline Dion. Rick Felajo, 54, attended every papal event, stating he felt 'blessed' just to be near the Pope. 'For me, he is the super Pope because he is very human and helpful. I want to follow his example. He is the ultimate guide to heaven,' Felajo shared. When the Popemobile drove by, cheers and applause filled the air. Fifteen-year-old Brenda Ganabban said, 'I felt happy, even just for a moment. I saw him smiling and waving. He might not remember, but I will.' Despite the tropical rain and humidity, people stood outside for hours, smiling and in good spirits. Joey Stefona, 55, waited in the rain for five hours and remarked, 'I feel like it's shining and warm. I don't feel the rain.' Many were creative, fashioning rain protection from plastic, towels, helmets, and even bubble wrap, as umbrellas were discouraged. With the main venue full, thousands wandered through a carnival-like atmosphere, weaving among souvenir stalls and snack vendors, in search of a place to stand and pray. Even when crowded, people remained helpful—some offered to assist journalists filming and directed foot traffic. Roxas Boulevard, usually busy with traffic, became peaceful as hundreds of thousands lined up calmly behind police barricades before, during, and after the Mass, showing patience and humility. From the altar, Pope Francis addressed the congregation, reminding them that God created the world as a beautiful garden for us to care for, but noted that human sinfulness has led to divisions and social issues like poverty and corruption. Many attendees hoped the Pope's visit would help heal the nation's 'illness.' Lucy Ripalda, a high school teacher, wished for government officials to act with integrity and without corruption. Seaman Joey Stefona prayed for improved jobs and better futures for children. As church music echoed, a sense of unity prevailed among the people. Rodolfo Gannabran, a 65-year-old retired Army officer who traveled 13 hours by bus, said, 'Today I feel peace and tranquility among Filipinos and all present. This happiness should continue.'

article_content: A recent study indicates that pregnant women with elevated perchlorate levels are more likely to have children whose IQ scores fall in the lowest 10 percent. Perchlorate, a chemical commonly used in rocket fuel and also present in fireworks, explosives, and as a byproduct of fertilizer use, has been found in the drinking water of some regions. Exposure to perchlorate may interfere with the normal production of thyroid hormones, which are critical during pregnancy. The study, published in the Journal of Clinical Endocrinology & Metabolism, examined pregnant women in Cardiff, Wales, and Turin, Italy, who experienced iodine deficiency and thyroid dysfunction. Researchers measured these women's perchlorate exposure and tested their children's IQ scores three years later. Results showed that those mothers with the highest 10 percent of perchlorate levels were over three times more likely to have children scoring in the lowest 10 percent for IQ. According to Scientific American, perchlorate is present in about 4 percent of U.S. public drinking water, affecting between 5 and 17 million people. The chemical is particularly prevalent in the Western U.S., especially near Las Vegas and Southern California. A survey by the Canadian Food Inspection Agency (CFIA) in May tested 611 samples—including fresh fruits and vegetables, dairy products, and infant formulas—from Canadian retail stores. The results indicated that, while a majority of samples contained trace amounts of perchlorate (ranging from 2 to 540 parts per billion), all were considered safe for consumption. For many years, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has debated whether to establish a legal limit for perchlorate in drinking water. In 2002, an EPA risk assessment suggested that 1 part per billion should be the safety threshold, but in 2008, the Bush administration decided not to regulate perchlorate at the federal level, advising instead that concentrations not exceed 15 parts per billion. Federal scientists estimated at the time that 16.6 million Americans could be exposed to levels they deemed unsafe. Meanwhile, California and Massachusetts have set their own state drinking water standards. The EPA intends to release new regulations for perchlorate in drinking water in the summer of 2015. Perchlorate contamination is most common near military bases.

article_content: Oceans have played a crucial role in limiting climate change, absorbing about 90 percent of the excess heat generated by human activities. While this has taken pressure off the atmosphere, it has caused significant harm to marine life and is now accelerating the loss of Greenland’s ice. The Greenland ice sheet—which rests on land—was responsible for more than 17 percent of global sea level rise between 2006 and 2018. Alarmingly, Greenland now loses approximately 270 billion tons of ice per year, a rate considerably higher than Antarctica's 150 billion tons annually. Research shows that Greenland’s northern ice shelves, which float on the ocean, have lost more than a third of their volume since 1978 due to warming sea water melting them from below. Since 2000, three of these northern ice shelves have collapsed entirely, and the remaining five are rapidly deteriorating, destabilizing nearby glaciers. Although the floating ice shelves themselves do not directly contribute to sea level rise, they act as barriers, regulating the flow of ice from the interior land-based ice sheet into the ocean. According to lead author Romain Millan, a glaciologist at Université Grenoble Alpes, weakening ice shelves are allowing glaciers to retreat and discharge more ice into the ocean. Millan and his colleagues analyzed satellite data and computer models to assess the health of northern Greenland’s ice shelves. They tracked changes in ice volume, area, and the position of the 'grounding line'—where the ice sheet transitions from land-based to floating. Satellite observations reveal that as ice shelves shrink and thin, grounding lines are retreating inland. This retreat is especially concerning because the land beneath the ice sheet slopes downward toward Greenland’s center. As the grounding line moves inland over this retrograde slope, more thick ice is exposed to warm ocean waters, which leads to accelerated melting, faster ice flow, and increased ice loss to the sea. If this process continues unchecked, it may result in an unstoppable retreat of Greenland's glaciers.

article_content: An Alabama man credits a stray dog with helping him overcome a bleak prognosis after being diagnosed with incurable cancer. Bill Hogencamp, 84, of Phenix, was told in May he likely would not live to see Christmas due to advanced cancer in several organs. Despite accepting his fate, he and his wife, Kathy, decided to keep fighting the illness. In October, after surgery to remove three large tumors, Kathy spotted a stray Maltese mix dangerously close to traffic. She rescued the dog, naming him Mahjong after her favorite card game. Though initially reluctant to adopt another pet, Hogencamp soon formed a close bond with Mahjong, who stayed constantly by his side. Hogencamp then underwent chemotherapy, and to the family’s surprise, later tests showed he was cancer-free. The Hogencamps view Mahjong as part of the 'miracle' and believe he gave the family hope and comfort during a difficult time. 'The dog seemed to know right away Bill was sick, and it was his job to take care of him -- and Bill knew it was his job to care for the dog,' Kathy told ABC News.

article_content: Don Cornelius, creator of 'Soul Train,' died at age 75 from an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound at his Sherman Oaks, California home early on February 1, 2012. Police ruled out foul play, and no suicide note was found. Authorities confirmed the 911 call was made by one of Cornelius's two sons from his first marriage to Delores. Cornelius left two life insurance policies totaling about $300,000, designated for his ex-wife, Viktoria Chapman-Cornelius, a Russian model. Their divorce was finalized in 2009 after a contentious legal battle that involved mutual allegations of domestic abuse. He had suffered serious health issues in recent years, including a stroke and brain surgery, which reportedly left him in significant pain. Aretha Franklin, Quincy Jones, Jesse Jackson, Clarence Avant, and others praised Cornelius, describing him as a transformative figure in television, music, and the civil rights movement. Soul Train started in 1970 as a local Chicago show and aired nationally from 1971 to 2006, becoming a cultural institution. It showcased African-American artists including Michael Jackson, Marvin Gaye, Aretha Franklin, James Brown, Patti LaBelle, and Barry White. Famous for the phrase 'We wish you love, peace, and soul,' Cornelius stepped down as host in 1993. He is credited for helping break down racial barriers in music and television. He is survived by two sons from his marriage to Delores. Don Cornelius was honored with a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame and is remembered for his profound impact on music and television.

article_content: The Indian government is preparing to launch a clear, risk-based framework with multiple options for social media and online platforms to enforce age verification and manage parental consent, according to individuals familiar with the matter. This framework will apply to major social media companies, including Facebook (Meta), Instagram, YouTube (Google), as well as edtech and health platforms. For children under 18, age verification may be carried out through documents stored in DigiLocker, Aadhaar-based verification, digital tokens, or at the app store level—depending on potential data misuse risks. Officials emphasized there is no one-size-fits-all solution. Social media platforms will have stricter requirements, as there is a greater chance children may have unsupervised contact with strangers compared to educational or news websites. Lower-risk platforms like educational or news sites may use more flexible verification by cross-checking documents such as school leaving certificates or birth certificates via DigiLocker. On social media, considered higher risk, stricter age verification may involve multi-layer authentication. This new framework will form part of the rules under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act (DPDP), which became law in August. The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) is likely to release the rules by month's end. The DPDP Act defines those under 18 as children and requires data fiduciaries—including social media and web platforms—not to process a child's data without parental consent. Industry representatives have expressed concerns about privacy impacts from age verification methods, but the ministry supports these provisions. Platforms will need to confirm user age, identify parents, and prove the connection between the two. App store-level age verification APIs are among the possible options. MeitY’s framework may also detail procedures for age verification and consent, set minimum requirements for third-party services, and prohibit self-declaration by users or intermediaries. The overall aim is to follow global best practices to protect users’ safety and security. Elsewhere, India’s IPO market is booming, with new offerings from Tata Technologies, Flair Writing Industries, and Gandhar Oil Refinery fully subscribed within hours. IndiGo, the country's largest airline, may introduce premium seating, hot meals, and a loyalty program by the end of 2024 to attract business travelers and compete with Air India. Since the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC) began, creditors have withdrawn over 26,000 insolvency cases worth a total of ₹9.33 lakh crore before court admission.

article_content: Formula One made a substantial $500 million investment in its new Las Vegas Grand Prix, organized directly by F1 and Liberty Media. However, the much-hyped event got off to a rough start when Carlos Sainz Jr. hit a loose water valve cover just nine minutes into the opening practice, bringing the session to a halt. Sainz's Ferrari suffered heavy damage, leading to a suspension of practice as officials inspected the entire street circuit. As a result, fans experienced a very brief session before being told to leave due to both safety concerns and rules around transport worker hours. Practice resumed in the middle of the night, but without spectators present. F1 President Stefano Domenicali and Grand Prix CEO Renee Wilm released a statement citing the need to balance safety, security, and logistics. No formal apology or ticket refunds were offered; affected attendees received a $200 merchandise store credit—a gesture that many felt was insufficient. Despite these setbacks, Ferrari rebuilt Sainz’s car in time for qualifying. Nevertheless, FIA regulations imposed a ten-place starting penalty on Sainz because of the extensive repairs, prompting criticism of the rules since the damage was caused by track conditions and not team error. Discontent among fans and local residents has simmered amid steep ticket prices, extended construction disruptions, and sessions scheduled to favor European television audiences. The Las Vegas Grand Prix represents F1's most significant push into the American market, boosted by the sport’s growing popularity from Netflix's 'Drive to Survive.' The race is also the most expensive to attend this year. Opinions from team leaders are sharply divided—while some, such as Fred Vasseur (Ferrari) and Toto Wolff (Mercedes), praised the organizational efforts, others like Max Verstappen criticized the event’s focus on spectacle over sport. Organizers remain hopeful that the remainder of the race weekend will win over fans, though whether the event can recover from its rocky start remains to be seen.

article_content: Gisela Voss, a Massachusetts mother, has written heartfelt open letters in memory of her late son, Luke Voss-Kernan, as his former classmates near college graduation. Luke tragically died in 2012 at the age of 19 during a cross-country trip when he fell from an old structure at Gas Works Park in Seattle. Reflecting on her son’s passing, Gisela first composed a deeply emotional note to Luke, describing her enduring grief and how she continues to miss him daily. She then addressed his friends and classmates, sharing these letters through her Facebook page, as reported by The Boston Globe. Luke, who graduated from Newton South High School in 2010, would have been celebrating his own college graduation this year. Instead, his mother chose to honor his memory by reaching out to his peers, encouraging them to value every moment of life. In her letter to them, Gisela urges Luke’s friends to appreciate the privilege of being alive, to pursue their dreams, forge meaningful memories, nurture friendships, and acknowledge that tomorrow is never guaranteed. Gisela’s words encourage young people to be present, ask profound questions, and truly listen to one another. She underlines that even in the face of loss, life continues, and the ability to love, experience joy, and create memories remains a gift. In closing, she implores them simply: ‘Stand in awe.’

The White House is considering combining aid requests for Ukraine and Israel into a single legislative package, sources told The Washington Post. This approach is intended to help secure enough Republican support for both measures, as the Biden administration works to fulfill its pledge to assist Ukraine in defending itself against Russia. 

An unnamed official indicated that this strategy could put pressure on the Republican 'far right,' which has opposed continued U.S. aid to Ukraine. Opposition from House Republicans, particularly the pro-Trump MAGA faction, has centered on prioritizing domestic spending over foreign aid.

In July, 70 House Republicans backed an amendment to the annual defense bill that would have cut off all U.S. military aid to Ukraine. More recently, $6 billion in Ukraine funding was excluded from a stopgap spending measure aimed at preventing a government shutdown due to Republican resistance.

The Biden administration is reportedly hoping to leverage widespread Republican support for Israel as a means to pass Ukraine aid through Congress. White House officials and pro-Ukraine lawmakers believe that linking the two aid packages could prompt some Republicans to approve the full measure, given their reluctance to oppose military support for Israel. 

John Kirby, the National Security Council’s coordinator for strategic communications, declined to confirm whether the packages would be combined, according to The Washington Post. Top officials expect the administration to seek congressional approval for more military aid to Israel as soon as next week.

William May, father of four-year-old McKenna from Haskins, Ohio, has spoken out about his decision to stop his daughter, a leukemia survivor, from taking a Make-A-Wish trip to Disney World. May reasoned that since McKenna is in remission and not terminally ill, the wish should be reserved for children facing more severe health struggles. He voiced concern that charitable funds ought to prioritize those with limited time or opportunities.

Nonetheless, donations from across the globe surpassed $12,000, allowing McKenna's mother, Whitney Hughes, and grandmother, Lori Helppie, to arrange the trip independently and donate any leftover funds to charity. McKenna endured two years of intense leukemia treatment, including fifteen spinal taps, numerous chemotherapy rounds, and steroid injections, often requiring hospitalization. Her final treatment was about a month ago, though full remission confirmation won't come for several years.

May’s refusal was deeply disappointing to McKenna, her mother, and her grandmother, particularly since Make-A-Wish required consent from both parents for the trip. McKenna's mother suggested that her ex-husband's objection might partially stem from ongoing disputes over visitation rights. May himself admitted frustration at feeling left out of key decisions regarding his daughter's wish.

Moved by McKenna’s story, local residents and strangers sent donations, with more collected at area banks. Susan McConnell, president and CEO of Make-A-Wish for Ohio, Kentucky, and Indiana, clarified that doctors are responsible for determining wish eligibility and expressed compassion for McKenna, who found herself caught in the middle of these disagreements. Thanks to the outpouring of support, McKenna is now set to make her trip to Disney World a reality.

article_content: Nigel Farage has admitted to setting up an offshore trust fund in the Isle of Man in an attempt to lower his tax bill, but later described the move as a mistake and claims he never benefited from it. Despite his public stance against tax avoidance, the UK Independence Party leader stated that the trust was meant for inheritance planning, later realizing he was not wealthy enough for it to be useful. Following advice from his financial advisors, Farage intended the trust to help pay for schooling costs for his children or grandchildren. He now says setting it up did not suit his circumstances. Political opponents, like Labour MP John Spellar, have accused Farage of hypocrisy, criticizing him for setting up an offshore fund while condemning similar practices. Documentation shows Farage temporarily moved shares from his company, Farage Ltd, to the trust in 2004—meaning the trust briefly owned half the business. Andrew Farage, his brother, was also named in the trust and reportedly received over £900,000 in dividends. According to an accountant, taxes on these earnings were paid. Farage expressed regret over establishing the trust, explaining both the changing public attitudes toward offshore finances and his lack of significant wealth. Tax avoidance through offshore schemes has been a key concern in the UK, with Prime Minister David Cameron addressing it at the G8 summit in Northern Ireland and estimating such practices cost the country £35 billion per year. Meanwhile, Farage Ltd is in a voluntary debt arrangement, owing more than £130,000. The Isle of Man’s appeal as a site for trusts comes from its lack of inheritance tax and very low corporation taxes.

article_content: Professor Bolaji Akinyemi, former Minister of External Affairs and past Director-General of the Nigerian Institute of International Affairs, reflects on Nigeria's journey 63 years after independence.  He notes that Nigeria's post-independence history has featured both progress and setbacks. There have been advances in housing, urbanization, and infrastructure, which is more widespread than in many other African countries. However, the country lags significantly in education, health, and welfare.  Akinyemi points out ongoing economic decline, with devalued currency and industrial closures—especially in sectors like textiles—and persistent unemployment. Inadequate power supply continues despite major investments.  He blames these issues on corruption and poor leadership. Past reform attempts, such as raising educational requirements for the presidency, have failed, and leadership positions still frequently go to those selected for ethnic or personal reasons rather than merit.  Other countries, some younger than Nigeria, have surpassed it through better management. A culture of hypocrisy exists in which former leaders who contributed to national problems now criticize the current state of affairs while avoiding accountability themselves, partly because Nigeria does not teach its own history effectively.  Akinyemi also critiques a persistent habit of circumventing the law, and warns that divisive ethnic competition and reliance on quotas have undermined meritocracy and hindered national advancement.  Despite immense human and natural resources, Nigeria’s economy remains weak due to corruption, resource mismanagement, and an inefficient federal revenue system. Akinyemi advocates for constitutional reforms that would let states control more of their resources, encouraging accountability and growth.  He urges a return to true federalism, with local issues handled by state governments and resources administered proportionally. Despite constitutional amendments—including proposals from the 2014 National Conference—transformative reforms have not yet materialized.  Akinyemi acknowledges notable improvements in Nigeria's democracy, especially with the use of technologies like BVAS in elections and the shift to resolving disputes in court rather than on the streets. However, public mistrust of the judiciary endures.  He recommends measures to discourage frivolous lawsuits and foster a culture of accepting both legal victory and defeat graciously.  The former minister warns against ethnic-based political parties and supports unity, recalling the brief success of the two-party system. He is critical of people who oppose monopolization only when they are not in power.  On attracting foreign investment, Akinyemi says Nigeria must streamline its bureaucracy, reduce corruption, and provide stable power to draw investors.  He notes Nigeria’s underfunded missions abroad weaken foreign policy and diplomatic effectiveness, and opposes shutting them down, pointing out the loss of influence on the global stage.  Akinyemi also clarifies that Nigeria is currently Africa’s third-largest economy after Egypt and South Africa, attributing the loss of position partly to over-reliance on oil and failure to develop other sectors or tap into its gas reserves.  In summary, Akinyemi insists that overcoming corruption, championing meritocracy, reforming governance, strengthening the constitution, and changing public attitudes are essential for Nigeria to reach its true potential.

Hurricane Otis, among the most powerful storms ever to strike Mexico, left catastrophic damage in the Pacific beach city of Acapulco, home to nearly 900,000 residents. At least 27 people have been confirmed dead, and four more are missing following landfall, when Otis battered the city with winds up to 270 km/h (165 mph). The hurricane tore roofs from homes and hotels, toppled trees, and severed communications and road links throughout the region.

Flooding submerged vehicles and required some hospitals to evacuate patients. President Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador stated at a Mexico City press conference, “What Acapulco suffered was truly disastrous.” Authorities reported many fatalities caused by overflowing rivers. While injuries have not yet been fully accounted for, a state of emergency remains in effect.

Otis rapidly intensified from a tropical storm to Category 5 on the Saffir-Simpson scale shortly before landfall, surprising authorities. President Lopez Obrador described the event as unprecedented in recent Mexican history, noting both the hurricane’s rapid escalation and its magnitude. The World Meteorological Organization labeled Otis “one of the most rapidly intensifying tropical cyclones on record.”

Residents recalled harrowing experiences during the storm. Citlali Portillo, a hotel manager, told Televisa she sheltered in a bathtub as the building shook violently. Erik Lozoya, a magician, described enduring hours of fear with his wife and young children in a hotel room as windows shattered and ceilings collapsed, barricading themselves in a bathroom for safety. “It felt like our ears would explode,” he recounted.

Survivors navigated mud and debris seeking food and shelter. “Acapulco is a total disaster. It’s not what it was before,” said resident Eric Hernandez, who also described looting and desperate scenes. President Lopez Obrador reached Acapulco by road, overcoming landslides and floods—media showed him in a military jeep stuck in mud during the journey.

By Thursday afternoon, authorities announced that Acapulco’s airport control tower was operational, and an air bridge to Mexico City would begin on Friday. Almost 8,400 military personnel, including army, air force, and national guard members, are assisting in recovery operations.

Acapulco, Guerrero’s largest city and a key tourist destination, suffered severe losses with 80% of its hotels damaged, according to Governor Evelyn Salgado, who called the storm “totally devastating.” Restoration of electricity and water supplies is underway.

During Saturday's launch, SpaceX’s Super Heavy rocket and Starship spacecraft—collectively known as Starship—produced 17 million pounds of thrust from 33 Raptor engines, making the launch tower an unsafe location. Instead of observing from the tower, SpaceX installed a robust 360-degree camera at the top, allowing space enthusiasts to experience the liftoff of the world’s most powerful rocket from a safe, close-up view. Viewers can use virtual reality headsets, smartphones, or PCs to explore the launch from all angles, witnessing the ascent of the 400-foot-tall Super Heavy booster and Starship at Boca Chica, Texas.

According to SpaceX, “This 360-degree view comes from the top of the launch tower at Starbase in Texas, providing a front-row seat to watch liftoff of the world’s most powerful launch vehicle ever developed.” The video, shared online Tuesday, was met with enthusiasm from space fans, with one describing it as “absolutely breathtaking.” Another called it “the coolest rocket 360 video I’ve ever seen.”

The second integrated flight test achieved major milestones: all 33 Raptor engines on Super Heavy ignited, a full-duration ascent burn was completed for the first time, and stage separation was achieved. However, both the booster and upper stage exploded after separation. SpaceX emphasized that the data collected is invaluable for Starship’s continued development. Ultimately, Starship is expected to transport crew and cargo to the Moon, Mars, and potentially beyond.

article_content: Veteran DJ Tony Blackburn injured his left thumb after accidentally trapping it in his electronic garage door at his Hertfordshire home on Monday. The 71-year-old broadcaster, known for launching BBC Radio 1 and winning multiple radio awards, received nine stitches and a bandage at a local hospital, with his wife Debra taking him to A&E. Blackburn later appeared on Sky News, where he showed his bandaged thumb, praised the NHS for their care, and maintained a cheerful attitude, joking that the injury was barely noticeable. His agent, Nick Canham, said Blackburn was unsure how the accident occurred, only that his hand became trapped when closing the door. Blackburn, who is right-handed, typically uses his other hand for DJing. The incident follows a recent hospital visit for sciatica. Blackburn kept fans updated via Twitter, thanking the NHS for their help. According to the Royal Society for the Prevention of Accidents (RoSPA), electronic garage doors cause nearly 5,000 injuries each year in the UK, with hundreds requiring hospital treatment.

article_content: Britain’s leading retailers are offering major discounts in an effort to sell large amounts of unsold summer stock, following an unusually cold season. Stores like Debenhams, House of Fraser, and Laura Ashley have launched half-price sales, while John Lewis has begun matching many of these reductions as part of its 'Never Knowingly Undersold' policy. Sales of non-food items have declined, with clothes and shoes dropping by 5.7%, and electrical goods by 5.2% compared to the previous year, according to the British Retail Consortium. The first overall decrease in average non-food prices in three years has been recorded. The British Retail Consortium is expected to confirm that many shoppers are avoiding town centres due to the cost of living pressures and a growing shift to online shopping. Products considered non-essential, such as DIY and garden supplies, are also seeing price drops. Profit margins are shrinking for many retailers as a result of these ‘desperation sales’. Shares in Home Retail Group, the parent company of Argos and Homebase, fell earlier this week after revealing significant reductions. Argos’s margins fell by 0.75 percentage points and Homebase’s by 2%, as outdoor-related sales suffered from the disappointing start to summer. Argos is running ‘The Big Sale’ with discounts up to 60% on garden patio furniture. John Lewis will launch its online clearance sale on Wednesday and in-store sales on Thursday. Marks & Spencer hosted special events like 20% off all menswear, while Gap held a 15% off online sale and Currys is offering up to 40% off large kitchen appliances and up to £300 off large flatscreen TVs. These widespread sales are aimed at customers affected by prolonged stagnation in wages and increased living costs. The retail environment remains difficult for some major chains, including Comet, Game, Clinton Cards, and JJB Sports, while value retailers like Primark and Aldi are performing strongly. Sainsbury's CEO, Justin King, has suggested introducing a new online sales tax to help bricks-and-mortar retailers compete with internet-based rivals that do not pay business rates. He proposes that the tax revenue could be used to reduce business rates or parking costs. King argued, 'The burden of taxation falls very heavily on bricks and mortar retailers. I think we need to rebalance the tax burden.'

article_content: In 2002, the family of German Robles, living in northern Mexico, set up a camera trap and unexpectedly captured images of a black bear on their farm. This discovery led the family, who had raised cattle for four generations, to let part of their land return to its natural state. Over time, they spotted ocelots, golden eagles, several rattlesnake species, and even a jaguar. Scientists took interest, and by 2011 the property was officially designated a federally protected Natural Area. Now, German Robles fears this sanctuary is at risk as contractors begin clearing land for a new freight railroad, which will cross near the Aribabi ranch and the nearby town of Imuris, about 40 miles south of the US-Mexico border. Robles says the project will fragment crucial habitats his family has helped restore, potentially creating a barrier to animal migration. The railroad is presented as a link between a Pacific port and the Arizona border. However, local residents and environmentalists argue that environmental concerns are being ignored. They have struggled to oppose the project due to limited information and a lack of public consultation; government officials have not publicly shared plans or performed environmental assessments, and the project is not on official websites. Construction began north of Imuris several months ago. Leaked route maps suggest the railway will follow the Cocospera river, cut through part of the Aribabi ranch, and continue towards Imuris, threatening local farmland, irrigation systems, and a reservoir that supplies water to roughly 12,500 residents. The track may also disrupt migration corridors for wildlife, including ocelots, jaguars, and black bears, as noted by the Center for Biological Diversity. The state's infrastructure department has offered to buy land along the route at low rates, drawing criticism from residents who describe the offers as unfair and disruptive. Some officials declined to comment, citing federal jurisdiction over the project, while Imuris's mayor acknowledged a lack of information for residents. The new railway is expected to run within about 10 miles of Santa Cruz, near a copper mine Grupo Mexico plans to open in 2025. Biologist Mirna Manteca and other advocates report difficulty accessing official details about the project, with government departments providing no clear answers. Community concerns echo those raised by opponents of the much larger Maya Train, a major infrastructure initiative in the Yucatan region. Both projects have moved forward with substantial military involvement and limited transparency, sometimes beginning construction before environmental reviews. Despite the challenges, local advocates like Yvonne Siquieros continue to press for more information and highlight risks, such as potential impacts on an aging dam that serves the community. Over half of freight through the region's port has been fossil fuels, and residents and scientists argue that the local desert habitat, though arid, supports remarkable biodiversity that deserves protection. Robles hopes that, even if the railway can't be stopped, part of his family's conservation legacy can be preserved.

article_content: An ambulance overturned on Florida’s Turnpike in Orlando Wednesday afternoon after colliding with a mattress that had fallen from a truck. Officials reported that the ambulance was traveling southbound near State Road 528 when a mattress became dislodged from a vehicle driving ahead. Inside the ambulance were a five-year-old boy and his 39-year-old father. The child was transported to Arnold Palmer Hospital with minor injuries. The ambulance, owned by American Ambulance, was not an emergency vehicle but was transferring the boy between facilities when the accident occurred at around 3 pm. The ambulance flipped onto its driver’s side after driving over the mattress. No other vehicles were involved. The driver of the truck, Jon Brumer, 36, of Cutler Bay, has been charged with dropping a load from a vehicle. The Turnpike was temporarily closed after the accident but has since reopened.

article_content: On January 18, 1976, over 6,000 fans filled Kilcohan Park, home of Waterford FC, for a remarkable football event. The club’s golden era had ended in 1973 after six league titles in eight years, leading to a period of decline and lower attendances. Excitement returned as the legendary Bobby Charlton—World Cup and European Cup winner, known for his career at Manchester United—appeared for Waterford. At 38, Charlton assisted a goal in a 3-2 victory over St Patrick’s Athletic. He received a share of the £1,900 gate receipts before playing three more matches, scoring once, and standing out each time, prior to returning to England. This brief chapter added to his celebrated football legacy; his life would be honored following his passing at age 86. Former Waterford star and manager Alfie Hale remembers the era well. Having scored over 100 goals for Waterford and managed the club twice, Hale pointed out that most of the club’s great players, himself included, had moved on by Charlton’s arrival. "By then, excitement for Waterford football had faded," he remarked. Attendances fell from over 10,000 in league-winning seasons to just 1,500–2,000. Charlton's move was driven by personal connections and opportunity. In the 1970s, Irish clubs occasionally attracted big names like George Best, Geoff Hurst, and Uwe Seeler, which invigorated local football. Charlton joined after a disappointing period managing Preston North End. Joe Delaney, the new chairman at Waterford in 1976, pushed for signings that could boost interest, offering a share of match receipts. Connections helped facilitate the move: Charlton’s close friendship with former Manchester United teammate Shay Brennan, who managed Waterford until 1974, played a role. Charlton had faced Waterford with United in a 1968 European Cup tie, with more than 50,000 fans attending the first leg at Lansdowne Road—a landmark event in Irish football. Charlton’s arrival thrilled those who hadn’t seen him before. After the win against St Patrick’s, Waterford also beat Finn Harps 3-1, with Charlton scoring. Unlike George Best's later struggles in Ireland, Charlton impressed with his fitness and performance. However, disputes over revenue sharing, particularly following a loss to Bohemians, cut his spell short. Charlton’s final Waterford match was a cup loss to Finn Harps. He later made brief appearances in Australia’s National Soccer League, retiring for good in 1980 at age 42. Alfie Hale later declined an offer from Charlton’s brother Jack to join the Republic of Ireland coaching staff, choosing to stay at Waterford. Reflecting now, Hale regards Charlton as the greatest player he encountered, and believes the respect of one’s peers is the ultimate measure. Charlton’s short stint at Waterford stands out as a unique period in Irish football and his exceptional career.

article_content: A mother who invested £40,000 converting her home into a garden cafe now faces the possibility of losing her property after her application for planning permission was refused. Kym McKenzie, 52, planned to use the cafe’s earnings to support her 15-year-old son Ramoan’s dream of attending university. Operating from her Southampton home near the Millbrook Trading Estate, McKenzie says she began work after being told by councillors that planning permission was unnecessary. However, permission was ultimately denied because of concerns about safe pedestrian access and the potential impact of delivery vehicles on neighbours. As a result, she is struggling to keep up with business loan repayments. McKenzie’s proposed access involved a gate leading onto a private grass verge, but the city council found this plan inadequate. They also disputed her claim, stating that she had not been advised to proceed before planning permission had been granted and generally recommend against commencing work beforehand. Her cafe, named Kym’s Garden Cafe, was completed in December of last year, outfitted with new kitchen equipment, tables, and chairs, but has yet to serve any customers. Despite outreach to local companies who expressed interest in ordering food, Ms. McKenzie has been unable to open the business. Local MP Alan Whitehead has expressed support for McKenzie’s business plans, calling the idea good for the area and suggesting further efforts be made to help her overcome the remaining hurdles. Kym McKenzie continues to hope for a positive outcome, expressing her desire to open and operate the cafe while retaining her home.

article_content:
A study suggests that the European Union (EU) could be partly responsible for Europe's growing obesity epidemic. Scientists found that due to lower import tariffs, the 27 EU member states have higher supplies of red meat and dairy compared to non-members. Member states also tend to have lower prices on calorie-dense foods, increasing the risk of obesity. A recent Eurostat report stated that more than half of the EU population is now overweight or obese.

Researchers analyzed dietary habits in Portugal before and after joining the EU in 1986. Before membership, the Portuguese diet focused on local produce, fish, and olive oil. After joining, many shifted to more affordable meats, cheeses, and grains imported from other EU states. Lead researcher Pedro Marques-Vidal from Lausanne University noted that after joining the EU, meat and dairy prices dropped in countries like Germany, Italy, France, and Portugal, leading to increased consumption and weight gain among citizens.

Other scientists, such as David Fah of Zurich University, support these findings and warn of similar risks if Switzerland joined the EU. Switzerland, which is not an EU member, currently has one of the lowest obesity rates in Europe, at around 8 percent. Fah explained that the Swiss diet contains more vegetables, fish, olive oil, and less red meat. He believes joining the EU would likely increase red meat consumption in Switzerland.

The late 1990s saw wheat prices in the EU hit record lows, driven down by cheap fuel and farm subsidies. This availability of inexpensive food contributed to rising obesity rates across Europe. Jo Leinen, a spokesperson for the EU Environment and Health Commission, acknowledged obesity as a major public health threat in the EU.

Obesity is recognized as a global epidemic and is the most common metabolic disease worldwide. A person is considered obese if their body mass index (BMI) is 30 or greater. The Foresight report predicts that by 2025, nearly half of men and over a third of women in Europe will be obese, increasing risk for chronic diseases like type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, hypertension, stroke, and some cancers.

UNITED NATIONS — Latvian President Edgars Rinkēvičs warns that Russia is preparing for a prolonged conflict in Ukraine and urges Western allies to sustain military support for Kyiv. In an interview with The Associated Press, Rinkēvičs emphasized that continued international support is necessary to prevent Russia from threatening other countries. He highlighted Russia's disruptive role in Africa via the Wagner mercenary group and noted Russian meetings with Hamas, whose October 7 attack in Israel killed around 1,200 people.

Rinkēvičs, inaugurated as Latvia's president in July after serving 13 years as foreign minister, underscored the nation's strategic importance on NATO's eastern flank. He noted that while EU members sometimes differ on Middle East policy, the bloc remains united in sanctioning Russia and aiding Ukraine after the February 2022 invasion.

He called on the West to support both Ukraine and Israel, defending shared democratic values and the international order. Rinkēvičs advocated for humanitarian pauses to aid Palestinian civilians amid high casualties in Gaza, as reported by Gaza health authorities.

The Latvian leader pointed out Iran's supply of arms to Russia in the Ukraine conflict and stressed that NATO must take both Ukraine and Middle Eastern tensions seriously. He argued that supporting Ukraine is crucial for European peace and warned that neglecting conflicts in Ukraine or the Middle East could embolden adversaries and destabilize other regions, including Asia and Taiwan.

Rinkēvičs observed that Russia has shifted to a war economy and is likely to resume attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure this winter. He called for increased defense spending by NATO members, with Latvia aiming to spend 2.4% of its GDP on defense next year, rising to 3% by 2027.

He warned that Russia is becoming increasingly totalitarian, employing aggressive propaganda and dehumanizing rhetoric toward Ukrainians reminiscent of Nazi-era language. Rinkēvičs, in New York to advocate for Latvia's 2026-2027 UN Security Council bid, is among Europe’s few openly LGBTQ+ heads of state and hopes his leadership encourages broader acceptance and inclusion worldwide.

article_content: A man whose mother died during Storm Babet has expressed frustration over delays in support for flood victims. Paul Gilbert discovered his mother Maureen, 83, deceased in floodwater inside her Chesterfield home last month. He said the community is struggling to come to terms with the tragedy and feels 'let down' by the council's response. Chesterfield Borough Council stated it is supporting residents. Mr Gilbert, who has been trying to clear wreckage from his mother's lifelong home on Tapton Terrace, said: 'It's horrible being down here. It's taking too long for help to arrive. You have to keep calling the council to get them to collect the rubbish. It's very difficult. We're having to fight for everything. We've been let down again.' Flooding occurred when the nearby River Rother overflowed during heavy rain, affecting 26 properties. Some residents reported insurance companies were overwhelmed and unable to promptly send loss adjusters. Mrs Gilbert's neighbor, Stephanie Winnard, said she is still in the process of drying out her home after it was flooded with 5ft (1.5m) of water. 'It's absolutely devastating. It's still very stressful. Every time you come in and see your house like this, it's hard,' she said. Local businesses are also feeling the impact. The cellar and ground floor of the Anchor pub on Factory Street were submerged and the pub had to close for a week. Co-owner Layonie Rawson explained previous flooding made it impossible to secure insurance. 'We've lost revenue, had repair costs, and are looking at around £20,000 in expenses. We've just had to keep going. Fortunately, we've received support from friends, family, and the community. Even people we don't know have brought cleaning supplies and food parcels,' she said. Chesterfield Borough Council leader Tricia Gilby commented: 'This has been an incredibly challenging period for the town and borough, but Chesterfield is resilient, and our community pulls together during times like these. Over the past month, we have supported residents and businesses with the clean-up, providing emergency and temporary housing for those affected.' She added that eight households remain in emergency accommodation and financial aid is available through the council for residents and businesses impacted by flooding. article_content: Opera singer Eliana Pretorian appeared outside the Royal Courts of Justice in London after escaping the threat of jail over a contractual dispute. Pretorian, based in the UK, was taken to court by Romanian businessman Ion Vasile, who sought a share of her earnings. Vasile applied for her committal to prison, alleging contempt of court. The dispute originated from a 1999 agreement that Vasile claimed entitled him to a percentage of Pretorian's future income in exchange for funding her music studies. The deal was made with Pretorian's father when she was 17. Pretorian, a soprano known for performing at Glyndebourne and Sadler's Wells, argued the contract was invalid because she was underage. Her barrister, Paul Stadden, criticized the agreement as exploitative. Pretorian's father is reported to have agreed to pay Vasile 35% of his daughter's professional income for a ten-year period chosen by Vasile, in return for $6,900 (£4,400) for her training. Now 31 and pregnant, Pretorian attempted to overturn the agreement, but Romanian courts ruled against her in 2009 and required her to pay Vasile’s legal costs. This ruling was recognized by English courts. Vasile's lawyers sought Pretorian's imprisonment for allegedly failing to fully disclose her professional income, but Judge Richard Seymour QC dismissed the case, ruling she had met her obligations and the application was without merit. Judge Seymour ordered Vasile to pay £6,525 in legal costs and questioned why the committal application was pursued. After the hearing, Pretorian called the original deal 'immoral to the root' and said it negatively affected her life, despite her successes. She emphasized her achievements were solely due to her own efforts.

article_content: A giant, partly-fossilised egg from the extinct elephant bird is set to be auctioned at Christie's. Measuring 30 cm high and 21 cm in diameter, the egg is more than 100 times the size of an average chicken egg. Elephant birds were massive, flightless birds that once lived in Madagascar. They could reach up to 11 feet in height and weigh around 880 pounds. They are believed to have been hunted to extinction between the 14th and 17th centuries. Whole, sub-fossilised elephant bird eggs are extremely rare. This specimen is estimated to fetch up to £30,000 at auction. The sale is part of Christie's Travel, Science and History auction, featuring over 260 lots including items from natural history, science, exploration, and art. Intact elephant bird eggs can be found in several museums globally: National Geographic Society (Washington), Denver Museum of Nature and Science, Harvard Museum of Natural History, Grant Museum of Zoology at University College London, Delaware Museum of Natural History, Melbourne Museum in Australia, and the Natural History Museum in London. Well-known broadcaster David Attenborough owns an almost complete elephant bird eggshell, which he reconstructed from fragments collected during filming for his 1961 BBC series 'Zoo Quest to Madagascar'. In 2011, he presented 'Attenborough and the Giant Egg', a BBC documentary tracing his personal investigation into the giant birds. The extinction of elephant birds is widely attributed to human activities, such as hunting and habitat loss. Archaeological discoveries, including eggshells among the remains of ancient fires, indicate their eggs were consumed by humans. Elephant birds, belonging to the genera Aepyornis and Mullerornis, were among the heaviest birds known, with eggs up to 160 times larger than a chicken egg. The precise reasons and timing for their extinction remain debated, but written records from the 17th century mentioned their presence. Historical writings, like those by explorer Marco Polo, describe enormous birds in Madagascar, which are now thought to have been elephant birds.

article_content: A migrant boat capsized off Yemen's coast, leaving dozens missing, most of whom are from the Horn of Africa, Yemeni officials said on Monday. Khalid al-Subeihi, a coast guard official in Mocha, reported that 75 migrants were onboard when the boat overturned on Sunday. Twenty-six people survived, but at least 49 are still missing, he told The Associated Press. Another coast guard official, Lt. Col. Olwan al-Qameri, stated that the search for survivors was ongoing on Monday. According to Yemen’s state-run SABA news agency, citing an unnamed official, strong winds caused the capsizing, with all passengers—including women and children—falling into the sea. This tragedy marks the latest in a series of maritime disasters involving African migrants seeking a better life in oil-rich Gulf countries. Every year, thousands make the dangerous journey from Ethiopia, Djibouti, and Somalia to Yemen, fleeing poverty and insecurity in search of work.

A journalist working for Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty (RFE/RL), Alsu Kurmasheva, has been detained by Russian authorities and charged with failing to register as a foreign agent, according to the news organization. Kurmasheva, a dual U.S.-Russian citizen and editor for RFE/RL's Tatar-Bashkir Service, was described as a 'highly respected colleague, devoted wife, and dedicated mother to two children' by acting president Dr. Jeffrey Gedmin, who called for her immediate release.

Kurmasheva, based in Prague, traveled to Russia in May for a family emergency. She was detained at Kazan airport on June 2 while awaiting a return flight, with officials confiscating her U.S. and Russian passports. RFE/RL reported that she was initially fined for not registering her U.S. passport with Russian authorities and was awaiting the return of her documents when, on October 18, new charges were brought against her.

U.S. State Department spokesperson Matt Miller said Thursday that the department has been quietly working on Kurmasheva’s case since May, choosing not to publicize details until recently. Miller criticized the Russian government’s actions as harassment and reiterated the U.S. government's strong travel warning against trips to Russia. Miller also noted the U.S. has not received formal notification from Russia about Kurmasheva's detention and highlighted that Moscow often denies consular access to dual nationals.

The incident follows the recent detention of another U.S. journalist, Evan Gershkovich of The Wall Street Journal, in Russia. The Committee to Protect Journalists, a New York-based nonprofit, condemned the charges against Kurmasheva as 'spurious' and demanded her immediate release, reaffirming that 'journalism is not a crime' and expressing concern over increasing restrictions on independent reporting in Russia.

Saad al-Hilli, a 50-year-old British engineer, was shot dead in his car near Annecy in the French Alps on September 5, 2012, along with his wife, Ikbal, and mother-in-law. Their two daughters, Zainab (7) and Zeena (4), survived the attack. French cyclist Sylvain Mollier was also killed at the scene.

Witnesses reported seeing Saad al-Hilli engaged in a 'heated' conversation with an unidentified man at the Le Solitaire du Lac campsite on the evening before the murders. The nature of the conversation remains unclear, and it was not described as particularly aggressive. The al-Hilli family had arrived in the area four days before, initially staying at a different campsite before spending their final night at Le Solitaire du Lac.

Investigators are exploring several motives, including a family inheritance dispute involving Saad’s brother, Zaid al-Hilli. Zaid has acknowledged arguing with his brother about their late father’s £1 million estate but denies any involvement in the killings. He was arrested for questioning but later released on bail.

Another theory suggests the attack might be related to Sylvain Mollier, possibly because he witnessed the murders. Witnesses noted a motorbike and a BMW 4x4 near the crime scene, and authorities intend to release an e-fit image of the suspected motorcyclist.

Investigators have not located the British passports of Saad al-Hilli or his wife despite extensive searches. The case remains unsolved, with a joint effort by British and French police continuing to pursue leads.

article_content: Construex, a software-as-a-service marketplace based in Ecuador, has made a major advance in modernizing the construction and design sectors after raising $4.6 million in seed funding, according to TechCrunch. The funding round was co-led by Zacua Ventures and Fifth Wall, with ABSeed and Terracotta Ventures also participating. Founded in 2019 by brothers Roberto and Nicolás Arroyo, Construex arose from challenges they encountered in their family's construction business. Roberto explained that difficulties sourcing building materials inspired them to create solutions for other developers facing similar issues. Construex aims to digitize Latin America’s $520 billion construction industry, where just 4% of suppliers use technology. The company has built a platform that connects construction product suppliers with clients, offering both free and premium services through subscriptions and transaction fees. With over 80,000 registered suppliers, Construex’s platform covers areas such as architecture, engineering, and furniture. Suppliers have access to a comprehensive CRM system, virtual reality showrooms, and WhatsApp integration. Initially self-funded, Construex became profitable and doubled its revenue over the last year. The company now operates in Chile, Guatemala, Argentina, and has established a base in Mexico City. The recent investment will accelerate expansion into Mexico, additional Spanish-speaking countries, and potentially Brazil. Construex’s goals include onboarding one million suppliers and quadrupling revenue in 2024. Geraldo Melzer, co-founder of ABSeed, praised Roberto Arroyo’s extensive industry knowledge and voiced enthusiasm for supporting Construex’s entry into more markets alongside Terracotta Ventures. This new funding positions Construex as a leader in digital transformation within Latin America’s construction and design markets, as it seeks to modernize and connect the industry.

article_content: You might want to watch the interview between Lex Fridman and Mark Zuckerberg, which takes place in the Metaverse. Is it fantastic or frightening? It's hard to decide. Initially, the technology showcased is exciting and innovative, but the possible implications for society are daunting. The setup of the realistic avatars raises questions about privacy, as it may soon be impossible to distinguish between real people and digital representations online. For this interview, both Fridman and Zuckerberg used high-definition, lifelike avatars for their conversation. Some observers believe Zuckerberg, CEO of Meta (formerly Facebook), may have crossed a line with this technology—raising ethical concerns about the direction of social media and communication. Many are wondering whether these advances can be paused or stopped, though the answer seems unlikely. The interaction demonstrates just how advanced online technology has become and how it is reshaping digital communication. Various media reactions have ranged from awe to alarm. Business Today called it 'pretty wild,' noting Fridman’s amazement at the realism of the Metaverse. The US Sun said it 'shocks the world with eerie first interview,' while Reddit users were more reserved, noting it will be 'kind of interesting to see the public react.' Meanwhile, The Verge reports slowing user growth, a decline in revenue for Meta, and a 60% drop in the company’s stock price this year. In an interview, Zuckerberg acknowledged that his metaverse strategy is a long-term bet, expecting it won't be profitable for several years, which sets up a 'trough of disillusionment.' Despite these challenges, Zuckerberg told The Verge that he still believes VR and AR headsets will become the next major computing platforms, and he wants Meta to lead that transition. The Meta Quest Pro—costing $1,499 in the US—was central to the metaverse interview experience, showing that this event was part of a broader plan for Meta’s future.

article_content: Tens of thousands gathered in Washington, D.C., on Saturday for one of the largest pro-Palestinian demonstrations in the United States since the recent escalation in Gaza. The protest, organized by several pro-Palestinian groups, drew participants from across the country calling for a cease-fire in Gaza, where officials report thousands of Palestinians have died in Israeli airstrikes. The event began with a rally at Freedom Plaza and continued with a march past notable landmarks, including the White House. Protesters held cloth bundles inscribed with the names of Palestinian children who died in the conflict and observed a moment of silence. Rally speakers called for an end to U.S. military aid to Israel and voiced criticism of President Biden's policies. Nour Jaghama from Code Pink questioned the lack of wider political support for a cease-fire among U.S. lawmakers. Attendees came from diverse backgrounds. Younass Barkouch from New Jersey attended to voice concern as an American. Ammara Rana, reflecting on her Muslim identity, described the strong sense of solidarity at the protest. Pedro Kremer, a Jewish protester, emphasized the universal value of human life and noted the personal repercussions of his views. While Israeli military operations in northern Gaza continue, the U.S. government has not called for a cease-fire but has urged Israel to implement a 'humanitarian pause' to permit aid into Gaza and secure the release of more than 200 hostages held by Hamas. Israel has stated any cease-fire is conditional on their release. President Biden has asked Congress to approve over $14 billion in additional military aid to Israel. Recent Israeli strikes, such as the one near Al Shifa hospital, have heightened international concern over civilian casualties and the targeting of sensitive organizations during the conflict.

article_content: Turks and Caicos, made up of two island groups south of the Bahamas in the Caribbean Sea, is famous for its spectacular white-sand beaches and uniquely blue waters—offering an idyllic setting for travelers. article_content: Lauren Graham, known for her role on 'Gilmore Girls,' was a close friend of Matthew Perry. She recently reflected on his happiness in the year before his unexpected death. 'This last year, he was so proud of the book he wrote and of how many people it touched,' Graham, 56, shared during a Thursday appearance on 'CBS Mornings.' 'It was a success that brought him a level of happiness I hadn’t seen in a long time, and that’s a wonderful memory.' Matthew Perry died unexpectedly on October 28 at the age of 54 in his Pacific Palisades home. Graham said she is still in shock, describing Perry’s passing as a tragic loss. She highlighted how grateful she is that he left behind such meaningful work. 'Again, the book really meant something to him, so it was a really happy year for him,' she added. She fondly recalled their friendship: 'No one made me laugh as hard—just tears, streaming. There was so much joy in being around him and being his friend.' Graham and Perry first met while filming 'Birds of America' in 2008 and kept in touch over the years. In his memoir, 'Friends, Lovers and the Big Terrible Thing,' Perry included a photo of the two, captioned, 'Me and the beautiful Lauren Graham.' Perry also spoke highly of Graham in a fan Q&A for his show 'The Odd Couple,' calling her 'one of my favorite people. We have great chemistry when working together and it’s fun to work with a close friend.' Other 'Friends' stars, including Lisa Kudrow, Jennifer Aniston, and David Schwimmer, publicly shared heartfelt tributes, thanking Perry for his humor, creativity, and lasting memories.

article_content: Dominica, a small Caribbean island, has announced plans to launch the world's first marine sanctuary dedicated to protecting endangered sperm whales. The new protected zone will span about 300 square miles (800 square kilometers) off the island's west coast, encompassing essential feeding and nursing grounds for these massive whales. According to Prime Minister Roosevelt Skerrit, the initiative aims to safeguard the whales and promote ocean and climate health. Scientists point out that sperm whales benefit the environment by releasing nutrient-rich waste near the surface, which supports plankton growth. These plankton blooms trap carbon from the atmosphere and transfer it to the ocean floor, helping mitigate climate change. Shane Gero, who leads the Dominica Sperm Whale Project, observes that sperm whales near Dominica seem to defecate more than elsewhere, perhaps because of their diet or the type of squid they consume. While the exact reason is unclear, their behavior enhances the positive environmental impact. Fewer than 500 sperm whales inhabit Dominica’s waters, migrating along the Lesser Antilles from St. Vincent to Guadeloupe. Unlike other sperm whale populations that roam widely, Dominica’s whales tend to stay within the eastern Caribbean. Gero emphasizes the importance of protecting them, especially since a single female calf’s loss can threaten a whole pod. Over the years, sperm whales have faced dangers like being struck by ships, getting caught in fishing equipment, and pollution from land runoff. Their numbers have dropped dramatically from an estimated 2 million before widespread whaling to roughly 800,000 worldwide today. Dominica’s marine reserve will allow small-scale fishing and establish a safer shipping route. The government will assign staff to oversee the area and enforce new rules around whale tourism, limiting the number of people who can interact with the animals. Scientists and conservationists, such as National Geographic’s Enric Sala, have welcomed the move, noting that Dominica considers the whales as part of its community and is taking unprecedented steps to protect them. Around 35 whale families reside in the island’s waters, some with individuals more than 60 years old. These whales communicate using unique clicking sounds and have even been given names by researchers, like 'Snow,' 'Fruit Salad,' and 'Soursop.'
