article_content: Nigel Farage, leader of the UK Independence Party (UKIP), claims that his party is attracting thousands of former British National Party (BNP) voters. Farage attributes this shift to UKIP’s strong anti-EU stance and its tough approach to immigration, which he believes appeals to voters disillusioned with far-right politics. He emphasized that while UKIP rejects the BNP’s ‘racist agenda,’ he is proud to gain support from those who no longer identify with the BNP. Speaking at Chatham House in London, Farage addressed BNP sympathizers: ‘If your frustration and disappointment with changes in your community have led you to support the BNP despite disagreeing with their racist policies, then we invite you to vote for us. I believe UKIP has won over about a third of the BNP’s former supporters.’ In the 2009 European elections, the BNP received 940,000 votes and secured two seats, but its support has since declined sharply. Meanwhile, Deputy Prime Minister and Liberal Democrat leader Nick Clegg criticized UKIP, accusing the party of exploiting the public’s anxiety by promoting a ‘politics of blame,’ similar to France’s far-right National Front. Clegg argued that encouraging voters to blame foreigners, immigrants, or EU institutions for societal problems is an appealing but ultimately insufficient solution, stating, ‘You can’t turn the clock back to the 1950s.’ Clegg also rebuked Farage for remarks made in a GQ magazine interview, in which the UKIP leader expressed admiration for Vladimir Putin’s strategic handling of the Syrian civil war—though not for Putin himself as a person. At a Westminster press conference, Clegg described Farage’s comments as ‘utterly grotesque,’ pointing out Putin’s support for Syrian President Assad as particularly troubling.

article_content: Taylor Swift revealed that the inspiration for her song 'All You Had To Do Was Stay' came from a dream—one that she found embarrassing. On the verge of her explosive rise to global stardom with her fifth studio album, '1989', released in 2014, Swift explained in a TIME interview that she dreamt her ex showed up at her door asking to reconcile. In the dream, all she could say in response was a high-pitched 'Stay.' 'It was almost operatic,' Swift recalled. 'I woke up and actually recorded myself saying the odd part into my phone, knowing I had to use it because it was just too strange to ignore. In pop music, you get to have fun with unusual sounds like that.' Some of the most memorable pop songs are born out of quirky moments. It's all the more surprising, then, that 'All You Had To Do Was Stay' has never fully received the recognition it deserves. With the release of Swift's re-recorded '1989 (Taylor’s Version)' nine years after the original, it's an ideal time to revisit and appreciate this overlooked track. There's thought behind why 'All You Had To Do Was Stay' occupies the fifth spot on '1989.' Fans, known as Swifties, have noticed a consistent pattern: track five on each of her albums tends to be the most emotional and cathartic song, often capturing the album's core mood and message. On 'Fearless,' it was 'White Horse'; on 'Speak Now,' it was 'Dear John'; and on 'Red,' 'All Too Well.' The tradition continued on her seventh album, 'Lover,' with 'The Archer.' Swift herself acknowledged that the pattern was initially unintentional, but after hearing from fans, she began to consciously place her most vulnerable songs as track five. Despite differing opinions, 'All You Had To Do Was Stay' fits this pattern. It is considered one of Swift's saddest tracks, yet its energetic pop sound is a departure from the country influences of her earlier work. This marks Swift’s clear move into pop territory, which began to show in 'Red' but was fully realized in '1989.' '1989' was crafted as a fun, pop-forward soundtrack for Swift’s life. Songs like 'Shake It Off' and 'Blank Space' offered playful responses to media scrutiny and heartbreak, while 'Welcome to New York' captured the excitement of young adulthood. Even tracks aiming at criticism, like 'Bad Blood,' retained a light, playful edge. Still, as many fans know, joy and pain often intertwine in Swift's music. That's where 'All You Had To Do Was Stay' stands out. The song’s lively production contrasts with its raw, honest lyrics about the complexities of breakups—longing, regret, and eventually, emotional release. Swift’s lyric, 'People like you always want back the love they pushed aside. But people like me are gone forever when you say goodbye,' sets a somber mood, heightened by the forceful 'stay!' in the chorus. The song explores how breakups can leave mixed emotions—the desire to move on and the temptation to look back, the pain and the urge to dance through it. 'All You Had To Do Was Stay' shows that catharsis in music doesn’t always come quietly; sometimes, it’s loud and full of drama. Its vivid storytelling and surreal inspiration are trademarks of Swift's style, demonstrating the power of pop to make even the strangest moments accessible and relatable—if you just allow yourself to embrace them and dance.

article_content: Pamela Hupp, whose case has garnered national attention and even inspired a television drama, is once again being prosecuted for first-degree murder in Missouri. Lincoln County Prosecuting Attorney Mike Wood revealed on Friday that the charges against Hupp—linked to the 2011 killing of her friend Betsy Faria—were dropped and then immediately refiled. This procedural change was used to request a closer trial venue, making it easier for witnesses and the Faria family to attend, after the previous venue in Springfield proved logistically difficult. Prosecutors accuse Hupp of murdering Betsy Faria to claim a $150,000 life insurance payout that had been switched to her just before Faria's death. They allege she tried to frame Betsy’s husband, Russ Faria, leading to his conviction and imprisonment in 2013. Russ was cleared and released two years later, and later received a $2 million compensation from Lincoln County for his wrongful conviction. Hupp is already serving a life sentence without parole for the 2016 murder of Louis Gumpenberger. According to prosecutors, Hupp lured Gumpenberger—who had disabilities—into her home under false pretenses, staging the event to draw away suspicion from herself in the Faria case.  The saga has been dramatized in NBC's series 'The Thing About Pam,' starring Renee Zellweger. Hupp’s attorney has not responded to requests for comment.

For over four years, self-driving cars have been tested on California’s roads, but now the Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) is taking official steps by issuing permits. Until this process, the exact number of test vehicles wasn’t clear. The updated, stringent guidelines require all autonomous cars to have manual override controls; as a result, Google has added steering wheels to its vehicles even though their design is focused on full autonomy. Google currently operates the largest fleet, with 25 upgraded Lexus SUVs, and both Mercedes and Volkswagen each have two vehicles permitted on California roads. Bernard Soriano, responsible for the DMV’s autonomous vehicle regulations, reported additional companies are applying for permits.

To ensure safety, the DMV mandates that all test drivers maintain impeccable driving records and complete mandatory training programs. Companies must also provide $5 million insurance per vehicle and report every incident where the car unexpectedly disengages self-driving mode, either due to technical problems or human intervention. Google is using a hangar leased from NASA at the Ames Research Center to continue developing and testing its vehicles, with NASA seeking insights for its own technology projects.

California joins Nevada and Florida in regulating driverless vehicle testing, while states like Michigan enforce fewer restrictions and rely mainly on manufacturer’s plates. Across the board, Google nears one million test miles. The federal government is yet to enact nationwide rules, putting regulatory authority mostly in the hands of states. The DMV is also finalizing rules that will oversee when autonomous cars become available to the public, with big questions remaining, like whether a human needs to be inside the vehicle.

article_content: Controlled substances were discovered on one of two tour buses traveling with rocker Bret Michaels and his band during a traffic stop in northeast Indiana late Wednesday, police reported. No arrests were made, but the evidence was forwarded to the DeKalb County prosecutor for review and possible charges. Drug detection dogs conducted scans of both buses after a sheriff’s deputy pulled over the tour convoy on northbound Interstate 69. According to Deputy Aaron Long, both canines indicated the presence of narcotics at the front of one bus. Another dog alerted to drugs in the second bus, which Michaels was occupying. The subsequent searches led to the discovery of marijuana on both buses, and a quantity of Schedule II controlled substances—drugs with a high potential for abuse but legal medical uses—on the first bus. Bret Michaels' publicist explained that the stop was due to a missing tag light on a trailer. The publicist emphasized that Michaels permitted the bus searches and that the situation was handled professionally. Michaels is currently on tour just months after suffering a major brain hemorrhage in April. CNN’s Jennifer Wolfe and Denise Quan contributed to this report.

article_content: With the beauty market full of products promising to slow aging, dealing with fine lines and pigmentation on the face is already complicated. Now, specialized creams and serums designed to target hand wrinkles are becoming widely available, encouraging people to give their hands as much attention as their faces. Hands are often one of the first areas to show signs of aging, with thinning skin making veins more prominent and increasing the likelihood of dark spots, sometimes called liver spots. Unlike the face, where makeup can mask these changes, it's harder to conceal them on the hands. A study from beauty brand No7 found that one in eight people worry more about their hands betraying their age than their faces. This has led to a surge in potent products aimed at plumping hands, reducing wrinkles, and targeting dark spots. Brands like Mavala, Hand Chemistry, Neutrogena, E45, and Palmer’s now offer various treatments for hand health. For example, Mavala's Repair Night Cream (£36.50) contains hyaluronic acid and silk amino acids to support cell renewal and moisture retention. Hand Chemistry's Hyaluronic Concentrate, with a 19% marine hyaluronic complex, aims for deep hydration, while Neutrogena's Norwegian Formula Anti-Ageing Hand Cream (£3.99) uses glycerin, shea butter, and soy complex to moisturize and reduce brown spots. E45’s Repair & Protect Overnight Hand Cream (£3.99) is meant to boost regeneration while you sleep, and Palmer’s Eventone Age Spot Hand Cream (£3.99) combines dark spot reduction with SPF for additional protection. Other specialized products include Mavala’s Cleansing Mask for Hands (£22.25), which refreshes and soothes the skin, and the Mavala Anti Blemish Cream for Hands (£17.00), tackling pigmentary blemishes with botanical extracts to regulate pigmentation and gentle exfoliation to brighten skin. The demand for hand-care has grown alongside clinical procedures. Cosmetic clinics have noted an 18% increase in inquiries about hand rejuvenation. Treatments range from dermal fillers and laser resurfacing to fat transfer, sometimes called the 'hand lift.' Dr. Dennis Wolf (The Private Clinic of Harley Street) explains that aging and sun exposure lead to more noticeable veins and wrinkles in the hands. Temporary solutions like fillers and lasers exist, but fat transfer—moving fat from other body areas into the hands—offers a longer-term fix and is minimally invasive. Dr. Yannis Alexandrides (111 Harley Street) emphasizes that skincare should go beyond the face, as hands often age faster due to exposure and less fat under the skin. Popular treatments include fillers or fat transfer for volume loss, and laser treatments like Fraxel for pigmentation. Permanent results are possible with some procedures, but recovery may involve redness and swelling.

article_content: On the second day of the October 2013 federal government shutdown, World War II veterans defied barriers to visit the WWII Memorial in Washington, D.C. The National Park Service, following White House orders, had fenced off the site and posted closure signs. Yet, veterans from honor flights—including those from Mississippi, Iowa, Illinois, and Missouri—reached the memorial, some using wheelchairs or canes. Unwilling to let the obstacles stop them, they and their supporters moved the barricades aside to gain entry. Several Republican lawmakers—Claire McCaskill, Roy Blunt, Michele Bachmann, and Steve Palazzo—were on hand and assisted the veterans. The closures were caused by a deadlock in Congress over funding and the Affordable Care Act, leading to the furlough of around 800,000 federal workers and the suspension of non-essential services. Many national parks and memorial sites were shut, disrupting long-awaited honor flights. Carol Johnson, spokesperson for the National Park Service, emphasized staff reluctance to enforce the closure but said regulations required it. After the veterans entered, officials allowed them to remain for commemorative activities, citing their First Amendment rights. Veterans like 90-year-old Bob Hunter of Mississippi and Tom Lucas, 87, one of five brothers who served, expressed both pride in their visit and disappointment at initially being blocked. During their visit, veterans laid wreaths, took photographs, and honored their comrades, drawing nationwide attention. Lawmakers from both parties expressed support—Senator Sherrod Brown pledged his pay to a veterans’ group and Senator John McCain publicly approved the gesture. Many saw the veterans’ actions as a powerful instance of civil disobedience, highlighting how the shutdown affected everyday citizens and the enduring appreciation for those who served.

article_content: The risk of hearing loss is not limited to loud machinery or obvious sources. It can also affect people in public environments such as theaters and concert halls. A recent study proposes absorbing excess sound in these areas to make them safer for hearing, while also using unwanted sound waves to generate electricity. The research, titled 'Piezoelectric system on harnessing sound energy in closed environment,' was published in Physics of Fluids. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), an estimated 12.5% of children and adolescents aged 6 to 19, and 17% of adults aged 20 to 69, have sustained permanent hearing damage from excessive noise exposure, said study author Rajendra Prasad P. 'Noise above 70 decibels for a prolonged period can start to damage our hearing. We need systems that can mitigate very loud sounds,' Prasad stated. In their study, the researchers focused on enclosed spaces like theaters and concert halls, building a system of piezoelectric sensors that can be installed in the walls, floors, and ceilings to absorb sound waves and capture their energy. Sound levels from loudspeakers in these locations typically range from 60 to 100 decibels, sometimes reaching as high as 120 decibels, Prasad explained. 'We classified the sound in closed environments based on intensity (decibels) that could potentially cause hearing loss,' Prasad said. 'The sound energy absorbed by piezoelectric sensors is processed by our system to convert it into electrical energy. Depending on the energy generation pattern, the system output switches between battery storage and direct use.' To optimize the system, the authors used computer simulations to adjust variables such as the input voltage needed, sound frequency and intensity, and sensor configurations in parallel and series. 'Surprisingly, the system works best at certain frequencies that match those typically found in theaters or auditoriums,' Prasad noted. 'Our design reduces sound vibration each time it reflects off the piezoelectric material, lowering the overall sound intensity in the space.' Beyond reducing the risk of hearing loss, the system is also environmentally friendly. It features a smart power management function that adjusts according to incoming sound levels, and it uses sustainable materials. 'The piezoelectric material we used is a form of quartz, a mineral made of silica,' Prasad added. 'It is easily biodegradable and can also be recycled.'

article_content: ATHENS, Greece — The European Union's border protection agency, Frontex, has joined the search for 12 crew members missing after a cargo ship sank in rough weather near the Greek island of Lesbos, authorities said on Monday. A 40-year-old Egyptian crew member was rescued on Sunday, while the body of another Egyptian crew member was recovered by a commercial vessel assisting in the search. The Comoros-flagged cargo ship Raptor was transporting salt from Alexandria, Egypt, to Istanbul, Turkey, and had a crew of 14, including eight Egyptians, four Indians, and two Syrians, according to the coast guard. The vessel reported a mechanical problem at 7 a.m. Sunday, sent a distress signal at 8:20 a.m., and shortly afterward disappeared about 4.5 nautical miles (8 kilometers) southwest of Lesbos. Frontex, which monitors the Lesbos area for irregular migration, sent a surveillance aircraft and a patrol boat to assist the Greek coast guard in the search and rescue efforts.

article_content: Photos recently released by the advocacy group Students and Scholars Against Corporate Misbehaviour (SACOM) allegedly show injuries suffered by workers at Biel Crystal, a company that manufactures touch screens for Apple. SACOM accuses Biel Crystal of multiple labor rights abuses at its factory in Huizhou, China, including exposing staff to excessive work hours, poor conditions, and a high rate of work-related injuries. The group further alleges that several Biel Crystal workers have committed suicide over the last two years. The photos, whose authenticity has not been independently verified, were made public as SACOM staged a protest outside Apple’s flagship store at Hong Kong’s International Finance Centre. SACOM’s investigation claims that Biel Crystal staff are required to sign 'blank contracts', work up to 11 hours a day, seven days a week, with only a 24-hour break at the end of each month. According to SACOM, workers do not receive fair compensation, and five suicides have allegedly occurred at the factory since 2011. Biel Crystal, based in Hong Kong, reportedly supplies touch screens for approximately 60 percent of Apple’s products and employs over 60,000 people across more than 15 production lines. On its website, Biel Crystal states that it is committed to providing industry-leading products and services using advanced technology and skilled engineers, and that it complies with competitive pricing standards. Apple has not provided an official comment on SACOM’s latest allegations. Instead, it referred to its 'Supplier Responsibility Progress Report', which details the company’s ongoing efforts to address supply chain issues such as excessive work hours and underage labor. The report highlights Apple’s tracking of weekly work hours for a million workers across its supply chain, publishing the results monthly. It also emphasizes Apple’s commitment to transparency and continuous improvement, though does not specifically mention Biel Crystal. Earlier this year, China Labour Watch made similar accusations against Pegatron, another Apple supplier, citing violations of labor laws and Apple’s own code of conduct. Foxconn, a major Apple supplier, has also faced significant scrutiny after a series of worker suicides and reports of poor working conditions. In response to these incidents, Apple joined the Fair Labour Association and increased scrutiny and audits of its suppliers. In summary, SACOM’s latest claims echo ongoing concerns about labor rights in Apple's supply chain, particularly among its suppliers in China. Apple maintains that it is committed to improving workplace standards and regularly audits its supplier facilities.

article_content: The Indian government has officially requested evidence from US authorities regarding the attacks on the Indian consulate in San Francisco, under the Mutual Legal Assistance Treaty (MLAT). This request follows findings from the National Investigation Agency (NIA). Authorities have identified 45 individuals linked to the attack, reportedly coordinated via crowd-funding. On the night between March 18 and 19, a group associated with pro-Khalistani elements trespassed into the San Francisco consulate and attempted to set it on fire. Violent incidents followed, involving breaches of security barriers, raising of Khalistani flags, slogans, property damage, and injuries to officials. According to NIA, another similar event occurred on the night between July 1 and 2, with an attempted arson while staff were present. The NIA filed a case on June 16 under provisions of the Indian Penal Code (IPC), the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, and the Prevention of Damage to Public Property Act. An NIA team visited San Francisco in August to further the investigation.

article_content: ROME: A suspected gas explosion partially destroyed a building housing asylum seekers in central Italy overnight, injuring 31 people, firefighters said Saturday. Video footage from the fire service showed sections of the two-storey building in San Lorenzo Nuovo, near Viterbo, reduced to rubble after the blast, which occurred shortly before midnight. The fire service reported that there was an "explosion and partial collapse" of the reception centre, likely due to a gas leak. Rescue searches, including sniffer dogs, confirmed 31 people were injured. One person is in serious condition, was airlifted to a hospital in Rome, and is currently in a coma, according to ANSA news agency. The building consisted of mini-apartments for asylum seekers, mostly men and some women without children. According to ANSA, a carpenter's workshop and a wine shop next door were also destroyed. Investigations into the cause of the explosion are ongoing.

article_content: Primary school pupils at Burton Joyce Primary School in Nottinghamshire were found watching inappropriate material during a school trip to Skegness, prompting calls for an investigation by education authorities. Many parents have withdrawn their children after the incident, which reportedly involved two girls aged eight seen watching the explicit film in a dormitory. The school, catering to children aged four to eleven, has faced over 30 withdrawals following serious complaints about its safeguarding and teaching practices. Burton Joyce Primary had previously received a 'good' rating from Ofsted in March 2009. Governor Eric Ashworth expressed concerns about the school's child protection measures, stating that proper records of governing body decisions were lacking, and called for the suspension of headteacher Margaret Gretton while Nottinghamshire County Council investigates. At least four governors have resigned over the incident. Parent Christopher Green withdrew his four children, citing deteriorating conditions. Another parent questioned the staff’s ability to safeguard children and described some teachers as inexperienced. Councillor Philip Owen confirmed an inquiry into the school's management, including the headteacher’s role, following complaints of 'inappropriate material' exposure during the trip. The Department for Education has deferred Burton Joyce Primary School's academy application until the investigation concludes. The school and its headteacher were unavailable for comment.

article_content: A Winnipeg woman, Lana Sinclair, alleges she was assaulted by a police officer in her home on Halloween. Sinclair says the incident happened in front of her eight-year-old son and describes it as senseless. The clothing and jewelry designer stated that police were called to her house following reports of screaming, but she explained she was only trying to get her son ready for trick-or-treating. Sinclair told CTV Winnipeg, 'He came up to me and poked me.' She said she was more concerned for her son's wellbeing while a police officer allegedly assaulted her after responding to the call on Halloween night. Hoping to prevent similar incidents, Sinclair has decided to come forward. She described sitting on a chair in her kitchen, jumping up and saying, 'You don't need to touch me.' Sinclair was then handcuffed, and said her feet were kicked out from under her, causing her to fall and hit her head on a table, just as her son came downstairs. 'All I was thinking about was his safety, and how he would be traumatized and how he would now view the police,' Sinclair said in her report. She noted she has no criminal record and has always tried to help others, adding that one of her other sons is a police officer. Sinclair has filed a complaint with the Law Enforcement Review Agency (LERA). In a television interview, she re-enacted what happened on Halloween. She claims she hit her head on a table after allegedly being kicked down by an officer. LERA commissioner Max Churler stated that, although hundreds of complaints are filed each year—most regarding excessive force—only four to six cases typically proceed to a hearing, as most are abandoned. Winnipeg police have not provided comment. Sinclair continues to recover from the injuries she sustained in the alleged incident and hopes sharing her story will help prevent similar experiences for others.

article_content: Despite recent diplomatic tensions between India and Canada, the process for obtaining Canadian student visas continues with no major interruptions. Approval rates remain impressively high—typically between 85% and 95%. Many students are being granted visas even if their language proficiency scores are slightly below the standard, such as an overall IELTS band of 6 with some scores of 5 in certain modules, or PTE results a few points under the recommended benchmark. Visa centers, especially those in the Doaba region of Punjab, report that their success rates not only remain steady, but have increased by up to 18–19% in the past month. The current strain between the two countries first arose when Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau alleged an Indian connection in the death of Canadian citizen Hardeep Singh Nijjar. Nevertheless, applications and approvals continue robustly. Education consultants like Sumit Jain of Jain Overseas and Sunil Kumar Vashisth from Pyramid e-Services note that they process hundreds of applications each month, with ongoing approval rates above 90%. In many cases, applicants receive their visas quickly—some within just 12 to 20 days, and a few consultancies have reported receiving over 200 approvals in a single day. Stories of determination abound, such as a student finally granted a visa after eight unsuccessful attempts. Not only are students receiving approvals, but their family members, including spouses and parents, are also obtaining visitor and work-related visas at the same pace as before. Recent cases include a spouse visa processed in just 22 days. Consultants credit the smooth visa process to Canada’s inclusive immigration stance and to the established Indian community in Canada. After an initial period of uncertainty, the steady flow of approvals encouraged more students to apply, resulting in a continued high number of issuances, not only for educational but also for visitor, tourist, business, and work purposes. All in all, the high approval rates and persistent application flow highlight that Indian students and their families still have excellent opportunities for studying and living in Canada, despite the ongoing diplomatic challenges.

Google Photos is receiving a new update that gives users more control over when and what kind of slideshows the app creates, addressing the common complaint of unwanted or poorly selected photo reels. Google recently announced on social media that the introduction of the 'Highlight video' feature allows users to quickly generate AI-powered highlight reels from their favorite photos and videos.

To use the Highlight video, open Google Photos on Android or iOS, tap the plus (+) icon at the top of your gallery, and select 'Highlight video' from the menu. Users can then search for specific people, places, or activities they wish to feature, and the app’s AI will automatically pick the best images and video clips. Additionally, the app adds background music and syncs the footage to the music for a polished look.

Users have the option to edit these videos further if they are unsatisfied with the AI’s selections before sharing them. At present, photos that aren’t in a vertical format may appear with black bars in the finished video, although future updates may improve how differently sized images and clips are displayed.

The Memories feature in Google Photos has also been enhanced, enabling users to collaborate with friends and family on creating albums. This uses generative AI to arrange photos and suggest titles for the album.

While automated highlight videos may not always select the perfect moments, Google’s goal is to make photo and video editing easy and accessible for everyone—not just professionals. According to reporting by 9to5Google, the new Highlight video replaces the former movie creator feature, which had limited user control and only included a few preset options.

article_content: Manchester United veteran Ryan Giggs has signed a new one-year contract, extending his career to 21 seasons with the English Premier League leaders. The 37-year-old Welsh midfielder, who aims to help United win a record 19th English league title—his 12th—made his debut for the club in March 1991. He has a club-record 862 first-team appearances and has scored 158 goals, serving as a key figure under manager Alex Ferguson, who signed him on his 14th birthday from Manchester City's youth academy. Ferguson told United's website on Friday, 'You run out of words to describe Ryan Giggs. He is a marvelous player and a wonderful man. To have the desire and the ability to play at the top level in such a physically demanding position at his age requires a special person. He is still turning in man-of-the-match performances, and his experience is vital for the younger players in the squad.' Giggs, a two-time European Champions League winner, remains the only player to score in every season since the Premier League began in 1992. 'All I've ever wanted to do is play for United, and I've been lucky enough to do that for 20 years,' he said after extending his previous one-year deal. 'It's great to know I'm still contributing to the team's success. I feel I've got a lot to offer on and off the pitch. This is an exciting time to be involved, with so many good young players coming through.' Giggs is included in the United squad for Saturday's FA Cup fifth-round match against non-league club Crawley Town, as he seeks to win England's famous knockout competition for the fifth time. Other FA Cup fixtures this weekend include Chelsea vs. Everton, Birmingham vs. Sheffield Wednesday, Stoke vs. Brighton, Arsenal vs. Leyton Orient, Manchester City vs. Notts County, and Fulham vs. Bolton.

article_content: Lian Watson, a 30-year-old former primary school teacher and accomplished horse rider, died after injecting herself with ketamine and other drugs used for animals. Watson had worked at St Patrick’s Catholic Primary School in Heysham, Lancashire, but lost her job after admitting to cocaine use on several occasions, including in front of a parent and a police officer. Following her dismissal, she retrained as a veterinary nurse and began using ketamine, a common horse tranquilliser. The evening before her death, Watson hosted a dinner party at her home in Scotforth, Lancashire, with her veterinarian friend and colleague, Olga Klecandova, and two other guests. One guest described Watson as being in good spirits, though later, she was seen near Klecandova's car acting suspiciously. That night, Watson took veterinary drugs from the boot of Klecandova's car, which she sometimes helped to stock for work. She was found deceased the next morning, with signs of multiple recent injections. At the inquest at Lancaster Magistrates Court, it was reported Watson had previously enrolled in a drug treatment program but discharged herself shortly after. A pathologist concluded that respiratory depression due to combined drug effects caused her death. Coroner Simon Jones ruled her death as misadventure, emphasizing that Watson acted alone and, due to her experience, would have been aware of the risks. Toxicology confirmed the presence of ketamine and other veterinary drugs. Police found no evidence of third-party involvement. Watson was known for her success in the equestrian community, including a third-place finish at the 2008 Horse of the Year show. She was once reprimanded by the General Teaching Council for cocaine use but recognized for her capability and passion as a teacher. After leaving teaching, she worked with animals and participated actively in equestrian events. World Horse Welfare expressed their condolences and thanked her family for donations made in her memory.

article_content: The United States has closed its embassy in Yemen to the public until further notice amid ongoing political unrest following the resignation of the country’s government under pressure from the Houthi rebel movement. The embassy stated that the closure was made 'out of an abundance of caution and care for our employees and others who may be visiting the embassy.' Due to the resignation of Yemen’s president, prime minister, and cabinet, and continuing security concerns, the US embassy in Sanaa is unable to provide routine consular services and can only offer limited assistance in emergencies involving US citizens. A general view of the US embassy compound in Sanaa, Yemen was captured in May 2014. The United States has suspended public operations at the embassy, citing recent attacks on Western interests in Yemen, according to the State Department. On Monday, Yemenis gathered in a rally in Sanaa to protest the occupation of the capital by the Shiite Houthi rebels. The Houthi militia blocked access to Sanaa University as opponents to their takeover called for further demonstrations against their increasing control. US officials recently reduced the number of embassy staff. Last week, President Abd-Rabbu Mansour Hadi’s government collapsed after confrontation with the Iran-aligned Houthi movement. The loss of the Yemeni government deprives Washington of a key ally in efforts against al Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula (AQAP). President Barack Obama stressed on Sunday that operations against al Qaeda in Yemen would continue despite the political upheaval, which saw Hadi and Prime Minister Khalid Bahah resign. Shortly before the embassy closure was announced, a drone strike reportedly killed three suspected al Qaeda members in eastern Yemen. The United States is the only country operating unmanned aircraft in the region. Yemen’s parliament has postponed a session to discuss Hadi’s resignation, raising concerns about a prolonged power vacuum after a Shiite militia kidnapped the president’s chief of staff and seized important buildings in Sanaa. The State Department today warned US citizens of the high security threat in Yemen due to terrorist activities and civil unrest, urging them not to travel to the country and advising those still in Yemen to leave immediately. Protesters in Sanaa have displayed posters featuring President Hadi and Abdul-Malik al-Houthi, the leader of the Shiite rebels, amid continued demonstrations and political uncertainty. The State Department said it is closely monitoring security conditions and will resume consular operations when it is safe to do so. Ongoing unrest has raised fears for Yemen’s stability, especially given its location next to oil-rich Saudi Arabia and key shipping routes. Yemeni authorities previously allowed US operations against al Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula, with Hadi playing a central role in these anti-terror efforts.

article_content: In past years, I've faded quietly from social media. My Instagram's been dormant since December, I barely tweet, and Facebook or Snapchat? Haven't checked them in ages. My profiles look deserted—and it turns out plenty of folks are backing away from social apps, too. For a decade, platforms like Facebook, Instagram, and Twitter brought us together, but chasing endless growth made them feel more like chaotic ad factories than friendly hangouts. Now, more people are ditching public feeds for cozy group chats, swapping performative posting for real conversations with friends and family. Here, there's no pressure to sell myself or share everything. These small circles feel genuine, like a relaxed dinner instead of the public spectacle social media’s become. Meanwhile, newer apps are popping up to recapture what old platforms lost, or to try brand-new ideas around social networking. While these don’t rival the big names in size, they're offering relief from the stress and noise of major networks. Big social companies have shifted away from their original mission of connecting people, according to researcher Ben Grosser at Harvard’s Berkman Klein Center. Now, maximizing engagement and profit is the priority, often at users’ expense. Studies link social media usage to mental health challenges like eating disorders, low self-esteem, and polarization. Social platforms' always-on model isn’t natural; we’re not built for nonstop public interaction. Still, I depend on big platforms for my job as a journalist, needing both an audience and news in real time. My social fatigue partly stems from not knowing where to post—I've hopped from Discord to Bluesky to Threads, only to find none is home. In the past, with Orkut, Facebook, Instagram, and TikTok, there was somewhere to land. Now, it feels like options are scattered. Chand Rajendra-Nicolucci from UMass Amherst observes a shift toward smaller, fragmented online spaces—group chats, niche communities, and apps serving different needs. For work, I hang onto LinkedIn or Twitter/X, but for personal chat, I rely on private threads and Close Friends lists. This patchwork setup works, but sometimes I miss the open community and viral potential of big platforms. Rebecca Rinkevich, at the Institute for Rebooting Social Media, predicts large platforms aren’t disappearing soon—their wide reach is crucial for major issues. But now, with attention split, it's harder to keep meaningful dialogue going. Flipboard’s CEO Mike McCue believes the future lies in combining close, trusted groups with public reach, though no single place can please everyone. New platforms may soon let users keep their identity and friends while chatting across apps—Threads, for example, uses a protocol allowing future interaction with Mastodon, a decentralized network. On Mastodon, private circles and public engagement can coexist, like living in a town: your 'home' is private, but you can wander the neighborhood or join the global town square when you want. These models move away from one-size-fits-all control. Instead, users decide which communities and feeds suit them. Platforms like Threads use ads, while Mastodon relies on donations, letting people pick what works for them. I've tried Mastodon and Bluesky; while the crowds are smaller, conversation quality matches old Twitter. The hard part: the platforms don’t fully connect with each other or reach the old giants' scale yet. Making these networks work together could push big companies to change for the better. Steve Teixeira at Mozilla says social media was at its best when it connected people and delivered useful info—but now it tries too much at once. Splintering these roles could mean better experiences for everyone. Users also need more control. Constant news and content leave many stressed and sleepless. Decentralized social media lets people control their feed, data, and who influences their experience. Activists can reach millions, private people can stay private, and everyone can choose their own algorithm and moderation style. Rather than negotiating with platforms for better features, decentralization gives power back to users and policymakers. Tailored feeds, algorithms for diverse needs, and federated networks might make interactions deeper and less superficial. The ‘Great Social Media Splintering’ is underway, encouraging more thoughtful, healthier online habits and less focus on chasing likes or virality. The next big thing is unknown, so for now, I’m living a fragmented online life like so many others, searching for a better way. -- Shubham Agarwal, freelance technology journalist, Ahmedabad, India

article_content: To encourage safer greetings in regions hit by Ebola, U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Samantha Power introduced the ‘Ebola handshake’ this week—a non-contact gesture where individuals touch elbows—to curb the virus’s spread. She demonstrated this in Monrovia with Liberia’s President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf during a press conference. Ebola only spreads when an infected person starts showing symptoms, and transmission happens through direct contact with bodily fluids like blood, sweat, saliva, vomit, urine, feces, and semen, or contaminated objects. After visiting Liberia, Sierra Leone, and Guinea—countries most affected by the outbreak—Power stressed that although the global response is having an impact, much more support and resources are still needed. She urged other nations to contribute, noting that while some are highly involved, many are not taking enough action. Power also pointed out the social stigma faced by Ebola survivors, mentioning Australia’s visa ban for affected countries and state-level quarantines in the U.S. for returning healthcare workers as examples of ongoing challenges. 'It’s heartbreaking when families can't even be together to comfort each other,' Power remarked. She applauded the effectiveness of new command centers in Liberia and Sierra Leone, which have led to dramatic improvements, such as increasing safe burial rates from 30% to 98% in a few days, and reducing diagnostic test times in remote areas from days to hours. Power said she’s hopeful about the progress so far, promising to deliver that message to the U.S. and the United Nations. She maintains, however, that the fight is far from over and asks countries worldwide to join the response, describing Ebola as a crisis unlike any other the world has seen. During discussions en route to Brussels, Power emphasized sharing and learning from each country’s experiences. While there are early indications of slowed transmission in Liberia, the urgency for prepared medical infrastructure and ongoing vigilance persists. Echoing these concerns, Andy Weber from the U.S. State Department stressed the need to keep building and distributing Ebola Treatment Units to meet both current and future needs. Power concluded that future generations will judge today’s global response to Ebola, comparing its significance to other historic humanitarian emergencies.

Afenifere, the pan-Yoruba socio-political organisation, is split between factions led by Pa Reuben Fasoranti and Pa Ayo Adebanjo. The Adebanjo group recently criticised the Supreme Court's decision to uphold President Bola Tinubu's election, claiming that electoral reforms achieved by technological improvements and significant investment have been undermined.

In a communique from their Secretary General, Chief Sola Ebiseni, the group expressed concern that progress towards credible elections was lost. The Fasoranti-led faction, which supported Tinubu in the February 25 election, opposed this view, stating it did not reflect Afenifere's official position.

Kole Omololu, Organising Secretary for the Fasoranti group, clarified that neither Chief Fasoranti nor other Afenifere leaders were involved in or agreed with the statement issued by the Adebanjo-led group. Omololu described the communique as the action of some Labour Party elements attempting to harm Afenifere's reputation for political reasons.

He emphasized that Chief Fasoranti had officially congratulated Tinubu and shown support after the Supreme Court’s ruling. Omololu acknowledged Adebanjo’s status as acting leader by tradition but urged him to consult Fasoranti on major issues. The statement called for alignment with Afenifere’s official leadership and challenged Chief Ebiseni to provide accurate records of the recent Ogbo Ijebu meeting to support the communique’s claims.

The Fasoranti faction concluded by urging the focus to shift from election disputes to governance, promising to provide constructive feedback and criticism for Nigeria's progress.

article_content: In startup business culture, failure is not just accepted—it’s celebrated as essential for growth. In Finland, this approach is honored annually on October 13 with ‘Failure Day.’ The event was first established at Aalto University in 2010, when members of the entrepreneurship society realized that acknowledging failure was key to success. Historically, a fear of failure in Finnish culture discouraged people from becoming entrepreneurs. Niklas Hamberg, a 20-year-old student and president of the entrepreneurship society at Aalto University, states: ‘We are promoting entrepreneurship, especially among young people, and to do that, we need to destigmatize failure.’ ‘In the past, failure was a significant taboo in Finland—nobody wanted to talk about it,’ he tells Euronews. ‘In the US, the culture is different. Entrepreneurs openly discuss their failures, and having failed is almost a rite of passage to success.’ In the past 15 years, Finland’s startup scene has expanded rapidly. The country now has more than 3,800 startups, valued collectively at €48.2 billion in 2022 (dealroom data). The sector provides close to 30,000 jobs. The capital region has seen a rise in startup hubs, incubators like Startup Sauna, and co-working spaces. Finnish government support, including funding, helps promising startups to scale globally. Investment in Finnish startups grew from €186 million in 2013 to €1.79 billion in 2022. ‘If you aim big, you’re likely to encounter failure along the way—but you shouldn’t be discouraged by it,’ says Hamberg, who ran his first online store selling second-hand clothes in high school in Espoo, Finland’s second-largest city. ‘Failure and mistakes aren’t the same. Failure just means things didn’t go as planned, but you learn from it,’ he explains. While Finland’s entrepreneurs are coming to terms with failure, Hamberg points out that large companies remain cautious. ‘When a small startup fails, it rarely makes the news. But a big company’s failure is headline news, so larger firms are still conservative about acknowledging and celebrating failure.’

article_content: Monday’s cabinet reshuffle was marked by the surprise return of former Prime Minister David Cameron to government. However, he was not the only ex-minister rejoining the cabinet. Esther McVey, who was the work and pensions secretary in 2018, has also taken on a ministerial role. Officially, McVey has been appointed minister without portfolio in the Cabinet Office. Unofficially, she has been dubbed the “minister for common sense.” Ms McVey was born in Liverpool in 1967 and, shortly after birth, was placed in a Barnardo’s foster home by her young parents who could not afford to care for her. She remained in the charity’s care for her first two years before returning to her parents. Speaking on the Political Thinking with Nick Robinson podcast, she expressed no resentment towards her family for their decision, describing it as an act of love. She attended a private girls’ school, where she became head girl. Faced with a choice between ballet and law school, she chose law, but while working as a waitress in a London restaurant, she decided to become a TV presenter. In her media career, she worked on a range of programmes, including a Channel 5 documentary about naturists, BBC One’s Heaven and Earth Show, and ITV’s breakfast show GMTV. In the early 2000s, she began her political career and won the Wirral West seat for the Conservatives in 2010. She served as a minister in David Cameron’s government and was criticized for implementing benefits cuts. She lost her seat in 2015, returned to Parliament in 2017 as MP for Tatton, and later became work and pensions secretary under Theresa May. Ms McVey has openly discussed her political ambitions, telling ITV’s Loose Women she would like to be prime minister and ran for Conservative leader in 2019. After leaving Boris Johnson’s ministerial team in 2020, she co-hosted a show on GB News with her husband, Conservative MP Philip Davies. Earlier this year, Ofcom ruled their show breached impartiality rules when they interviewed Chancellor Jeremy Hunt. Following her return to government, McVey is expected to step down from her TV role. Her appointment was among the last announced on Monday and is viewed as an effort to appease right-leaning Conservative MPs concerned by Lord Cameron’s return and Suella Braverman’s dismissal. The government has not detailed her new responsibilities, but Downing Street is expected to provide more information soon. Conservative Party chair Richard Holden suggested her role could include issues like freedom of speech on university campuses, describing McVey as a ‘plain-speaking northerner’ who would be a valued addition to the cabinet. Other former ministers rejoining the government include Andrea Leadsom and Damian Hinds. Dame Andrea, who has held senior roles under Cameron, May, and Johnson and ran for Conservative leader in 2016, becomes a junior health minister. Mr Hinds, a former education secretary, returns as minister of state after a stint at the Ministry of Justice.

Ramjit is candid about his health and the curiosity it draws from others, mentioning that neighbors often inquire about the secret to his longevity, which he attributes simply to his healthy lifestyle and outlook. He views fatherhood late in life as a special blessing and sees it as a way to carry forward his family's legacy.

article_content: Rescue operations to save 41 workers trapped in the Silkyara tunnel in Uttarakhand are back on track following repairs to the 25-tonne platform carrying the auger drilling machine. The machine had been stopped after cracks were discovered during the drilling process, but authorities have confirmed it is now fixed and operational. An official noted that the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) will first scan beyond the 46.8 meters already cleared—out of a total of 55 meters of debris—using special equipment before resuming horizontal drilling. Pipes already placed in the cleared passage will help create an escape route, allowing the trapped workers to crawl to safety. Authorities stress there are no guaranteed timelines, but if no further problems arise, the workers could be rescued as early as Saturday afternoon. This is the 13th day since the tunnel collapsed on November 12, trapping workers inside a finished and reinforced segment of the tunnel.

One official explain say DRDO aguh use special device fi scan over di 46.8 meter dem clear out already, from a total a 55 meter a debris, before dem dig more. Pipe weh dem put in di space ago make a escape way fi di worka dem crawl out. article_content: Following recent critical and commercial disappointments, Variety reports that Marvel Studios is considering featuring the six original Avengers in an upcoming film. This would mean the Marvel Cinematic Universe might bring back Tony Stark and Natasha Romanoff, both of whom died in Avengers: Endgame. Bringing back dead characters has long been a trend in comic books, and now it appears in the films as well. However, reviving Tony and Natasha, who ended their stories on such a high note, might diminish the impact of their sacrifices. If the MCU reunites the Avengers, it should use the opportunity effectively. For example, Tony Stark acted as a mentor to Peter Parker, providing him with wisdom and advanced suits. Since Tony’s death in Endgame, Peter has matured and established himself as a humble, street-level hero independent of Stark’s technology. It would be touching for Tony to see Peter’s growth, especially since he’s one of the few who remembers Peter after the memory wipe in Spider-Man: No Way Home. Fans were thrilled when Captain America wielded Thor’s hammer to fight Thanos. Seeing Cap use Mjölnir again, possibly against a powerful villain like Kang, could be a cinematic highlight. If Kang is as dangerous as rumored, Cap will need every advantage. Natasha and Yelena’s bond was highlighted in Black Widow after years apart. While Yelena grieves Natasha’s sacrifice in Endgame, Natasha’s potential revival could give the sisters an emotional reunion they missed, showing how Yelena has grown as a hero. Thor has already lost Loki to Thanos, but an alternate version, introduced in Endgame and developed in the Loki series, has matured significantly. If Thor and the Avengers reunite, reconnecting with this version of Loki could give both brothers some closure. Seeing the original six Avengers return to the big screen would be exciting, but the team broke up for reasons. Actors like Robert Downey Jr., Chris Evans, and Scarlett Johansson invested years in these roles and seemed satisfied moving on. Returning for too long might be a step back for them. Rumors suggest that Secret Wars may softly reboot the MCU. If this happens, the reunion could serve as a farewell before a fresh lineup of actors takes over in the franchise’s new timeline.

article_content: Ryanair, despite efforts to improve its public image and customer service, has been ranked the least client-friendly airline according to a new survey by Spanish consumer group Reclamador.es. The survey evaluated how airlines respond to customer complaints, with Ryanair being criticized for failing to resolve complaints amicably and often requiring legal action but typically settling out of court before any judgment. Passengers commonly report issues with Ryanair’s ticket surcharges and lack of support during flight delays. The airline is also said to deny passengers meals and refreshments during delays exceeding two hours in most cases. Ryanair imposes a surcharge of €2.50 (about £2) per ticket each way to fund potential compensation for delays. Ryanair responded, stating: 'This survey, conducted by a Spanish claims website, lacks merit since Ryanair’s passenger numbers continue to rise, expected to reach 90 million this year.' The survey also placed British Airways, Lufthansa, Air France, Finnair, and Alitalia in joint sixth place, noting similar policies in handling complaints. Reclamador.es stated these airlines generally do not mediate and often reply to travellers by denying compensation without detailed explanation. Iberia, Spain’s national carrier and part of International Airlines Group after merging with British Airways, ranked as the third least client-friendly airline. The report accuses Iberia of making the complaints process excessively bureaucratic, requiring handwritten forms, identity documents, tickets, and additional paperwork before responding to customers. Reclamador.es further criticized Iberia for providing ambiguous standard responses to different customers on the same flight and for often settling claims just before court hearings. These practices, the report says, lead to delayed payments to travellers and add strain to the Spanish legal system, reflecting a lack of respect for passengers.

In Australia, buying a first home is getting harder as property prices keep rising. Many young Australians now rely on their parents to help with deposits. John Symonds, who started Aussie Home Loans, says the iconic goal of owning a home is slipping away for many, which he finds troubling for the nation’s sense of identity.

Research by ING Direct reveals that four in five parents are willing to help their children financially when buying a home, and almost half of them would even change their lifestyle or let their adult children stay at home longer to assist with saving for a deposit.

Compared to the past, this help from parents has shot up; only a small portion did so a decade ago, and it was rare twenty years back. Now, a third of first-home buyers get such assistance, with parents collectively contributing $122 million each year.

Experts point out that gifting cash is now more common than using their own home equity, since it’s a simpler solution if the mortgage can’t be paid or if there’s a divorce. This kind of support jumped by 15% over the past year.

To make homeownership more achievable, a law proposed by Senator Nick Xenophon would let first-time buyers borrow up to $25,000 from their superannuation for a deposit, which they’d pay back over 15 years.

article_content: An increasing number of new mothers are reporting 'mummy's thumb,' also called de Quervain's tenosynovitis—a painful inflammation of the thumb tendons brought on by repetitive lifting and gripping. Sammy Margo, a chartered physiotherapist, observes that many women today lead less physically active lives, possibly making them less prepared for the physical demands of infant care. After childbirth, relaxin hormone makes ligaments and tendons more flexible, especially while breastfeeding, which can add to the risk. Margo estimates that new mothers lift their babies around 25 to 30 times daily. Such repetitive motion, combined with softer ligaments, can aggravate thumb tendons, causing pain when turning the wrist or gripping objects. While in the past, daily chores often helped maintain strength, modern conveniences may reduce such incidental conditioning. Many mothers look up their symptoms online and only seek treatment when pain becomes severe, turning to physiotherapy or using hand splints as needed. De Quervain's tenosynovitis is particularly prevalent among women aged 30 to 50 and is associated with repeated hand tasks like baby care, gardening, or texting. Prevention strategies include strengthening exercises before pregnancy and using supportive aids, such as feeding pillows, to limit lifting strain. Symptoms often subside after breastfeeding ends and tissue firmness returns, but more persistent cases may require ongoing therapy. The Mayo Clinic notes that women, especially those who are pregnant or engaged in frequent hand movements, have a higher risk for this condition, with chronic overuse as a key contributor.

Microsoft is working on technology that could turn your living room into a futuristic, Star Trek-style 'Holodeck.' A recently published patent application reveals Microsoft's vision for future game consoles: projecting gameplay onto your room’s walls to create an immersive experience that goes beyond the TV screen.

The technology would use Microsoft’s Kinect sensor—which currently lets players control games with body movements—to map the room and identify where you are. Multiple projectors would then overlay a 3D video game environment throughout your living space. This means the entire room, including furniture and plants, could become part of the game, letting you hunt aliens or join virtual Westerns right at home.

Patently Apple reported spotting the patent application. It shows that Kinect could also recognize and adapt to furniture—either incorporating it into the game or hiding it with video projection. The idea is that players could turn around in their own living room and potentially see in-game enemies behind them.

Kinect has already been a big success for Microsoft, allowing players to use their bodies—like pulling a virtual bow or dancing—instead of controllers. The new system would combine projectors and Kinect’s depth-sensing technology to track movement and bring those actions into the game world.

It’s unknown how far along this technology is. The patent was filed early last year and published last month by the Patent and Trademark Office. Jack Purcher of Patently Apple commented that gaming made a dramatic leap when it switched from CRT to HDTV, and he is excited about the idea of games immersing players by projecting environments onto all four walls—a potential breakthrough for gaming experiences.

article_content: Frank Borman, the renowned astronaut who commanded Apollo 8—the first mission to orbit the moon—has died at age 95 in Billings, Montana, according to NASA. Launched on December 21, 1968, Apollo 8, with crew members James Lovell and William Anders, spent three days flying to the moon, orbited it ten times on Christmas Eve and Christmas Day, and provided the world with the unforgettable 'Earthrise' photo. The mission was a crucial step leading to the 1969 lunar landing. Borman, Lovell, and Anders were the first humans to witness Earth as a distant sphere in space. During a live Christmas Eve telecast from lunar orbit, the crew read from the Book of Genesis—a historic moment watched by millions. Borman closed the broadcast by wishing the world 'Good night, good luck, a Merry Christmas, and God bless all of you—on the good Earth.' Prior to Apollo, Borman and Lovell also flew together on the Gemini 7 mission in 1965, achieving the first space orbital rendezvous with Gemini 6. Borman later described Gemini as cramped compared to the more spacious Apollo module. Initially, Apollo 8 was planned to orbit Earth. However, after the success of Apollo 7 in October 1968, NASA took the bold step to attempt a lunar mission to outpace the Soviet Union in the space race. Borman noted that his main concern was beating the Russians and returning safely. After retiring from NASA, Borman became president, CEO, and later chairman of Eastern Airlines during a turbulent era of rising fuel costs and industry deregulation, leading to increased challenges for the airline. He stepped down in 1986 and later settled in New Mexico. Borman’s passion for flight began in his teens, flying solo at age 15 after saving money from part-time jobs. He continued flying well into his 90s. Born in Gary, Indiana, and raised in Tucson, Arizona, Borman was a West Point graduate and served as a US Air Force pilot and instructor. He later earned a master's degree in aeronautical engineering from Caltech. In 1962, he was selected for NASA's astronaut program and later received the Congressional Space Medal of Honor from President Jimmy Carter. In retirement, Borman ran a cattle ranch in Montana with his son Fred. He is survived by his two sons, Fred and Edwin, and their families. His wife, Susan Bugbee Borman, passed away in 2021. NASA Administrator Bill Nelson described Borman as 'a true American hero' whose dedication to aviation and exploration was matched only by his devotion to his family.

article_content: In a striking new series of fashion photographs, models dressed in couture appear dazed and ethereal, floating upside down in streets and shops across the Far East. The images, shot by Montréal-based photographer Martin Tremblay—also known as Le Pinch—for the British fashion magazine Schön!, blend reality with surreal settings to create a curious, inverted world. Tremblay revealed that the gravity-defying images were created using a combination of studio props and digital editing. 'First, I photographed multiple backgrounds using flashes,' explains Tremblay, 44. 'We then shot the models in the studio using a trampoline to match the chosen images. I also made a cardboard ceiling to flatten the models' hair, and later photographed the shoes. Everything was composited together in Photoshop.' Despite appearing weightless, the models maintain elegance as the surreal setups in the East Asian urban environment complement the high-fashion looks. Tremblay experiments with reality by creating unusual hairstyles and using props, even including pets, to enhance the optical illusion. 'I simply wanted to do something different by connecting two opposite worlds,' says Tremblay. 'As one woman experiences the world we know, someone else is facing something at the exact opposite end of the globe.' Tremblay, a professional photographer for over 20 years, originally pitched the concept to Schön! magazine, which commissioned the project now called 'Fortune Cookie'. The series has received widespread acclaim. The project took two years of research and required 160 hours of retouching. Tremblay and his creative team aimed for impeccable, timeless execution in every detail. 'It was my idea. My motivation was to design a non-traditional fashion shoot,' Tremblay stated. Tremblay made a drastic career change to pursue photography, having previously worked as an underground miner in northern Quebec. He now primarily shoots advertising campaigns, corporate projects, and art. 'I'm a perfectionist, and light is essential to my work. I find it fascinating to construct different worlds,' he says. 'Even if my images are often surreal, I always strive for truth and the highest standards in design and detail.' For the shoot, Tremblay chose clothing from Givenchy, Marie Saint Pierre, and Dolce & Gabbana for models Bayan and Cat, styled by Pascal & Jérémie. Image retouching was performed with the help of Visual Box. Founded in 2009, Schön! began as an online platform to showcase international creative talent in fashion, art, and illustration. It has since evolved into a luxurious print magazine distributed in 43 countries, including the USA and much of Europe.

article_content: The attack on Israel on October 7 left the nation reeling, with community trauma and urgent humanitarian needs arising almost immediately. In response, Israelis banded together—civil groups and tech companies alike—organizing relief efforts to supply essentials like food, medical aid, and supplies, and mobilizing volunteers to help communities along the border. Much of this response centers on children deeply affected by the violence, many of whom lost parents or are still uncertain about their families’ fate. Experts and organizers argue that immediate access to emotional, psychological support and the restoration of daily routines are essential for these children’s recovery. Recognizing these needs, organizations Sheatufim and Zionism 2000 created 'Resilience for Our Children (Yeladenu)', a large-scale emergency operation. Acting with urgency, the initiative delivers ongoing care and therapy to over 10,000 children aged 6-18 impacted by recent trauma. Ronny Douek, leading both groups, has stressed that supporting children’s resilience is key to securing a positive future for the country. As the conflict continues, the program adapts to emerging challenges, providing parents peace of mind that their children are being supported and cared for, which in turn helps stabilize entire families. Rapid action has already delivered tangible results: resilience centers with tents, group classrooms, and therapy rooms have been constructed to host group activities, counseling sessions, and safe spaces for recreation. Commitment from top professionals ensures ongoing stability and care for these children. The initiative builds partnerships with trauma organizations, government agencies, and youth movements. Technology plays a key role, with companies like Monday.com, Google, and Palo Alto Networks helping manage the complex logistics involved in supporting traumatized children. Funding is a collaborative effort, with donations from local and international benefactors, civil organizations, and tech businesses. However, an extra NIS 20 million is needed for ongoing work throughout the next year. Prominent voices, including President Isaac Herzog and former US Ambassador Thomas Nides, have recognized the resilience and quick action of Israeli civil society, emphasizing the significance of caring for children’s well-being as the cornerstone of a healthier, more united nation. The leaders behind these efforts remain focused on rapid, inclusive support, determined to prioritize vulnerable children as Israel works to recover and rebuild.

article_content: Kanye West is making public apologies to fellow artists Beck and Bruno Mars. In a series of tweets, West reached out to both musicians to express regret for his past criticism. “I would like to publicly apologize to Beck. I’m sorry, Beck,” West tweeted Thursday night. West previously attracted negative attention when he briefly stepped on stage after Beck won the Grammy Award for Album of the Year, later claiming in an interview that Beck should “respect artistry” and give the award to Beyonce. Although West did not interrupt Beck directly, the behavior was reminiscent of his 2009 MTV Video Music Awards outburst, when he interrupted Taylor Swift and stated on stage that Beyonce deserved the award. Since then, West and Swift have reconciled, sharing a hug at this month's Grammys. On Thursday, West also addressed Bruno Mars, tweeting, “I used to hate on him but I really respect what he does as an artist.” West even invited Bruno Mars to sing on a track he co-produced. As of now, neither Beck nor Bruno Mars has responded publicly to West’s statements.

A 14-year-old autistic Michigan girl, Isabelle Stapleton, is recovering after authorities say her mother tried to poison her with carbon monoxide in an apparent murder-suicide attempt. According to Benzie County prosecuting attorney Sara Swanson, Isabelle is now awake and responding after spending time in critical care for carbon monoxide poisoning following the incident last week. Swanson reported that Isabelle’s condition has improved each day since the weekend.

On the evening of September 3, police found both Isabelle and her mother, Kelli Stapleton, unconscious in their locked vehicle in a wooded area, as confirmed by Michigan State Police Sgt. Malcolm Irwin. Officers discovered two charcoal grills burning inside the car, producing dangerous carbon monoxide levels. Earlier that day, Matt Stapleton, Isabelle's father, contacted the police after noticing that neither Isabelle nor her mother had been seen all day.

Isabelle was taken to DeVos Children’s Hospital in Grand Rapids, Michigan, where she opened her eyes over the weekend. Kelli was arrested after receiving medical clearance and was arraigned on Thursday, facing a charge of attempted murder. She is currently being held without bail and is scheduled for a preliminary court examination on September 16 to determine if there is enough evidence to proceed with the charges. 

Kelli maintained a blog called “The Status Woe,” where she expressed feeling 'a severe case of battle fatigue' surrounding her daughter’s autism treatment on the day of the incident. Her attorney, Anthony Cicchelli, declined to comment. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, an estimated one in 88 children is diagnosed with an autism spectrum disorder.

Dr. Naeem Dalal, Advisor on Non-communicable Diseases, Injuries, and Mental Health for Africa CDC, emphasized the urgent need to challenge cultural stereotypes that deter African men from seeking emotional and mental health support. Speaking to the News Agency of Nigeria during a youth mental health session at the International Conference on Public Health in Africa (CPHIA 2023) in Lusaka, Zambia, Dr. Dalal noted that societal expectations often discourage men from expressing vulnerability, resulting in fewer men accessing mental health services.

According to Dr. Dalal, statistical evidence shows that suicide rates are higher among men across Africa. This is mainly because men tend to use more lethal means and are less likely to seek help. He made a distinction between active suicide—which involves taking action leading to death—and passive suicide, characterized by suicidal thoughts or self-harm ideation that are not acted upon.

He explained that, in many African societies, men are expected to be strong, supportive, and to act as breadwinners, making it culturally difficult for them to seek help for mental health concerns. These attitudes are often taught from childhood, with boys encouraged to be ‘strong and responsible’, further contributing to the reluctance to access mental health care.

Dr. Dalal outlined Africa CDC’s ongoing initiatives, which include a strategy for non-communicable diseases, injuries, and mental health. The approach features programs focused on mental health advocacy, especially for men. Efforts are also being made to train more healthcare workers in mental health and to expand mental health fellowships, as there is limited interest among healthcare professionals to specialize in this field.

He observed that suicide is the third leading cause of death among people aged 15 to 29 in Africa, highlighting the importance of advocacy among younger generations. Africa CDC, in partnership with the African Union, is also working on policy reforms to make mental health care more relevant to current conditions.

Dr. Dalal commended Nigeria for recently passing a new mental health bill. The CPHIA 2023, held from November 27 to 30 in Lusaka and organized by Africa CDC with support from the Zambian government, was themed ‘Breaking Barriers: Repositioning Africa in the Global Health Architecture.’

Restoring global forests could sequester 22 times the amount of carbon the world emits in a year, new research shows. The study says forest restoration—where forests would naturally grow if not for human activity—could remove about 226 gigatonnes of excess carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, about a third of CO2 released since the industrial revolution.

Lead author Thomas Crowther (ETH Zurich) and over 200 researchers stress that planting trees must complement, not replace, cutting fossil fuel use. Their paper, published in Nature, updates a 2019 study that was criticized for overestimating tree restoration’s potential. Crowther argues that it’s counterproductive to use forests to offset new emissions—since more emissions will worsen climate change and harm forests’ ability to absorb carbon.

Crowther adds, “Relying on tree-planting as offsets is now at odds with the science.” He plans to share this view at the COP28 climate summit in Dubai, emphasizing the need to reject ‘greenwashing.’

The earlier 2019 paper inspired initiatives like the World Economic Forum’s Trillion Trees project, but also sparked criticism for inflating potential carbon sequestration—critics include Joseph Veldman (Texas A&M), Nicola Stevens (Oxford), and Greta Thunberg. Veldman still believes the latest estimate may be double the realistic figure, citing inclusion of unsuitable regions like savannas. “It’s the absolute upper limit—unlikely and unfeasible,” he says.

The authors underscore that forest restoration should be diverse (not monoculture) and tailored to local communities’ needs. Cristina Banks-Leite (Imperial College London) cites these debates as valuable teaching tools for understanding the difficulties of global-scale environmental estimates, noting they can improve with better technology.

The updated study also finds that protecting standing forests and allowing degraded woods to recover accounts for most of the carbon sequestration (61%), whereas only 39% comes from planting in bare areas. "The crucial message—that we must protect existing forests—is absolutely correct," says Stevens.

article_content: Amelia’s parents are contesting a hospital ethics committee’s decision that would permit doctors to stop her breathing support—an action that could end her life. Amelia, diagnosed with the rare, terminal disorder PCH1B last December, was initially expected to live only a year. Accordingly, doctors and her parents created an end-of-life care plan stating she wouldn’t be given intensive interventions if her condition worsened. Now almost two, Amelia has shown unexpected stability and progress. Observing this, her parents, Shelley Beilby and Robert Dainton, feel the prior restrictions on her treatment should be reconsidered. They argue that because Amelia is more aware and interactive than expected, she deserves every chance at additional care, especially if something minor, like a cold, threatens her. A recent event saw Amelia admitted to the ICU after she stopped breathing, which prompted a compromise in the care plan—ICU intervention may be considered in some situations. Despite this, the core ethics committee ruling stands. The family awaits a formal written decision, while legal action remains an option. A spokesperson for Alder Hey Hospital reiterated that all care decisions are made collaboratively with families and, if disagreements continue, can be determined in court. The hospital highlighted the compassion and difficulty present in such cases, emphasizing the commitment to the child’s comfort. The family remains determined to advocate for more supportive care, hoping Amelia’s improvements will influence the final outcome.

article_content: The foreign ministers of South Korea, China, and Japan convened in Busan, South Korea on Sunday, aiming to revive cooperation among the three Asian neighbors and pave the way for a future trilateral summit. Since 2008, the three countries had agreed to hold annual summits to strengthen diplomatic and economic ties, but these have stalled since 2019 due to bilateral disputes and the COVID-19 pandemic. This weekend's meeting marked the first such gathering since 2019. In September, senior officials from all three countries agreed to arrange a trilateral summit at the earliest convenient time. As part of the renewed engagement, South Korean Foreign Minister Park Jin held separate meetings on Sunday with his Japanese counterpart, Yoko Kamikawa, and China's Wang Yi. Park and Kamikawa strongly condemned North Korea's recent launch of its first spy satellite and agreed to enhance their response to arms transactions between Pyongyang and Moscow, according to a statement from South Korea's foreign ministry. However, lingering historical tensions surfaced during the talks. Kamikawa criticized a South Korean court order requiring Japan to compensate women forced to work in wartime Japanese military brothels, calling it 'extremely regrettable' and urging the South Korean government to take appropriate action, Japan's Kyodo news agency reported. On Saturday, Kamikawa also met with Wang, expressing hope for renewed security dialogue between Tokyo and Beijing 'in the near future.' Wang emphasized the need for both sides to avoid posing threats to each other and to respect each other's legitimate concerns, according to China's foreign ministry. South Korean President Yoon Suk Yeol and Japanese Prime Minister Fumio Kishida have recently taken steps to repair their countries' strained relations, most notably participating in a historic trilateral summit with US President Joe Biden in August. In July, Wang cautioned that US efforts to strengthen ties with Seoul and Tokyo could raise regional tensions and confrontation, reflecting lingering unease in Beijing about closer US-South Korea-Japan cooperation.
