article_content: Retail businesses and shoppers are heading into the holiday season amid economic turbulence similar to that seen before the 2008 Great Recession. High interest rates, rising credit card debt, weaker job growth, and stagnating income are casting doubt on what was once the most lucrative time for retailers. The National Retail Federation (NRF) expects holiday retail sales to rise between 3% and 4% in November and December 2023—a slower pace compared to past years, and reflecting a more conservative outlook after last year's overoptimistic forecasts. NRF president Matthew Shay says consumers have been resilient, but mounting financial pressures could turn this into the last strong holiday for a while. Comparisons to 2007 abound: that year’s softer forecast was followed by positive sales, but hidden economic stress worsened. This year, consumers are struggling with steep interest rates keeping home purchases out of reach and a record $1 trillion in credit card debt as reported by the New York Fed. Close to 60% now worry about accessing more credit, and nearly 14% fear job loss in the coming year, as job growth slows and unemployment ticks upward. Higher inflation and escalating conflicts in places like Ukraine and the Middle East cloud the outlook further. While inflation is lower than last year’s surge, prices are still notably higher than a couple years ago. NRF chief economist Jack Kleinhenz suggests that, despite many economic headwinds, resilient consumer spending could keep sales positive. He cites the Personal Consumption Expenditure (PCE) index as moderating fears about rising retail prices, although this doesn't fully address how inflation strains overall household budgets. Retail spending gains appear to be slowing, but may not disappear entirely. Other analyses point to changing consumer habits. Deloitte foresees a 9% rise in gift spending, but at a total below NRF estimates. Accenture, meanwhile, expects Americans to cut back on spending, focus on simpler celebrations, and delay shopping. Many are shifting to practical gifts or making presents by hand. Surveys reveal broad unease: the Conference Board’s data shows consumer confidence falling for the third straight month, with concerns mounting about increased prices, the political climate, and international instability. NRF executives remain hopeful that holiday sales growth will materialize, but acknowledge the risks for 2024. As in 2007, seemingly positive trends ahead of the holidays may mask deeper problems that could worsen after the new year.

article_content: Three Filipino fishermen died after their fishing boat was struck by an unidentified foreign commercial vessel and sank in the South China Sea, according to the Philippine Coast Guard. The incident occurred on Monday while the vessel was 85 nautical miles (157 km) northwest of the disputed Scarborough Shoal. Some crew members survived the accident. President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has promised a thorough investigation, stating, “We assure the victims, their families, and everyone that we will exert every effort to hold accountable those who are responsible for this unfortunate maritime incident.” The coast guard reported that the incident is still under investigation to determine the details and circumstances surrounding the collision. Based on preliminary accounts from survivors and vessel monitoring data, the coast guard suspects that a crude oil tanker registered under the Marshall Islands may have been involved. Efforts are underway to locate the vessel and its crew. Tensions have recently risen in the South China Sea after the Philippines removed a 300-metre-long barrier set up by China’s Coast Guard near Scarborough Shoal, a significant fishing area and a highly contested maritime feature. Scarborough Shoal, named after a British ship that ran aground there in the 18th century, was seized by China in 2012. Chinese coast guard and fishing vessels have maintained a presence at the site since. Meanwhile, the United States and the Philippines have begun their annual “Samasama” (Tagalog for “Together”) joint naval exercises, involving over a thousand sailors. The drills include anti-submarine, surface, and electronic warfare activities off Manila and southern Luzon. US Seventh Fleet Vice Admiral Karl Thomas emphasized at the opening ceremony the importance of all nations protecting their sovereignty on the high seas, stating, “There’s no better way to ensure sovereignty and security than to sail and to operate together.”

article_content: Australian Foreign Minister Penny Wong stated on Tuesday that China continues to modernize its military on an unprecedented scale, with limited transparency. She emphasized that Australia's partnership with India is vital for maintaining the strategic balance of power in the region. Speaking at an event at Lady Shri Ram College at Delhi University, Wong reaffirmed Australia's strong commitment to partnerships like the Quad, which aim to ensure sovereignty and territorial integrity in the Indo-Pacific. "China continues to modernize its military at a pace and scale not seen globally in nearly a century, and with little transparency. North Korea persists in destabilizing activities through its nuclear weapons program and frequent ballistic missile launches," Wong noted during her discussion with students. Wong called for regional partnerships to create a free and open Indo-Pacific, rooted in sovereignty and not dominated by any single power. She added that collaboration with India is critical because it supports the strategic balance of the area, and Australia encourages mutual strategic reassurance and military risk reduction measures. Earlier on Tuesday, Wong met with her Indian counterpart S Jaishankar for the Foreign Ministers' Framework Dialogue in New Delhi. On Monday, the India-Australia 2+2 Ministerial Dialogue took place, with Jaishankar and Defence Minister Rajnath Singh meeting their Australian counterparts, Penny Wong and Defence Minister Richard Marles. Separately, India's income tax department discovered nearly ₹10,000 crore in tax evasion over three years by online retailers selling products via platforms like Instagram and Facebook. Intimation notices have been sent to 45 brands, with more expected. Amid increased scrutiny, Indian businesses are prioritizing GST compliance and considering tax liabilities before finalizing mergers, acquisitions, and other business deals. In other news, Raymond managing director Gautam Singhania's estranged wife, Nawaz Modi, has accused Singhania of assaulting her and their daughter two months ago during a reported outburst.

article_content: According to the Air Quality Early Warning System (EWS) for Delhi, air quality is forecasted to remain in the 'very poor' category until at least November 4, with similar conditions expected for the following six days. Meteorological conditions are not expected to change over the next two days, which suggests that air quality in north-west India will likely stay in the 'severe' category, primarily due to increasing incidents of farm fires. This sudden drop to 'severe' levels was not anticipated. Experts cite low temperatures, calm winds, and a reduced mixing layer height as contributing factors to the accumulation of pollution. Mostly calm winds were observed at night, and during the day, wind speeds were as low as 4 kmph, hindering the dispersal of pollutants. The EWS bulletin on Thursday continued to predict 'very poor' air quality until November 5, with the possibility of conditions worsening to 'severe' in the subsequent days, as reported by TOI. In Safdarjung, mainly easterly winds were observed on Thursday, while Palam experienced north-westerly winds. Experts noted that pollutants accumulated because of winds blowing from opposite directions. Visibility dropped to 500 meters in Safdarjung at 7 am and 1,000 meters in Palam. Visibility remained poor throughout the day. At 12:30 pm, the meteorological department described conditions as 'smoke.' Kuldeep Srivastava, head of the Regional Weather Forecasting Centre at IMD, told TOI that visibility was 700 meters at Safdarjung and 1,000 meters in Palam around 3 pm. article_content: Action movies are infamous for high body counts, but filmmakers often keep audiences at arm’s length from the true gruesomeness of these deaths. This distance helps make action films thrilling, but not emotionally draining. Occasionally, however, certain directors shatter that comfort zone, creating deaths so intense that they stick with you long after the credits roll. Here are seven particularly unforgettable deaths from acclaimed action films—moments that are both shocking and deeply impactful. ‘Mad Max: Fury Road’ (2015) offers a standout example, with Immortan Joe’s end. As Furiosa yanks off his breathing mask in their final confrontation, the horrific implication and raw violence create some of the movie’s most memorable scenes. In ‘Raiders of the Lost Ark,’ the danger of the Ark proves real. When Indiana and Marion avert their eyes, the Nazis meet a gruesome fate as their faces melt—a scene that’s still unnerving decades later. ‘John Wick: Chapter 2’ raises the bar for inventive action sequences. With only a pencil, John Wick fatally stabs two attackers—dispatching one through the ear and pinning the other—making this scene especially brutal. ‘Blade Runner’ isn't saturated with violence, but its darkest scene arrives when Roy Batty kills Eldon Tyrell by crushing his skull. The personal confrontation is both horrifying and unforgettable. In ‘Kill Bill,’ Elle Driver faces one of Tarantino’s most harrowing fates: after Beatrix Kiddo gouges out her last eye, Elle is left locked in with a snake, plunging her into terror and blindness. ‘The Mummy’ starts on a grim note as Imhotep, the titular character, has his tongue cut out before being mummified alive and consumed by beetles—a surprisingly graphic sequence in an otherwise adventurous film. Finally, ‘Logan’ delivers one of superhero cinema's most powerful endings. Logan’s impalement and slow death is gut-wrenching yet brings his journey to a fitting and memorable close.

article_content: Katie and Roy Marks, a couple from Milton Keynes, Buckinghamshire, lost a combined 13 stone by learning to cook healthier versions of their favorite takeaways at home. Their transformation began after realizing most of their meals came from fast food outlets or microwave dinners. At the start, Katie, 30, weighed more than 22 stone and Roy was 23 stone. Together, they started preparing home-cooked meals—like kebabs—which led to a significant lifestyle change as they now cook together each night and stick to a healthier diet. Before this, they ordered at least two large takeaway meals per week and relied heavily on processed foods. Katie’s weight once reached 22 stone and she wore a size 26. She admits they initially lacked cooking skills, finding it embarrassing. The couple’s first attempt at a home-cooked meal—a kebab with homemade chips—was a pleasant surprise and became a favorite. Working as a team, they motivated each other, turning daily cooking into a shared activity and supporting one another through challenges. Katie was particularly motivated by her struggle to get pregnant; doctors told her that weight was affecting her fertility. After being diagnosed with polycystic ovary syndrome, and experiencing several miscarriages and an ectopic pregnancy, she learned IVF was possible only if she reduced her BMI to under 30, while Roy’s needed to be under 35. Having worn a size 24 dress at their 2007 wedding, Katie hadn’t previously worried about her weight. But fertility issues signaled a shift. At first, Katie tried to lose weight at home, managing to shed just 2.5 stone in two years. Frustrated, she joined Slimming World and shared tips with Roy. A main focus was learning to create healthy meals themselves. Previously, their typical day included no breakfast, frequent crisps, sweets, and chocolate as snacks, sandwiches made with lots of bread and cheese, and nightly takeaways. Now, their meals incorporate yogurt and fruit for breakfast, nutritious lunches, whole-food snacks, and dinners like grilled chicken with vegetables. At first, neither Katie nor Roy had cooking experience, making the change difficult, but they soon discovered a love for preparing meals together. Katie lost over five and a half stone and dropped to a size 12 in just a year, while Roy lost five stone as well. Shared dog walks and evening meals have fostered new healthy habits and strengthened their relationship. Their new mindset avoids strict food bans; instead, they practice moderation—with Slimming World’s plan allowing some favorite foods without guilt. Feeling healthier and happier, Katie now runs her own Slimming World class at Old Stratford Community Hall. With their BMI goals met, the couple is ready to start IVF treatment and hope to begin their family soon.

article_content: Various people worldwide shared their views on the Beijing Olympics. Many commended the event's scale, organization, and the enthusiasm shown by both the public and organizers. For example, Laurentius Metaal praised the International Olympic Committee's decision to hold the games in Beijing, seeing its outcome as successful despite initial criticism. However, concerns were raised about China's significant spending on the Olympics in light of persistent poverty. Other critiques included alleged manipulation of gymnast ages, edited performances during ceremonies, and suppression of protests. John from Jakarta argued that awarding the games to China was a mistake, highlighting reports of human rights violations and underreported forced relocations. Some, like Wallace Rhodes, viewed these Olympics as among the best, commending China's organization and hoping the event's success would positively influence the country. There were also ideas for improving medal tracking by assigning point values to gold, silver, and bronze medals. Dan Ingram pointed out that China's large population and government control played roles in the event's success, speculating about different outcomes with less centralized management. Joel Shattles praised the artistic achievements but called for more independence for athletes. Specific issues, such as controversy over gymnasts' ages, were cited with references to documentaries, raising concerns that some regulations may have been disregarded for competitive advantage. The event faced criticism for heavy commercialization and politicization. Despite this, most contributors acknowledged China's strong performance as a host, even as debates about related social and political concerns continued.

article_content: Last week, Snoop Dogg surprised fans worldwide by declaring he was ‘giving up smoke.’ Many assumed the legendary rapper was quitting marijuana, causing a massive buzz and outpouring of support on social media. However, this statement turned out to be a clever ad for a smokeless fire pit, rather than a lifestyle change.  Snoop’s humorous twist quickly captured attention, showing how impactful humor can be in marketing today. Interestingly, while most consumers—91%—enjoy brands with a fun approach, a huge 95% of companies hold back from embracing humor. This stands out even more as many young people, like Gen-Z and Millennials, go to social media primarily for entertainment and laughs.  Research supports humor’s effectiveness: a 1993 Journal of Marketing study found that humor improves memory of ads, boosts brand perceptions, and raises the chance of purchase, particularly when it aligns naturally with the brand message. Further work by Professor Martin Eisend at Viadrina University confirms humor’s positive effects on brand engagement.  Beyond jokes, humor helps brands appear more personable and relatable. Snoop Dogg’s approach was not just attention-grabbing—it created a connection. Brands can stand out and build loyalty by using a personable, light-hearted tone.  With growing reports of unhappiness, humor is ever more vital for brands to build emotional connections. Companies like Netflix show how embracing wit and self-irony—like in the popular ‘Netflix and chill’—can foster loyal communities and cultural trends.  In the end, Snoop Dogg’s creative move underlines the value of humor in helping brands bond with audiences. As Jeetendr Sehdev—media figure, speaker, and author—observes, adding some joy and laughter should be part of every brand’s game plan.

article_content: Before Diwali, the Indian Finance Ministry announced changes to several small savings schemes to boost their appeal. Under the revised Senior Citizens Savings Scheme (2023), depositors can now renew their accounts multiple times for three-year periods, instead of being limited to a single renewal. The interest rate for the scheme is currently 8.2%. The window for retirees to open SCSS accounts has been extended from one month to three months after they receive retirement benefits. Additionally, spouses of government staff who die after the age of 55 are now eligible to open accounts with some conditions. Updates to the Public Provident Fund (PPF) scheme now permit account holders— and guardians of minors or incapacitated individuals— to close accounts before maturity, though the payout interest is 1% less than the credited rate since the account's beginning or last five-year cycle. For National Savings Time Deposit accounts, early withdrawals of five-year deposits after four years will now accrue interest at the Post Office Savings Account rate, instead of at the three-year deposit rate. All these rule changes take effect from November 9, 2023, the Department of Economic Affairs reports. Separately, India's industrial growth rate dropped more sharply than expected in September, falling to 5.8% as compared to 10.3% in August. This slowdown was blamed on rainfall and changes in the festive calendar. Meanwhile, Ranjan Pai has poured Rs 1,400 crore into Aakash Institute, which is part of Byju's, and manufacturing companies are turning to younger graduates for their tech-focused skills, according to JSW Group’s HR chief, Dilip Pattanayak.

article_content: Sheryl Sandberg, Facebook's chief operating officer and author of 'Lean In', received an enthusiastic welcome at BlogHer, the world's largest conference for women bloggers held in Chicago. Despite facing criticism—often from other women—Sandberg was met with applause, standing ovations, and many seeking personal interactions. During her keynote speech, Sandberg emphasized that 'Lean In,' her best-selling book now reaching over one million copies sold, is not solely about climbing the corporate ladder. 'Lean In is about believing in ourselves and reaching for any ambition,' Sandberg said, explaining that her message is intended for all women—whether they're stay-at-home moms advocating for better education, or professionals aiming for executive roles. Sandberg acknowledged critiques that her message comes across as elitist or dismissive of women with different goals, clarifying that anyone can 'lean in' by pursuing whatever dreams they choose. 'It's not a recalibration, but if the message got lost, I have to take some responsibility,' she remarked during a press conference. She indicated that while her book shared mostly her and her colleagues' stories, her intention was for the message to include all women. Many conference attendees felt Sandberg's message resonated more clearly in person. Danielle Herzog, a mother of two and blogger at Martinis and Minivans, said she learned that leaning in is about following one's own dreams, whatever they may be. Norine Dworkin-McDaniel, co-creator of Science of Parenthood, echoed this sentiment, saying she doesn't aspire to be a CEO of a major company, but wants to excel at what matters to her. Sandberg also addressed the 'leadership ambition gap' between boys and girls seen in surveys as early as middle school, linking it to how daughters are raised compared to sons. Leigh Baker, a parenting blogger, realized she was unintentionally discouraging her daughter from leadership except in sports, while treating her son differently. Sandberg's rising public profile has sparked speculation about whether she might pursue a political career, but she told BlogHer co-founder Lisa Stone that she is focused on her current roles at Facebook and with the Lean In online community, which now exceeds 250,000 members. Rachel Thomas, president of Sandberg's nonprofit LeanIn.org, described the vibrant growth of the community, including more than 7,000 Lean In circles across all 50 states and at least 50 countries. At the conference, Sandberg joined small groups in Lean In circles, encouraging women to share challenges and support each other. According to Thomas, these circles foster empowerment and solidarity, with participants expressing feelings of strength and possibility. Attendees remarked on Sandberg's humility and accessibility, contrasting with the criticism she often receives in broader national discussions. Some suggested that criticism is sometimes rooted in personal insecurity or reluctance to embrace new messages. As Jessica Ziegler, co-founder of Science of Parenthood, noted, 'It's much easier to be negative than to support a movement aimed at empowering many.'

article_content: As adults, it’s easy to express our food preferences — we can plainly refuse or set aside items we don’t enjoy. Babies, however, find it harder to communicate what they like or dislike — until now. Engineers from the Thrill Laboratory have created the world’s first ‘Baby Thrill-O-Meter.’ This device measures a baby’s physiological reaction to different vegetables, fruits, and spices, giving parents insights into their children’s food preferences. Engineer Brendan Walker attached sensors to the feet of seven babies and fed them a range of foods, including mangoes, carrots, lemons, and cinnamon. The Thrill-O-Meter uses these sensors to track changes in each baby’s Galvanic Skin Response (GSR), which indicates emotional reactions to food through changes in sweat and skin conductivity. Results were calculated by analyzing changes in GSR, facial expressions, and body language. Mango produced the most positive response, followed by cinnamon, lemon, coconut, and banana. Foods with less distinctive flavors, like sweet potatoes and carrots, ranked lower. The study found that when a baby enjoyed a food, their excitement was shown by increased sweat levels, resulting in a higher GSR score. Ella’s Kitchen, which makes organic baby foods, partnered with the Thrill Laboratory on this research and plans to use the findings to improve its products. Brendan Walker commented that different foods can trigger unique physiological responses, revealing how thrilling tastes can be for babies.

Deep within a cave in Brazil, a crust-encrusted creature moved across the damp, rocky floor. Scientists, intrigued by this underground animal, took notice during their exploration of the reddish, iron-rich caves of the Carajás Mountains. According to a study published September 13 in the journal Zoosystema, researchers conducted extensive wildlife surveys in the area from 2005 to 2019, gathering a significant collection of specimens.

During these surveys, over 1,300 millipedes were collected and preserved in museum collections, but initially left unidentified. Later, another team of researchers analyzed these millipedes and determined they represented a new species: Pseudoporatia kananciuê, also known as the Kananciuê millipede.

The Kananciuê millipede features 19 body segments, or 'body rings,' which are crusted with iron ore sediments. The number of legs is unspecified, as they are not visible from above. Considered 'relatively large' for a cave millipede, they grow to about 0.3 inches in length, according to study co-author Luiz Iniesta.

Photographs of the Kananciuê millipede show a whitish cream-colored body with orange-red speckles, matching the surrounding cave soil. Its body rings appear waxy and are held together by a thinner, worm-like body beneath. Close-up images reveal a pair of antennae extending horizontally from its head. Notably, male Kananciuê millipedes possess rather complex genitalia, located near the head segment and oval in shape, as shown in the study photos.

Kananciuê millipedes live underground, favoring moist, low-light areas of the cave, often clustering around large deposits of bat guano. They are widely distributed throughout the interconnected, iron-rich caves of the Carajás Mountains. Despite living underground, the species shows no obvious physical adaptations for life in caves, according to Iniesta.

The species is named after Kananciuê, the main deity of the indigenous Karajás tribe who inhabit the Carajás Mountains. This region is part of a national forest in the state of Pará, about 700 miles northwest of Brasília, Brazil's capital.

Researchers identified the new species through its distinctive body segments, genitalia, and other subtle physical characteristics; however, no DNA analysis was conducted. The team notes that millipede diversity is still largely underestimated in the Amazon rainforest.

Study authors include Iniesta, Rodrigo Bouzan, Claudio Souza, Robson Zampaulo, Igor Cizauskas, and Antonio Brescovit.

Superheroes are dominating the box office. 'The Avengers'—featuring Captain America, Iron Man, Thor, and The Hulk—is on track to surpass $1 billion in worldwide revenue on its 19th day of release, according to Walt Disney Studios. The film set a new industry record with an estimated $103.2 million in its second weekend in North American theaters, following a $207.4 million opening weekend.

Robert A. Iger, Disney's chairman and CEO, said in a statement, “We’re obviously thrilled with the global success of ‘The Avengers.’ It’s a fantastic movie and an extraordinary franchise that will continue with more great stories and compelling characters for years to come.”

So far, the film has brought in about $628.9 million internationally. Based on its massive success, Disney is already planning a sequel. This triumph is a significant boost for the movie industry, which earned around $2.3 billion at the U.S. box office in the first three months of 2012—a nearly 46% increase over last year, according to Box Office Mojo. The industry’s rebound comes after 2011 marked the lowest movie ticket sales in 16 years.

Prior to ‘The Avengers,’ ‘The Hunger Games’ from Lionsgate had delivered the largest box-office opening of the year, with about $155 million domestically in its first weekend. Other high-profile releases coming soon include ‘Men in Black III’ over Memorial Day weekend, Pixar’s ‘Brave’ in June, and two other anticipated superhero films: ‘The Amazing Spider-Man’ and ‘The Dark Knight Rises.’

The success of ‘The Avengers’ follows Disney’s costly misstep with ‘John Carter,’ which lost an estimated $200 million and led to changes in its studio division. Disney secured the rights to The Avengers’ characters by acquiring Marvel in a $4 billion deal three years ago.

article_content: For 370 years, Itteringham in Norfolk has kept its village shop open in the same spot. When supermarket competition threatened its future, the villagers stepped up—over half of the 120 residents volunteer to keep it running. Volunteers handle everything from stocking shelves and setting prices to baking, cleaning, and delivering orders. Their efforts save the shop about £350 a week on wages, making up 20% of its £2,000 weekly income—just enough to break even. The shop’s more than a business: it's the hub of local life. When times get tough, the village throws fundraising events like garden parties or pop-up restaurants to support it. The Fairhead family managed the shop from 1908 to 1994, becoming central figures in its story. In 1994, after Brian Fairhead fell ill, locals raised £5,000 and formed the Itteringham Community Shop association, rescuing the shop from closure. Still in its original building, the shop sells local produce as it has since Richard Bell owned it in the 1600s. Shop manager Mike Hemsley, 55, says community ties keep the shop alive—most villagers volunteer, and young people join as soon as they turn 18. He believes enthusiasm is greater when people freely give their time. Maggie Vaughan-Lewis, a local, chronicled the shop’s long story in her book 'The Village Shop,' collecting memories and old photos. Although Chiddingston post office in Kent (opened 1593) and the Three Old Arches in Chester (built 1274) are older, Itteringham’s shop stands out for its longevity and community run model. The Plunkett Foundation reports over 280 similar community shops now exist in Britain, showing the success of these grassroots efforts.

Both Skakel and Moxley were 15 at the time of the crime, which happened following a night with friends in their affluent neighborhood. Skakel was tried and convicted as an adult decades after the incident. According to the Connecticut Department of Correction, this was Skakel’s first opportunity for parole since his conviction. Martha’s mother, Dorthy Moxley, said she believes Skakel should serve at least 20 years, feeling that ten years is not enough. Skakel continues to maintain his innocence. John Moxley, Martha’s brother, wrote to the parole board requesting the denial of parole, attributing Skakel’s behavior to his privileged background. Conversely, Skakel’s lawyer, Hope Seeley, argued that prosecuting Skakel as an adult led to an injustice and stated he should have received a shorter, juvenile sentence. Supporters, such as Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and others who sent letters to the parole board, described Skakel as religious, kind, and incapable of violence. He is depicted as a model inmate who has taken up mural painting while in prison. The case remains emotionally charged, with strong feelings on both sides, and the parole board ultimately decided to deny Skakel’s request for release.

Substitute Sammy Ameobi seized the moment, scoring the equalizer only six seconds after the restart, followed by Remy Cabella assisting Ayoze Perez for the winning goal. Newcastle's victory was all the more impressive considering they lost striker Papiss Cisse to a knee injury shortly before kickoff, prompting last-minute changes to the lineup. Pardew acknowledged the team had lost their way in the first half, giving Tottenham too much control, but praised the squad’s improved mindset after the break. Tottenham had taken an early lead with Emmanuel Adebayor's 18th-minute header and dominated much of the first half. However, manager Mauricio Pochettino lamented his team's lack of mental toughness following Newcastle’s swift equalizer. He pointed out that overcoming such psychological setbacks is challenging and requires more than tactical tweaks. In the end, Newcastle’s energized approach in the second half made the difference, while Tottenham were left to reflect on lost momentum and the need for greater resilience.

A French-built warship intended to boost Russia's ability to deploy helicopter gunships, troops, and tanks is set for its first sea trial today. The Vladivostok helicopter carrier, scheduled to depart from the French Atlantic port of Saint-Nazaire, is being sold to Russia under a €1.2 billion agreement—the biggest NATO weapons sale to Moscow, finalized in 2011. The test run aligns with heightened tensions as Western countries threaten economic sanctions against Russian President Vladimir Putin due to Russia's military involvement in Ukraine, particularly Crimea.

The vessel is being constructed by the French state-backed shipbuilder DCNS along with South Korean-controlled STX and is expected to be delivered to Russia by the end of the year. A sister ship, Sebastopol, named after a major Crimean port now under Russian control, is slated for delivery the following year.

Although France has joined others in criticizing Russia's incursion into Crimea, officials say there are no current plans to cancel the controversial arms deal, which supports approximately 1,000 French jobs. The situation places France between diplomatic pressure to sanction Russia and the need to protect its own economic interests. At the same time, Paris is hosting diplomatic talks with American, Russian, and other world representatives as the crisis intensifies.

In response to the threat of Western sanctions, Russian lawmakers have proposed new measures allowing the seizure of Western assets if penalties are enacted. European leaders have threatened to freeze Russian assets and impose further restrictions unless Russia de-escalates tensions in Ukraine. French Foreign Minister Laurent Fabius confirmed the EU's readiness to introduce visa restrictions and suspend economic ties if necessary. Russian officials, in turn, are considering reciprocal measures and have begun reviewing the legality of seizing foreign company assets under Russian law. Ukrainian Prime Minister Arseny Yatseniuk has warned that Russia's troop deployment in Crimea is severely impacting Ukraine’s economy.

article_content: The twin polar bear cubs at Munich's Hellabrunn Zoo have officially been named Nela and Nobby. Born December 9, these playful siblings live with their mother Giovanna and have charmed visitors with their lively antics. Naming was postponed while the zoo selected special 'godparents'—individuals or organizations given the honor of naming the cubs. article_content: Defining and determining death is more complex than it appears. In an article published in MIT Technology Review, Rachel Nuwer explored the evolving boundaries between life and death. As scientific knowledge increases, long-standing notions about death are becoming less concrete. The traditional view of death as a binary state—either 'alive' or 'dead'—is being challenged by new scientific insights. Nuwer discusses how understanding of death is shifting from a static event to a dynamic process, which has significant implications for medical practice and society's perspective on the end of life. Traditionally, death has been seen as the sudden loss of vital functions, with a doctor declaring the moment of death. However, recent research suggests that death is actually a process, and in some circumstances, it may even be reversible. Scientists are finding that the body can sometimes survive longer periods without oxygen than previously thought, potentially extending the timeline for medical intervention. This changing understanding has implications for organ recovery and resuscitation. Historically, legal and biological definitions of death focused on the irreversible loss of heart, lung, and brain function. The introduction of CPR in the 1960s and mechanical ventilators blurred the line between temporary and permanent loss of function, resulting in conditions like cardiac arrest and brain death. Defining death—especially in terms of brain activity—remains a subject of ongoing research and international debate. The World Brain Death Project has proposed a minimum set of requirements for determining brain death across institutions and countries. For example, Lewis et al. (2023) published recommendations aimed at improving consistency in death determination by neurologic criteria. Recent studies have challenged the assumption that the brain is highly vulnerable to oxygen deprivation. In one notable study published in Nature, researchers managed to restore certain brain functions in pig brains hours after death, suggesting more resilience than previously believed. Similar observations in humans have shown that some brain activity can persist, or even increase, during near-death states. These findings have practical implications. More precise understanding of the dying process could improve medical rescue protocols, potentially saving lives that might otherwise have been lost. For example, people suffering from heart attacks, severe blood loss, or suffocation might benefit from advanced interventions. Researchers are also exploring ways to restore metabolic function in other organs, such as the heart and kidneys, which could expand possibilities for successful organ donation. While these developments are promising, researchers caution against overly ambitious claims. Progress in this area requires rigorous research and careful consideration of ethical issues. As our understanding of death evolves, it raises questions not only for medicine and science but also for legal, religious, and societal systems. Policies and regulations will need to adapt to these advancements. Ultimately, the transition from life to death is less clear-cut than once believed. Ongoing research reveals that dying is a complex, sometimes reversible process, which may reshape medical practices, increase the window for organ recovery, and challenge commonly held notions about life's end. However, continued research, ethical discussions, and realistic expectations are necessary as this field advances. Though death remains a universal experience, the process is proving to be far from simple or static.

article_content: Chemists at RUDN University, together with colleagues from Belarus, have developed derivatives of the natural polymer chitosan that exhibit greater antibacterial activity than existing antibiotics. These new compounds are non-toxic, and their production method is considered safe. The results were published in the journal Polymers. Modern antibiotics are sometimes ineffective and can cause side effects or allergic reactions, spurring the development of new approaches to bacterial treatment. Polymer chemistry, including work on natural polymers like chitosan (derived from crab shells), contributes to this search. Chitosan derivatives already play a role in making antibacterial drugs. The research team proposed a new method: combining chitosan with benzothiazole, a cyclic organic compound with antibacterial properties. This approach aimed to create derivatives with improved antibacterial activity. "Chitosan has drawn the attention of researchers due to its biocompatibility, biodegradability, non-toxicity, and antibacterial effects. Antibacterial chitosan derivatives exist, while benzothiazole has also produced effective, low-toxicity antibacterial compounds. This led us to synthesize benzothiazole derivatives of chitosan to examine their antibacterial properties," said Andrey Kritchenkov, Ph.D., from RUDN University. Chemists used an electrochemical coupling reaction—a first for these substances—to produce the new compounds. They tested the antibacterial activity of these compounds in both lab cultures and animal models, including gram-positive Staphylococcus aureus and gram-negative Escherichia coli. The new antibacterial systems proved more effective than unmodified chitosan and commonly used antibiotics like ampicillin and gentamicin. In lab tests, the bacteria-affected area from the new compounds was just a few millimeters smaller than that from antibiotics, but in rat models of peritonitis, the new substances reduced bacteria counts by tenfold—to 8 viable bacteria per milliliter, compared to 82 when using ampicillin or gentamicin. Crucially, these derivatives maintained a similar low toxicity level as natural chitosan. "Our synthesized chitosan-based polymers and nanoparticles demonstrated strong antibacterial effects and low toxicity, indicating their potential as alternatives to current antibiotics. Nevertheless, additional studies and preclinical trials are needed before their use in clinical settings," noted Anton Egorov, a research intern at RUDN University.

article_content:
An international coalition of climate scientists has published a paper in BioScience warning that Earth's vital signs have declined to unprecedented levels, putting life on the planet at risk. The lead authors, William Ripple of Oregon State University and Christopher Wolf, formerly of OSU and now with Terrestrial Ecosystems Research Associates, along with 10 other U.S. and international scientists, say urgent action is needed to address humanity's excessive demands on nature.

“The root problem is that humans are taking more from Earth than it can safely give,” Wolf states. Without addressing this, he warns of the potential collapse of both natural and socioeconomic systems, resulting in unbearable heat and shortages of food and freshwater.

Their report, 'The 2023 State of the Climate Report: Entering Uncharted Territory,' notes that 20 of 35 planetary 'vital signs' used to track climate change have reached record extremes. The paper highlights new data showing that in 2023, numerous climate-related records were broken by substantial margins, especially with rising ocean temperatures and shrinking sea ice. It also points to an extraordinary wildfire season in Canada, which produced record carbon dioxide emissions.

This report comes four years after Ripple and collaborators published the 'World Scientists' Warning of a Climate Emergency' in BioScience, which was endorsed by over 15,000 scientists in 161 countries.

"Life on our planet is clearly under siege," says Ripple. "The statistical trends are deeply alarming, and we find little progress in addressing climate change."

Key findings from the report include:
- Fossil fuel subsidies doubled from $531 billion in 2021 to just over $1 trillion in 2022.
- Canadian wildfires this year have emitted over 1 gigaton of carbon dioxide, exceeding Canada's total 2021 greenhouse gas emissions of 0.67 gigatons.
- So far in 2023, there have been 38 days with global average temperatures more than 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels—a once rare occurrence.
- July 2023 saw the highest average Earth surface temperature on record, possibly the highest in the last 100,000 years.

Wolf emphasizes, "The increasing frequency and severity of climate-related disasters may be outpacing temperature rises. By century’s end, 3–6 billion people could face extreme heat, food insecurity, and elevated mortality rates."

The authors argue that policies must target the underlying issue of 'ecological overshoot'—human consumption exceeding planetary capacity—which leads to environmental crises like biodiversity loss. Focusing solely on carbon or climate without addressing broader demands may only shift the pressures elsewhere.

Ripple notes, "It's a moral duty for scientists to alert humanity to existential threats and provide leadership." The team urges a transition to a global economy prioritizing human well-being, reducing overconsumption, and curbing excessive emissions mainly by the wealthy. Recommendations include phasing out fossil fuel subsidies, promoting plant-based diets, enhancing forest protection, and adopting international agreements on coal and fossil fuel non-proliferation.

They stress that all climate actions must be grounded in equity and social justice, since the harshest impacts fall on poorer populations who have contributed least to climate change.

article_content: The Police Service Commission (PSC) has announced that 188,874 applications have been rejected so far in the ongoing recruitment into the constable cadre of the Nigeria Police Force. This was disclosed by PSC spokesman Ikechukwu Ani in a statement on Sunday. Since the application portal opened on October 15, a total of 547,774 applications have been received. The portal is scheduled to close on Sunday, November 26. Ani stated that 84,606 applications were rejected due to applicants exceeding the age limit. Kaduna State leads with the highest number of applicants at 40,272, while Anambra State has the lowest at 1,664. Out of the total applicants, 358,900 have qualified for the next stage, which includes physical screening, credential verification, medical tests, and background checks. Following Kaduna, Adamawa State had 36,398 applicants, Borno State 32,048, Benue 31,122, Katsina 30,202, Bauchi 30,604, and Kano 30,004. From the bottom, after Anambra, Ebonyi recorded 2,132 applications, Lagos 2,324, Bayelsa 2,651, and Abia 2,796. PSC Chairman Dr. Solomon Arase expressed satisfaction with the large number of applications. He commended Nigerian youths for their interest in joining the police force, calling it a positive sign for ongoing police reforms. Arase urged youths in the South-East to reconsider their lack of interest in police work, warning that involvement with criminal gangs is detrimental. He stressed that the region's future depends on stability and security. He also assured that the entire recruitment process will be transparent, based on merit and justice.

Their winter vacation becomes a tense adventure when Anya unwittingly becomes involved in her adoptive father’s secret operation. Both new and returning voice actors will feature in the film, with much of the main TV cast reprising their roles. The production team assembles seasoned talent in areas like character design and music, promising a high-quality cinematic experience. article_content: Liberian President George Weah has called his presidential challenger, Joseph Boakai, to congratulate him on his victory. Addressing the nation, Weah stated, "The Liberian people have spoken and we have heard their voice." Boakai, the opposition candidate, leads by more than 28,000 votes with nearly all ballots counted. President Weah, a former football star who has served since 2018, will step down in January. He entered office with broad support, especially among younger voters, following a decisive win against Boakai in the previous election. However, perceptions that he failed to address corruption, rising prices, and economic difficulties have stained his leadership. Demonstrating statesmanship in defeat, Weah began his five-minute address by expressing "the utmost respect for the democratic process that has defined our nation." He confirmed he has spoken to Boakai, whom he called the 'president-elect'. Earlier, the electoral commission announced that Boakai, a 78-year-old political veteran, had 50.89% of the votes, compared to Weah's 49.11%. Weah noted the close margin, saying it "reveals a deep division within our country," and called for Liberians to work together, emphasizing that unity is essential for the nation. Liberia's civil war, which ended about 20 years ago after claiming some 250,000 lives, still casts a long shadow. When the latest results were announced, celebrations broke out in the capital, Monrovia, where Boakai's supporters gathered at party headquarters, confident of the win. They called for Weah to step down, chanting slogans referencing a song tied to his campaign. The electoral commission reported results from 99.58% of polling stations for Tuesday's run-off election. The run-off was required after no candidate surpassed 50% in last month's initial round, where Weah narrowly led Boakai by about 7,000 votes among 18 candidates. This has been Liberia's tightest presidential contest since the civil war. Boakai's campaign centered on rescuing Liberia from what he characterized as 'mismanagement' by Weah's government—a claim Weah denied, highlighting accomplishments such as introducing free university tuition. This election marks the fourth presidential vote since the civil war. Regional bloc Ecowas noted the run-off was largely peaceful, though observers reported isolated incidents leading to injuries and hospitalizations in Lofa, Nimba, Bong, and Montserrado provinces, according to AFP.

Frank Rodriguez, previously the long-serving Head of Distribution at Searchlight Pictures, is joining Amazon MGM Studios as General Sales Manager. He will now report to Kevin Wilson, who became Amazon MGM’s Head of Distribution following Erik Lomis’s passing. Rodriguez’s appointment is part of a wider reorganization of Amazon MGM’s theatrical distribution division. Mark Boxer, already on the team, holds the role of Head of Specialty Theatrical Distribution.

Rodriguez’s career highlights at Searchlight include overseeing the distribution of award-winning movies: Wes Anderson’s 'The Grand Budapest Hotel', Guillermo del Toro’s 'The Shape of Water', Taika Waititi’s 'Jojo Rabbit', Steve McQueen’s '12 Years a Slave', Michael Keaton’s 'Birdman', and Yorgos Lanthimos’s 'The Favourite'. Before joining Searchlight, Rodriguez worked at DreamWorks, managing sales in New York from the studio’s foundation through its acquisition by Paramount, later advancing to SVP of Eastern Sales.

Recently honored with the 'Bingham Ray Spirit Award' at ShowEast for his contributions to film distribution, Rodriguez leaves Searchlight as the studio searches for his successor, who will report to Tony Chambers, EVP of Theatrical Distribution at Disney. Rodriguez had already devised plans for the studio’s upcoming slate, including Taika Waititi’s 'Next Goal Wins', Yorgos Lanthimos’s 'Poor Things', and Andrew Haigh’s 'All of Us Strangers'.

Kevin Wilson expressed confidence that Rodriguez’s experience and leadership will further strengthen Amazon MGM as they seek to grow their theatrical presence and bring quality films to viewers.

article_content: Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav on Sunday emphasized the need for a caste census in India to bring people from backward communities and classes into the mainstream. Yadav spoke at a rally in Jind, Haryana, organized by Balraj Kundu, an Independent MLA from Meham who recently launched the Haryana Jansewak Party. The rally occurs ahead of next year’s Haryana assembly elections, where the BJP-JJP alliance is currently in power. Yadav asserted that his party will continue working to guarantee the rights and respect of backward communities. He noted, 'After decades of independence, many backward people have not been counted or included in the mainstream.' He pointed out that the call for a caste census, which began in Uttar Pradesh, has also spread to Bihar and now Haryana. Yadav promised that, after the 2024 Lok Sabha elections, the Samajwadi Party will ensure a caste census so that people receive their due rights and respect. He also criticized the Centre’s Agniveer recruitment scheme for soldiers, saying the SP will promise to end the scheme and restore the previous recruitment system if it comes to power. Congress has also pledged to conduct a caste census if it is elected at the Centre, while Bihar's JD(U) government under Nitish Kumar has already released the results of its own caste survey. Former Gujarat chief minister Shankersinh Vaghela and other leaders were present at the event.

article_content: How artificial intelligence (AI) affects employment is less about the capabilities of the technology itself and more about decisions made by company leaders. Though many people are concerned about AI replacing human workers, whether it does so largely depends on whether organizations use AI to automate jobs or to enhance human performance. Debates around AI often feature extremes—either excessive optimism or fear. But it's not inevitable that AI will cause mass unemployment; management strategies play a key role. When a single company holds significant influence in a local job market, it may choose to automate more, using that power to reduce wages. The root of the issue lies in corporate dominance rather than the tools they use. Instead of limiting technological advancement, experts advocate for strong anti-trust measures to address the negative effects of excessive automation caused by corporate concentration. Recent legal action in this area is a step forward, but further initiatives could prove beneficial. Even when AI enhances jobs instead of eliminating them, there's concern that productivity gains will lead to fewer employees being required. Yet, as the 19th-century economist William Stanley Jevons observed, efficiency improvements—like those brought by AI—can paradoxically increase overall demand for work, as was the case with coal after the industrial revolution. In today's context, AI is making programming more efficient, which can lead to greater demand for software solutions and possibly more programming jobs. While fewer people may be needed for certain tasks due to automation, new opportunities and types of work emerge. The rise of personal computers and spreadsheets in the early 1980s revolutionized accounting, allowing complex data analysis and scenario modeling that were once impossible. This shift enabled professionals to add more value to their roles and organizations. Leaders today should focus on truly understanding AI and its potential applications. It's important that managers—and particularly those at the top—stay informed about the technology’s possibilities and encourage innovation that brings value to customers and employees alike. To ensure AI adoption benefits all, managers should design and introduce AI tools that genuinely help workers, making them more willing to adapt and learn. Though transitions can be tough and may meet resistance, prioritizing empathy, social understanding, and emotional intelligence can ease the process. As AI changes workplaces, it highlights not just the importance of technical know-how, but also of human skills that technology can’t replace.

article_content: Pizza delivery could soon enter a new era as CopterExpress, a Russian company, debuts drones designed for transporting lightweight goods. These drones can carry up to 5 kilograms and fly as fast as 40 km/h, making them suitable for delivering food and small packages. A recent company video features a CopterExpress representative explaining their pioneering work in developing commercial drone delivery services, with two years of experience building and operating multicopters. The drones come with GPS and onboard cameras, enabling users to track their deliveries in real time. Working with Dodo Pizza in Syktyvkar, northern Russia, CopterExpress helped launch what the pizzeria claims is the world’s first pizza delivery by drone. Dodo Pizza posted a video in June showcasing the drones dropping off pizzas to customers. Manager Ilya Farafonov stated that six pizzas were sold via drone in just one and a half hours, demonstrating the business potential. Dodo Pizza guarantees deliveries within 30 minutes, offering free pizza if a delivery takes over an hour. The company aims to expand drone-powered delivery to 18 additional Russian cities, with menu prices starting at £6 (325 rubles). Similar endeavors have surfaced abroad, including Domino’s UK’s DomiCopter and a drone test flight by a Brooklyn, NY pizza shop. Charles Walters, the CEO of Williamsburg Pizza in Brooklyn, predicts that drones will be delivering food high above ground within five years and hopes to operate a fleet of at least 25 delivery drones by 2018. Excitement for the future of airborne food delivery is growing, but there are also considerations regarding the impact on traditional delivery jobs.

Photobox, one of Europe’s leading personalized online publishers, is determined to expand its footprint across the continent, according to CEO Stan Laurent. In an interview with CNN’s Nina dos Santos, Laurent highlighted that while the UK and France remain important, European countries outside these two markets are the group’s fastest growing regions. Nevertheless, he believes there is still significant market share to capture.

"We’re also expanding internationally very rapidly, and that requires talent," Laurent said. "We need to develop local expertise, even if we initially build from the UK. Local talent can better support local markets and deliver the right level of service."

Laurent also noted that the UK is "a great place to find the talent we need." He emphasized that a key driver for Photobox is product quality, not simply producing the cheapest product.

Through recent acquisitions, Photobox now owns Moonpig.com, a personalized card service, and StickyGram, a platform allowing users to create fridge magnets and phone covers from Instagram photos.

Looking to new markets, Laurent said, "We've begun launching in Canada, Australia, New Zealand, and other regions. With services like StickyGram, we believe we can eventually build a global platform."

Photobox is broadening its service range, especially in mobile technology, to tap into a $7 billion market. Laurent, CEO since 2006, stated, "We're heavily investing in mobile and seeking experts who can help us advance in this area."

In 2012, Moonpig’s app saw 1.5 million downloads, supporting Photobox’s double-digit growth and generating £147.5 million in revenue, according to the company’s annual report. However, Laurent noted that 95% of greeting cards are still purchased in stores. "What mobile brings is convenience—it’s a great tool, especially since people have all their photos on their phones," he said.

Founded in 2000 by Graham Hobson and Mark Chapman, Photobox started as an online photo ordering service. Thirteen years on, Laurent describes it as a visionary idea in a time when both broadband and digital cameras were emerging. He attributes Photobox’s success to its focus on personal connection: "It’s about the entire customer experience and making sure our products carry the emotional value customers presume, since these often feature their family and loved ones."

article_content: Israeli security forces and intelligence officers conducted a nighttime raid on the Palestinian television station Wattan TV in Jerusalem, seizing computers, tapes, transmitters, and paperwork, according to station director Muamar Orabi. The raid began at 2 a.m., with four night-shift employees detained for more than three hours after their mobile phones were confiscated. The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) confirmed the operation. According to Israeli Ministry of Communications spokesman Yehiel Shavi, Wattan TV's broadcasts were interfering with Israeli broadcasters and flight communications at Ben Gurion airport in Tel Aviv. The Israeli authorities stated that repeated requests had been made to Wattan to stop the transmissions, which were resolved 'with the assistance of the IDF.' However, Orabi maintained that Wattan TV had never received any complaints about their transmission frequencies, questioning the necessity and proportionality of the raid. He emphasized, 'Why destroy the TV station when they could have just confiscated the two transmitters?' Orabi also recalled that Wattan TV was previously destroyed in March 2002. Palestinian Prime Minister Salam Fayyad condemned the raid, calling it 'piracy.' He compared it to similar Israeli actions at the start of the second Intifadah, which targeted several Palestinian media outlets, including Wattan TV. Fayyad added that officials would work to restore Wattan TV's broadcasting immediately. Wattan TV denounced the operation as an aggressive act against an effective media organization and committed to working with local and international media and human rights groups to expose what it described as a criminal act. The station announced efforts to recover the seized equipment and resume interrupted broadcasting. Fayyad further criticized the Middle East Quartet—the United States, United Nations, European Union, and Russia—holding them responsible for not preventing Israel’s actions. He said these violations highlight the Quartet's failure and inability to fulfill its duties. CNN's Enas Muthaffar contributed to the report.

article_content: To help calm concerns over climbing oil prices, Saudi Arabia’s oil minister has stated that both his nation and other OPEC countries have the ability to increase oil production if necessary. The Saudi Press Agency relayed that Minister Ali al-Naimi said Saudi Arabia alone can provide an extra 4 million barrels of oil a day. However, it wasn’t specified whether this surplus is currently being produced or simply available if needed. In a recent move, 87 countries including Saudi Arabia signed an agreement aimed at preventing extreme fluctuations in oil prices and stabilizing the global market. This step followed a 6% surge in oil prices, where the cost per barrel hit $98 amid concerns that upheaval in Libya could spread to other important oil producers in the Middle East. Peter Beutel, analyst at Cameron Hanover, commented that the situation is becoming more troubling, pointing out fears that unrest could eventually reach Saudi Arabia, which would have major market repercussions. Libya produces around 1.6 million barrels daily; by comparison, Saudi Arabia outputs about 8.4 million, while the world consumes almost 87 million barrels each day. According to Win Thin of Brown Brothers Harriman, financial markets have frequently relied on Saudi Arabia’s role as a 'swing producer'—stepping up production when global supplies are threatened. The International Energy Agency in Austria confirmed its ongoing willingness to make additional oil available if a serious supply disruption occurs and normal distribution cannot compensate. Additionally, OPEC has announced its readiness to convene an emergency session to discuss boosting production if the situation demands.

article_content: The tense standoff in Crimea escalated on Wednesday as pro-Russian activists stormed Ukraine’s navy headquarters in Sevastopol, taking control with nearly 300 armed supporters. Ukrainian officials reported that their navy chief, Sergey Gaiduk, was detained by the pro-Russian forces. Despite a deadline set by Ukraine’s acting President Oleksandr Turchynov to release all hostages, no immediate consequences followed after the deadline passed. Ukrainian personnel at the base tried to resist as the armed group replaced Ukrainian flags with Russian ones, but no shots were fired during the takeover. According to Russian state media, Gaiduk was taken to the Sevastopol prosecutor's office for questioning about potentially relaying orders from Kiev to use weapons. In response to the ongoing crisis, Ukraine announced new measures against Russia, including implementing a full visa regime for Russian citizens and initiating its withdrawal from the Commonwealth of Independent States. Kiev also prepared to accommodate up to 25,000 evacuees if needed and plans to estimate damages from the Russian annexation of Crimea. NATO Secretary General Anders Fogh Rasmussen expressed deep concerns about the risk of further Russian intervention in eastern Ukraine, warning that 'business as usual is not an option.' On the same day Russian President Vladimir Putin announced Crimea’s annexation, a Ukrainian soldier was killed and others captured when masked gunmen seized another military base. The controversial referendum in Crimea, held under Russian military presence and internationally condemned, reportedly saw 96.7% vote in favor of joining Russia. The ballot was criticized by Ukrainian and Western officials, who said that there were no realistic options for those wishing to remain part of Ukraine. Russia’s Constitutional Court ruled the accession lawful, clearing the way for the Russian parliament to complete the process. Meanwhile, crowds celebrated Crimea’s inclusion in Russia at rallies across the country. U.S. officials, including Vice President Joe Biden, reaffirmed support for NATO allies and condemned Russia's actions as military aggression. Observers note that up to 20,000 Russian troops are positioned close to Ukraine’s eastern border, raising fears of a wider incursion. Diplomatic efforts continue, with U.N. Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon visiting Moscow and Kiev to encourage peaceful resolution. Ukrainian and U.S. ambassadors at the U.N. called for non-recognition of Crimea's annexation, labeling it the result of force and intimidation. Amid heightened tensions, Ukrainian government officials were prevented by Crimean authorities from landing in the peninsula to negotiate. Some Crimean officials have labeled Ukrainian troops as occupying forces and demanded their withdrawal. Separately, Ukraine’s far-right Svoboda party lawmakers allegedly assaulted the head of state TV over the airing of a Russian concert, sparking condemnation from the U.S. embassy in Kiev.

article_content: India chose to support Saima Wazed, daughter of Bangladesh’s Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, as the new World Health Organization (WHO) Regional Director for Southeast Asia, opting not to back Nepal’s candidate, Dr. Shambhu Acharya. With India’s support, Wazed easily won, gathering votes from the majority of member nations; Dr. Acharya only received one other vote alongside Nepal’s. Though Indian officials did not confirm their vote, sources said Wazed was their preferred choice. India’s decision was notable, as it has been trying to build stronger ties with both Bangladesh and Nepal. Bangladesh’s concrete actions to prevent the use of its territory by terrorist groups targeting India may have convinced India to vote for Wazed. The political context, including interest from China, Sheikh Hasina’s personal involvement with her daughter’s candidacy, and Bangladesh’s upcoming elections, may have also influenced the decision. article_content: Serena Williams avenged her 2011 U.S. Open final defeat to Samantha Stosur by defeating the Australian sixth seed in straight sets at the WTA tournament in Miami on Monday, advancing to the quarterfinals. Last year, Williams entered the Flushing Meadows final as a favorite to add to her 13 Grand Slam titles but was outplayed by Stosur, who claimed her maiden major. Since then, both players have struggled—Stosur with declining form and Williams sidelined by injuries. However, Williams, a five-time champion in Miami, appears to be regaining top form. She overcame Stosur 7-5, 6-3 in a one-hour, 45-minute fourth-round match, converting four of 13 break points and improving her career record against Stosur to 5-3. Next, Williams will face Caroline Wozniacki, who beat Belgian 23rd seed Yanina Wickmayer 7-6 (8-6), 6-0. Victoria Azarenka, now world No. 1, made a dramatic comeback to reach the quarterfinals as well and stretched her perfect 2012 start to 26-0—the best season opening since Martina Hingis's 37-match run in 1997. Azarenka trailed Dominika Cibulkova 6-1, 4-0 but rallied to win 1-6, 7-6 (9-7), 7-5, making it four wins in their last five meetings and a career 7-1 edge. Afterward, Azarenka said, 'It kind of felt like she closed her eyes and just went for everything, and I couldn't open my eyes. I was blinded a little bit. My coach came on court, gave me a push to try to change something. It was more about fighting with my heart today than any particular shot.' Azarenka will next play French seventh seed Marion Bartoli, who beat Russia's Maria Kirilenko 6-1, 6-2. Second seed Maria Sharapova also advanced with a 6-4, 7-6 win over Russian compatriot Ekaterina Makarova. Sharapova, a runner-up in Miami in 2005 and 2006, will meet Chinese French Open champion Li Na, who came from behind to defeat Germany's Sabine Lisicki 3-6, 6-4, 6-2. Meanwhile, three-time Miami champion Venus Williams continued her comeback from illness by defeating Ana Ivanovic 6-7 (4-7), 6-2, 6-2. Venus, who has beaten Ivanovic in seven of their previous eight matches, will now face Polish fifth seed Agnieszka Radwanska.

article_content: Jacaranda season is beginning across Australia, with vibrant blue blossoms spreading from north to south. Jacarandas have become signature trees in many Australian cities, including Sydney, Melbourne, Adelaide, and Perth, and are common in botanic, public, and university gardens. Grafton, New South Wales, hosts an annual jacaranda festival, and Herberton in Queensland is also noted for its seasonal displays. The most common jacaranda species in Australia, Jacaranda mimosifolia, usually does not flower in Darwin due to the climate, and Hobart is generally too cold. Although jacarandas are widespread and can be mistaken for native trees, they originally come from South America and were introduced to Australia through 19th-century plant-exchange networks. The first specimens were sent by botanist Alan Cunningham, who shipped jacarandas from Rio de Janeiro to Kew Gardens in Britain around 1818. It's possible jacarandas arrived in Australia via Kew, or through Cunningham’s later postings or seed exchanges. The species was widely disseminated throughout temperate colonies, exported by the British, other colonial powers such as Portugal, and directly from South America. Jacarandas grow well from seed, but in the 19th century, propagation by cuttings was often preferred. However, for jacarandas, cuttings were not as effective. The tree remained rare until nurseryman Michael Guilfoyle or gardener George Mortimer managed to propagate it in 1868. This made jacarandas more widely available, leading to their spread throughout Australian suburbs. The earliest claimed jacaranda in Australia is in Brisbane, planted in 1864, though the Sydney Botanic Garden jacaranda is said to date from around 1850, and trees were listed for sale in Sydney by 1861. While early park and garden plantings drew attention, jacarandas became truly popular through later street plantings, especially in affluent or established suburbs. Internationally and in Australia, jacaranda avenues were often a marker of wealthier neighborhoods, as seen in places like Dunkeld (Johannesburg) and Kilimani (Nairobi). In Australia, such displays feature in suburbs like Subiaco and Applecross (Perth), Kirribilli and Paddington (Sydney), North Fitzroy (Melbourne), and St Lucia (Brisbane). The trend of planting single-species street avenues expanded in the mid-19th century with the rise of planned urban landscaping. Joseph Maiden, director of the Sydney Botanic Gardens from 1896, moved towards planting avenues of single tree species in the early 20th century, motivated by aesthetic preferences for uniformity and display. By the late 19th century, deciduous trees also gained popularity for their variety and ability to allow winter sunlight. It typically takes about ten years for jacaranda trees to become established, and between two and fourteen years to flower. Melbourne saw a rise in jacaranda plantings after the First World War, though these declined after WWII in favor of native trees. Despite localized popularity in some suburbs, jacaranda is not among Melbourne's top 50 plantings. In Queensland, early street tree planting was inconsistent, offset by active forest clearance. Organized beautification, including jacaranda avenues in places like New Farm (Brisbane), increased in the early 20th century. Notable plantings at the University of Queensland's St Lucia campus occurred in the 1930s. Jacarandas can be classified as invasive in some parts of Australia due to their ability to seed rapidly, especially in warm, dry climates. South Africa has also limited or banned jacaranda planting due to water use and invasiveness, while eucalyptus trees have a similar status there. Writer Carey Baraka observes that large jacaranda plantings in places like Kenya can reflect histories of colonial settlement. Despite environmental concerns and their colonial associations, jacarandas remain widely admired and are the subject of local myths. For example, in the southern hemisphere, university folklore holds that the first jacaranda blooms signal study time, while blossoms falling on students bring good luck. article_content: Spanish railway officials appeared before lawmakers on Thursday to address safety concerns, two weeks after a tragic derailment in northwestern Spain claimed 79 lives and injured dozens more. The ongoing investigation centers on both the actions of the train’s driver, Francisco Jose Garzon, and the adequacy of Spain’s national railway safety systems. Gonzalo Ferre Molto, president of the state-owned rail infrastructure company Adif, and Julio Gomez-Pomar, president of the state railway operator Renfe, explained current and planned measures to ensure the safety of rail passengers. 'My desire is to uncover the full truth and prevent such tragedies from ever happening again,' Ferre told lawmakers, calling it the best way to honor the victims and serve Spanish society. Officials outlined that the Madrid-to-Ferrol rail route combines both conventional and high-speed tracks. High-speed trains can exceed 200 kilometers per hour (124 mph) on certain sections. Spain employs two different safety systems: the European Rail Traffic Management System (ERTMS) for high-speed lines and ASFA for conventional tracks. The train involved had to switch between these systems during the journey, and the transition from ERTMS to ASFA occurred about four miles before the crash site, near Santiago de Compostela. Court officials say the train was travelling at 153 kph (95 mph) when it derailed—almost twice the permitted speed on the curve. Following the accident, a temporary speed limit of 30 kph was imposed on the affected section, and a permanent 60 kph limit will replace it later. Ferre described the ongoing internal investigation into rail safety, emphasizing that safety is an ever-evolving field. Renfe’s Gomez-Pomar admitted improvements could be made to existing safeguards. He noted the driver took control of the train at Ourense station approximately 35 minutes before the accident. Though Garzon began his shift about eight hours earlier, his actual time driving by that point was less than three hours. Garzon, who has worked for Renfe since 1992, had recently passed a health examination and obtained certifications to operate on the line and the specific train type. According to Gomez-Pomar, over 7,000 trains have passed safely through the area where the derailment occurred. Some lawmakers, including Rosana Perez of the Mixed Group and Gaspar Llamazares of United Left, expressed concern that the investigation and public discussion were placing excessive blame on the driver alone. They suggested measures like increasing the number of crew members on board to reduce risk from human error. As the investigation into the July 24 crash continues, 38 people remain hospitalized—six in critical condition. Driver Garzon faces 79 charges of homicide by professional recklessness and additional charges of causing injury. He has been released conditionally and handed over his passport. Authorities heard from three witnesses in a closed court session on Thursday: a station manager and two local residents who assisted survivors. Shortly before the derailment, Garzon reportedly received work-related instructions via phone from a Renfe staff member. The accident occurred near the end of the scheduled six-hour journey. The nation continues to mourn, with further inquiries underway.

The Canadian Coast Guard successfully completed the evacuation of passengers from the cruise ship Clipper Adventurer on Monday, after the vessel ran aground on an unmapped rock. Officials aboard the ship first reported the incident on Friday. Attempts by the crew to refloat the ship during high tide on Saturday were unsuccessful. On Sunday, the Coast Guard icebreaker Amundsen arrived to assist and began transporting people to safety.

"All 128 passengers were safely moved from the Amundsen to the community of Kugluktuk," said Theresa Nichols, spokeswoman for the Canadian Coast Guard. The ship also had 69 crew members, according to Nichols.

Kugluktuk, located on the shore of the Arctic Ocean, served as the initial landing point for evacuees. The cruise company has arranged accommodations for the passengers, who are now expected to fly to Edmonton, Canada.

Although the Clipper Adventurer remains grounded, the ship is in a stable condition but is listing slightly, according to Adventure Canada, the company that operates the vessel. During the ordeal, passengers participated in on-board activities and some even enjoyed time on the ship's deck.

article_content: Donald Trump, the leading Republican presidential candidate, announced at a campaign event in Fort Dodge, Iowa, that he would end the Indo-Pacific Economic Framework (IPEF) trade pact—calling it 'TPP Two'—if he is elected in 2024. Trump criticized the Biden administration's negotiations with 13 countries on the trade agreement, arguing it would negatively affect U.S. manufacturing and cause job losses. The IPEF, intended as an alternative to China's economic influence, has faced setbacks as countries like Vietnam and Indonesia declined to commit to strong labor and environmental standards. Trump, who withdrew the U.S. from the original Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP) in 2017 during his presidency, said he would immediately cancel this new trade pact if he takes office. He warned that the agreement could harm American farmers and manufacturers, describing it as another effort to increase outsourcing to Asia. The Biden administration hoped to finalize key aspects of IPEF before the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, but resistance from some countries and pressures due to the upcoming U.S. election make a final agreement unlikely, according to experts and business groups. In related news, hotel and airfare prices in Ahmedabad soared before the India-Australia cricket World Cup final; OpenAI dismissed CEO Sam Altman amid internal debate; and the Indian government approved IT hardware manufacturing proposals from 27 companies, including Dell, HP, and Lenovo.
