article_content: India's High Commissioner to Canada, Sanjay Kumar Verma, has reiterated that India had no involvement in the killing of Khalistani separatist Hardeep Singh Nijjar in Canada. Speaking to CTV News, Verma criticized Canada for making accusations before its investigation was complete, expressing concern that India was being judged without due process. Diplomatic relations between India and Canada have been tense since Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau alleged in September that Indian agents could be linked to Nijjar’s killing on June 18 in British Columbia. India had classified Nijjar as a terrorist in 2020 and has strongly denied the allegations, dismissing them as 'absurd' and 'motivated'. Verma clarified that India is prepared to assess any specific and relevant information provided by Canadian authorities, but views the demands for 'cooperation' as unwarranted. He emphasized that India would examine concrete evidence if supplied. Highlighting India’s legal and constitutional framework, Verma stated that India’s core concern is the alleged use of Canadian soil by some citizens to challenge India’s sovereignty, referencing the activities of the Sikh separatist movement. He asserted that individuals associated with the Khalistani cause in Canada are involved in criminal enterprises, including drug trafficking, arms smuggling, and human trafficking, which also affect India. Verma referenced Interpol red corner notices shared with Canada, including one for Nijjar, as evidence of these threats. According to Verma, India considers these individuals terrorists rather than separatists, due to their involvement in financing and supporting criminal networks operating against India. He questioned the legitimacy of holding referendums in Canada aimed at partitioning India, arguing this contravenes international law. Verma also noted that India resumed e-visa services for Canadians after a reassessment found improved security conditions, following the previous suspension. He expressed optimism about ongoing discussions between the two countries, saying relations are improving and dialogue has become more constructive. Additionally, the article briefly highlights trends showing reduced electronic goods imports, a potential leadership change at PepsiCo India, banking sector concerns over related-party loan renewals, and various business news updates.

article_content: Henri Lansbury has solidified his future at Nottingham Forest by signing a new three-year contract with the club. This enhanced deal reportedly raises him among Forest’s top earners. The 23-year-old midfielder had drawn attention from Burnley, who previously had a £3.5 million bid rejected. Even though Burnley contemplated increasing their offer to £4 million at the last minute, they did not go ahead with it. Despite being tempted by the possibility of joining a Premier League team, Lansbury chose to remain with Forest after this week’s improved terms, following an earlier reluctance to sign a prior offer from owner Fawaz Al-Hasawi. Manager Stuart Pearce was instrumental in convincing Lansbury to stay, expressing pleasure that such committed players are continuing with the club on a long-term basis. Lansbury has yet to play for Forest this season, having picked up an injury in a friendly against Porto B last month. Nevertheless, after featuring in a practice match on Thursday, he is expected to be back to full fitness soon.

article_content: On Monday, science fiction met reality when William Shatner took part in NASA’s latest space shuttle mission. Renowned for his role as Captain James T. Kirk in the original "Star Trek" TV series and movies, Shatner, now 79, reprised his iconic monologue to wake up the crew of the space shuttle Discovery at 3:23 a.m. ET. Speaking over the classic "Star Trek" theme, he said: "Space, the final frontier. These have been the voyages of the space shuttle Discovery. Her 30-year mission: To seek out new science. To build new outposts. To bring nations together on the final frontier. To boldly go, and do, what no spacecraft has done before." This event marked Discovery’s final scheduled mission. Over its career, the spacecraft has completed 39 flights, including 13 journeys to the International Space Station. Discovery undocked from the station for the last time at 8:37 a.m., according to NASA, and is now preparing to return to Earth. The shuttle is set to land at Florida’s Kennedy Space Center just before noon on Wednesday, a day later than first planned. NASA’s nearly three-decade shuttle program is scheduled to come to a close later this year. CNN’s Ric Ward contributed to this report.

article_content: Prime Minister David Cameron delivered a notably religious Christmas message, quoting from the Gospel of St John as he addressed the nation. His statement comes during ongoing debate about the government's plan to introduce gay marriage, which is set for a vote in the Commons in the New Year. Cameron has been criticized by church leaders and MPs over the proposed legislation. In his message, he called Jesus 'the light of all mankind' and the 'Prince of Peace.' He reflected on the year's major events, including the Olympic Games and the Queen's Diamond Jubilee, applauding the efforts of the Armed Forces. The Prime Minister emphasized the importance of the Christmas story and the hope offered by the birth of Jesus Christ, noting, 'Christmas gives us the opportunity to remember the Christmas story—the story about the birth of Jesus Christ and the hope that he brings to the countless millions who follow him.' Quoting the Gospel of John, Cameron said, 'in this man was life, and that his life was the light of all mankind, and that he came with grace, truth and love. Indeed, God’s word reminds us that Jesus was the Prince of Peace.' He concluded with a wish for a happy and peaceful Christmas to everyone, regardless of how they celebrate. The Bishop of Leicester and other church figures have accused Cameron of being out of touch with most practicing religious people, despite assurances that no church would be obliged to conduct same-sex marriages. Previously, Cameron described himself as a 'vaguely practising' Christian who appreciates the role of the Bible in British values, even while admitting doubts about theological issues. In his Christmas message, Cameron also paid tribute to servicemen and women overseas, their families who would be apart from them, and emergency service workers supporting those in need, asking the public to keep them in their thoughts and appreciation during the festive season.

article_content: More foreign nationals are preparing to leave the besieged Gaza Strip on Thursday, as authorities in the enclave reported at least 195 Palestinians killed in Israeli strikes on the Jabalia refugee camp—attacks United Nations human rights officials say could amount to war crimes. At least 320 foreign nationals from an initial list of 500, along with dozens of severely injured Gazans, crossed into Egypt on Wednesday under an agreement among Israel, Egypt, and Hamas. Passport holders from Australia, Austria, Bulgaria, the Czech Republic, Finland, Indonesia, Italy, Japan, Jordan, the United Kingdom, and the United States were among those evacuated. Gaza border officials indicated the crossing would reopen Thursday to allow more foreign citizens to exit. A diplomatic source estimated about 7,500 foreign passport holders will leave Gaza over the next two weeks. As Israel pushes forward with its offensive against Hamas, the military has conducted attacks by air, land, and sea to dismantle the Islamist group after its assault across the border into southern Israel on October 7. Israel reported that Hamas killed 1,400 people, mostly civilians, and took over 200 hostages during the attack. Loud explosions were reported early Thursday near al-Quds hospital in densely populated Gaza City, according to the Palestinian Red Crescent. Israeli authorities have previously ordered the hospital to evacuate, but UN officials state this could endanger patients. ISRAEL: TWO HAMAS COMMANDERS KILLED Israeli military sources reported that two Hamas commanders were killed in strikes on Tuesday and Wednesday in Jabalia, Gaza’s largest refugee camp. Israel claims Hamas operated command centers and infrastructure under and around civilian areas, putting residents at risk. On Thursday, Gaza’s government media office reported at least 195 Palestinians killed in the two attacks on Jabalia, with 120 still missing and at least 777 wounded. On Wednesday, Palestinians searched the rubble for survivors. 'It is a massacre,' one witness said. UN human rights officials said the strikes on the camp could constitute war crimes. 'Given the high number of civilian casualties and scale of destruction after Israeli air strikes on Jabalia refugee camp, we have serious concerns these are disproportionate attacks that could amount to war crimes,' the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights posted on X. As the international community increasingly calls for a humanitarian pause, conditions in Gaza have worsened under Israel’s assault and stricter blockade, with shortages of food, fuel, clean water, and medicine. Dr. Fathi Abu al-Hassan, a US passport holder waiting to cross into Egypt on Wednesday, described extreme hardships within Gaza. 'We open our eyes on dead people and close our eyes on dead people,' he said. Many hospitals are struggling as fuel shortages force shutdowns, including Gaza’s only cancer hospital. Israel has blocked humanitarian convoys from delivering fuel, fearing Hamas could divert it for military purposes. Ashraf Al-Qudra, spokesperson for Gaza's health ministry, said Thursday that the main generator at the Indonesian Hospital had stopped working due to lack of fuel. The hospital switched to a backup generator but could no longer power mortuary refrigerators or oxygen generators. 'If we do not get fuel in the next few days, we will inevitably reach disaster,' Al-Qudra warned. DIPLOMATIC AND LEGISLATIVE MOVES US Secretary of State Antony Blinken is scheduled to depart Thursday for his second visit to Israel in less than a month. He will meet Israeli officials, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, to express solidarity while stressing the need to minimize Palestinian civilian casualties, according to his spokesperson. Blinken will also visit Jordan, which has normalized ties with Israel. On Wednesday, Jordan withdrew its ambassador from Tel Aviv over Israel’s actions in Gaza, a decision Israel called regrettable. In Jordan, Blinken will underline the importance of protecting civilians and reaffirm US opposition to forced displacement of Palestinians from Gaza. He will also work with Egypt and Qatar to negotiate the release of hostages held by Hamas, said spokesperson Matthew Miller. On Thursday, the US House of Representatives may pass a $14.3 billion aid package for Israel, backed by Republicans, but it is unlikely to become law due to opposition in the Democratic-controlled Senate and a veto threat. President Joe Biden has proposed a broader $106 billion package, including aid for Ukraine, border security, humanitarian efforts, and Israel. Israeli ground forces entered Gaza late last week, following weeks of air and artillery strikes, in response to the October 7 attack by Hamas. Gaza’s health ministry reports at least 8,796 Palestinians, including 3,648 children, have been killed by Israeli strikes since October 7.

Abdalrahim Alfarra, the chief Palestinian diplomat to the European Union, whose family remains in Gaza, has expressed deep disappointment over the Western response to the ongoing conflict. After a deadly explosion at Gaza’s al-Ahli Arab Hospital this week, Alfarra voiced his hope that EU leaders would show visible solidarity with Palestinian victims, but he awoke to the reality that such support was absent.

Following Hamas’s deadly assault in Israel, EU officials in Brussels held vigils to honor Israeli victims, and landmarks across Europe were illuminated in Israel’s flag colors. Alfarra noted a lack of similarly strong sympathy for the thousands of Palestinians who have since died amid Israeli military operations in Gaza. His own family is currently in Gaza, facing ongoing hardship. He holds the EU accountable for what he calls its 'silence' on the suffering of Gazan civilians.

The cause of the blast at al-Ahli Arab Hospital remains disputed, with both Israel and Palestinian Islamic Jihad blaming each other. Alfarra said he was dismayed by what he views as insufficient response from both the EU and the US. During a virtual EU summit held during the hospital incident, leaders opened with a minute of silence for victims in Israel and Palestine, as well as recent attacks in France and Belgium, but continued their meeting and focused statements on support for Israel’s right to self-defense under international law. Statements of solidarity with hospital victims from EU leaders followed later, in some cases a day after the explosion.

Alfarra has been working with other Arab diplomats in Brussels to urge the EU to support Palestinians more assertively. He cited a recent shift where the EU reversed a decision to cut aid to the Palestinian territories, instead pledging 75 million euros in humanitarian support. He calls for the EU to put pressure on Israel to fully open border crossings and ensure humanitarian aid reaches Gaza.

Alfarra also warned about the impact of the conflict on diaspora communities and accused Israel of waging an 'information war.' He referred to the killing of a six-year-old Palestinian American boy in the US, attributing it to the spread of negative portrayals of Palestinians. Alfarra argued that ongoing silence from the international community could further endanger civilians in Gaza, and he urged global leaders to condemn all violence and seek a swift resolution to the conflict.

article_content: CM Punk has made a dramatic return to WWE after nearly ten years away. Fans erupted with cheers when his entrance music played at the Survivor Series event in Chicago on Saturday night. Punk originally left WWE in 2014, having voiced frustrations over creative decisions and concerns about the quality of medical care he received. Recently, speculation mounted about the 45-year-old's return after he departed rival wrestling promotion All Elite Wrestling (AEW). WWE’s chief content officer, Triple H, described Punk’s comeback as a last-minute decision, saying, 'This was one of those lightning in a bottle moments that came together very quickly, but we are incredibly excited about it.' He explained that plans only started to come together after most people had stopped expecting it. Triple H also noted that Punk had often said he wouldn’t return to WWE. He added, 'If you are the same person you were 10 years ago, 10 years later, you’ve messed up. Everybody grows, everybody changes. I’m a different person, he’s a different person, this is a different company, and we’re all starting fresh.' After his 2014 exit, CM Punk—real name Phil Brooks—briefly competed in MMA with UFC before signing with AEW in 2021. He left AEW earlier this year after their All In event at Wembley Stadium. Punk did not wrestle during his unexpected WWE appearance and did not enter the ring, but his return still caused a frenzy among fans. Social media was abuzz, with one person calling it 'the biggest pop in history of wrestling.' Fan Joe Clarkson told BBC Newsbeat Punk’s return was 'a complete and utter shock.' Having attended Punk’s last AEW match, Clarkson never expected to see him in wrestling again. 'There are plenty of people in wrestling who cannot stand him, but so many love him. He’s always a conversation starter—a star like CM Punk doesn’t come around often,' he said. WWE fan Sabrina Nicole said Punk’s return makes it 'an exciting time to be a wrestling fan.' She was watching Survivor Series and got chills hearing his music. Nicole looks forward to what’s next for Punk, possibly including a rivalry with Seth Rollins, who was seen looking displeased at his return. 'It feels surreal to see CM Punk back. I’ve always been a fan despite the ups and downs.' During the show, Randy Orton, who also made a comeback after over a year away due to injury, was in the ring as Punk appeared, and the two shared a smile. WWE star Cody Rhodes commented, 'If he can help with where we’re going and what we’re doing, absolutely welcome aboard. I have a feeling the CM Punk we’re getting is hungry, and that’s the best.' On Tuesday, India successfully test-fired its surface-to-surface short-range ballistic missile (SRBM) 'Pralay' from Abdul Kalam Island off the Odisha coast, a Defence official confirmed. Developed by the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO), the missile is designed to address India's defense requirements along its borders with China and Pakistan.

The 'Pralay' missile was launched around 9:50 am and achieved all mission objectives. Tracking instruments monitored its trajectory along the coastline. 'Pralay' offers a range of 350-500 kilometers and carries a payload capacity of 500-1,000 kilograms. This solid-fuel battlefield missile is based on the Prithvi Defence Vehicle platform.

According to the official, 'Pralay' has been developed for deployment along the Line of Actual Control (LAC) and Line of Control (LoC). The missile is comparable to China's 'Dong Feng 12' and Russia's 'Iskander', which is currently in use in the conflict in Ukraine. Pakistan also possesses tactical ballistic missiles as part of its defense arsenal.

article_content: President Barack Obama has decided to postpone any executive action on immigration until after the November congressional elections, according to White House officials. This shift delays Obama's previous pledge to act by the end of summer and has sparked frustration among immigration advocates, while providing relief to vulnerable Democrats facing tough Senate re-election battles. Two White House officials, speaking on the condition of anonymity, explained that the president determined taking executive action on immigration during the campaign season would politicize the issue and potentially jeopardize future efforts for comprehensive reform. Obama reached this decision on Friday while returning from a NATO summit in Wales, notifying allies via phone calls from Air Force One and later from the White House. The officials added that while there is no specific new timeline, executive action is still expected before the end of the year. Back in June, Obama had instructed Homeland Security Secretary Jeh Johnson and Attorney General Eric Holder to provide recommendations for executive action by summer's end, pledging to adopt those recommendations promptly. However, competing pressures emerged: advocacy groups demanded swift action while Democrats fretted that action before midterms would mobilize Republican opposition against embattled incumbents. Senators Mark Pryor of Arkansas, Mary Landrieu of Louisiana, and Kay Hagan of North Carolina were cited as particularly vulnerable. White House advisers were unsure that presidential action would significantly impact election outcomes, but discussions about timing grew more urgent as the elections approached. Officials referenced the Democratic losses of 1994, attributed to votes on gun-control legislation, as a cautionary example. The president’s decision drew sharp criticism from advocacy groups. Frank Sharry of America’s Voice said, 'We are bitterly disappointed in the president and in Senate Democrats,' accusing them of choosing politics over resolving real problems. Cristina Jimenez of United We Dream called the move 'another slap in the face to the Latino and immigrant community,' citing broken promises and insufficient political courage. Recent months saw partisan conflict over how to address a surge of unaccompanied minors crossing from Central America at the U.S.-Mexico border. Obama had requested $3.7 billion to manage the crisis, but the Republican-controlled House approved much less and made it easier to deport minors—measures opposed by Democrats and advocates. Congress adjourned without passing a final bill. The number of unaccompanied minors crossing has declined since June, and Congress’s summer recess has shifted attention away for now. Broader tensions remain over comprehensive immigration reform and the fate of approximately 11 million undocumented immigrants. The Senate passed bipartisan immigration reform in 2013, but the House, led by Speaker John Boehner, refused to act, prompting Obama’s vow to proceed unilaterally. At the NATO summit in Wales, Obama reaffirmed his intent to take executive action, emphasizing increased border security, streamlined processing, and a pathway to legal residency for some undocumented immigrants, including payment of taxes and learning English. He stressed, 'In the absence of action by Congress, I'm going to do what I can within the legal constraints of my office, because it's the right thing to do.' Legal and political debates continue over the extent of the president's authority. Some Democrats prefer allowing Congress to act, while pro-immigration groups urged Obama to fulfill his promise without delay. National Council of La Raza and the League of United Latin American Citizens joined advocacy letters urging him to show leadership and courage during this critical moment.

article_content: Walking along a country road in hiking shoes with a rucksack, Kathleen Chitty may seem like an unlikely muse, yet she inspired one of America’s legendary songwriters and helped launch his international career. Her quiet life in a Welsh-speaking village now gives few clues to her global notoriety. Chitty inspired Paul Simon—half of the famed Simon and Garfunkel duo—and played a major role in his formative years. Paul Simon was so taken with her that they appeared together on his first album cover. She is referenced in several of his works, such as 'America,' and their romance was immortalized in 'Kathy’s Song.' The overwhelming attention from fans and the media led Chitty to withdraw from the spotlight. She now resides in a peaceful three-bedroom house and commutes to her longtime job as an administrator at a technical college, where she has worked for over 25 years. Simon called their relationship his 'most peaceful time,' a sentiment echoed in his lyrics. This contrasts with his more recent experiences—at 72, Simon appeared in court alongside his third wife, Edie Brickell, following a domestic dispute. Decades after they met, Chitty, now 68, still resembles the teenager Simon once loved. In 1963, passionate about folk music, she met Simon at a Brentwood, Essex folk club while selling tickets; Simon had arrived in England after facing challenges gaining fame in the U.S. Her gentleness and reserved nature captivated Simon, and the two entered into an intense relationship. During this period, Simon wrote many songs that he later performed with Art Garfunkel. Kathy is mentioned by name in 'America,' and 'Homeward Bound' describes his longing to return to her. 'Kathy’s Song' reflects Simon’s feelings for her from afar, longing for England while in New York. As Simon's popularity grew, Chitty, uncomfortable with the spotlight, left the U.S. in the mid-1960s. Now, Chitty lives near a mountain village in North Wales with her partner of over 40 years, Kenneth Harrison, with whom she has three children. Harrison explained their move from Essex in the early 1970s was to gain privacy and confirmed there was never any rift between them and Simon. Harrison, a former journalist and friend to both, reminisced about the folk scene, noting that the song 'America' has lasting significance. At 68, Chitty maintains her distinct features and continues part-time administrative work at a technical college. She still receives interview requests about her time with Simon but always declines. Harrison affirms that she remains a private person, unwilling to speak publicly about her past. Friends note the breakup with Simon was traumatic and public attention was difficult for Chitty. She walks daily to catch her bus, is known for her friendly but shy demeanor, and her three grown children now live in London. Paul Simon later married Peggy Harper, with whom he had a son, Ben, divorcing in 1975. He then married actress Carrie Fisher for two years, and since 1992 has been married to Edie Brickell, with whom he has three children: Adrian, Lulu, and Gabriel. A recent incident led police to Simon and Brickell's home after a 911 call, with both reported to have minor injuries. In court, Simon said the two were 'fine together.' They are set to appear again on May 16 on disorderly conduct charges. Simon has received 12 Grammy Awards as a solo artist and as part of Simon and Garfunkel. His notable songs include 'Mrs Robinson,' 'Bridge Over Troubled Water,' and 'Graceland.'

article_content: On Monday, New Jersey formally expressed 'profound regret' for its involvement in slavery, becoming the first state north of the Mason-Dixon line to pass a slavery apology resolution. The measure does not require a signature from New Jersey Governor Jon Corzine to become official. A committee of the New Jersey Assembly approved the resolution last Thursday, one of several necessary steps before the end of the legislative session on Monday. Both the Assembly and Senate voted overwhelmingly—29 to 2—to approve the resolution. The resolution declares that the 'fundamental values of Africans were shattered; they were brutalized, humiliated, and dehumanized.' It notes that New Jersey had about 12,000 enslaved people, one of the largest populations in the northern colonies, and was the last northern state to emancipate slaves in 1846. If the measure had failed, the process would have had to start over. The resolution becomes official when filed with the secretary of state. This symbolic apology follows similar actions taken in 2007 by Alabama, Maryland, North Carolina, and Virginia.

article_content: Iran's state TV broadcaster, Press TV, was taken off air in the UK after the British media regulator Ofcom revoked its licence, in a move that could heighten diplomatic tensions with Iran. Ofcom determined that Press TV failed to declare that its editorial base was in Tehran, not London, when granted its licence. The regulator noted that 'editorial control of the channel rested with Press TV International (based in Tehran)'. Press TV presenters have included former MP George Galloway and Lauren Booth, Tony Blair's sister-in-law. Ofcom fined Press TV £100,000 after the channel broadcast an interview with a journalist held in an Iranian prison, which the regulator said was 'obtained under duress'. Ofcom reported that Press TV indicated it is unwilling and unable to pay the fine. This development comes after the UK closed Iran's embassy in London and expelled staff in November, following a protest at the British embassy in Tehran. Mr. Galloway expressed his dissatisfaction on Twitter, criticizing the British government's decision to remove Press TV from Sky. Other presenters for Press TV include former London Mayor Ken Livingstone and journalist Yvonne Ridley, who was kidnapped by the Taliban in Afghanistan in 2001. Press TV states on its website that it aims to broadcast underreported perspectives from around the world. The channel has previously been reprimanded by Ofcom for breaching impartiality regulations, notably in a programme hosted by Mr. Galloway that was found to lack due impartiality regarding Israel. Press TV's English-language service was removed from Sky TV's satellite platform, but continues to be available online. Ofcom stated that Press TV was offered the option to obtain a licence based on its operations in Tehran, but did not respond. In a letter, Press TV's chief executive Mohammad Sarafraz claimed Ofcom’s actions were part of an effort to silence alternative viewpoints in the UK, particularly the channel’s critical coverage of the UK’s foreign policy in Iraq and Afghanistan. Press TV said it will strive to continue reaching UK audiences and claimed it had been targeted due to airing critical views on Britain's role in international conflicts.

Some users have stated that after using BMW’s wireless charging pad, their phones display a 'Could Not Set Up Apple Pay' error and can no longer access tickets stored in Apple Wallet or use the device as a digital car key. The affected phones reportedly enter recovery mode and cannot be fixed by rebooting or resetting. These concerns have been raised on MacRumors forums and on Twitter/X. Overheating in the iPhone 15 models, previously linked to an iOS 17 glitch, may be worsened by wireless charging, especially in warm cars. Although the main reports involve the iPhone 15 Pro and Pro Max, users of the iPhone 15 and iPhone 15 Plus are also advised to avoid charging via BMW’s wireless charger. Multiple BMW models, including the X5, have been implicated in these reports. BMW confirmed to Gizmodo that they are currently investigating the issue with Apple and hope to provide answers soon.

article_content: Google Maps and Waze have suspended live traffic updates for regions in Israel and the Gaza Strip at the request of the Israeli military, as reported by Bloomberg. The decision was made ahead of a possible ground invasion to enhance the safety of local communities. A Google spokesperson told Gizmodo, "As we have done previously in conflict situations, and in response to the evolving situation in the region, we have temporarily disabled the ability to see live traffic conditions and busyness information out of consideration for the safety of local communities." Live traffic data can expose sensitive information, such as troop movements or areas where people have gathered in large numbers. These technologies aggregate anonymous location data to detect traffic delays. This approach has precedent: last year, Google disabled live traffic in Ukraine to protect citizens following the Russian invasion. Early in the war, some civilians reportedly used Google Maps to identify the invasion by observing traffic patterns before any official announcements. According to Motherboard, an open-source intelligence expert and college professor detected a traffic jam inside Russia using Google Maps' live traffic layer. In the affected areas of Israel and Gaza, Waze displays a pop-up alert reading, "Due to the security situation: Other drivers, traffic jams, and other alerts will not be displayed," according to 9to5Google. Waze is reportedly still operational in other parts of Israel, such as Tel Aviv, though Google Maps has disabled live traffic data across the entire country. Users in these regions can still use both apps for navigation and to receive estimated arrival times based on current conditions, but without detailed information about traffic congestion. Apple Maps has also reportedly turned off its live traffic features, as first observed by Israeli tech publication GeekTime. Apple has not yet commented on the change in response to Gizmodo's inquiry.

article_content: Australian-born actor Rod Taylor, best known for starring in Alfred Hitchcock's thriller 'The Birds', died this week in Los Angeles at the age of 84. He passed away at home on Wednesday, surrounded by his family and loved ones, according to his daughter, Felicia Taylor. No cause of death was provided. Felicia Taylor described her father as passionate about acting, calling it his life's work and an honorable art form. Rod Taylor appeared in numerous films, including 'The Time Machine', 'The Train Robbers', 'Sunday in New York', and 'The Catered Affair'. Tippi Hedren, Taylor's co-star in 'The Birds', shared fond memories of their friendship, calling him fun, thoughtful, and classy. Taylor was born in Sydney, the only child of a steel contractor father and a writer mother. He attended a fine arts college and theater school in Sydney before moving to Hollywood in the 1950s, where he steadily gained recognition with a series of prominent roles. In his final role, Taylor played Winston Churchill in the 2009 film 'Inglourious Basterds', alongside Brad Pitt. Taylor is survived by his wife of more than thirty years, Carol, and his daughter Felicia, a former CNN News correspondent. CNN's Veronica George contributed to this report.

article_content: With swine flu fears on the rise worldwide, demand for face masks has surged. In Mexico City, so many masks were distributed that supplies quickly ran low, and similar shortages are being reported by European pharmacies and U.S. manufacturers. Nonetheless, medical experts generally agree that masks are mainly effective at preventing sick individuals from spreading viruses, rather than shielding healthy people. Dr. Richard Besser, acting CDC director, said there isn’t strong evidence that masks protect the general public, unless someone is in close contact with an infected individual. He noted, 'We don't recommend the routine use of masks by people at work as a precaution.' The World Health Organization and the UK's Health Protection Agency have also advised against masks for the healthy public, with WHO spokesperson Sarah Cumberland telling CNN that masks are most valuable for people already showing symptoms to avoid passing germs to others. Dr. Arthur Reingold of UC Berkeley’s School of Public Health mentioned that, although the benefit of surgical masks for stopping swine flu isn’t fully known, it does make sense for sick people to wear them to help prevent spreading the virus via coughs and sneezes. N95 respirators, which offer higher filtration and a tighter fit, provide more protection but are less comfortable, more expensive, and require special fitting. These are better suited for high-risk settings such as laboratories. Dr. Julio Frenk, former Mexican health minister and current dean at Harvard, pointed out that masks serve as a reminder to maintain social distance and avoid behaviors like handshakes and kisses during an outbreak. For healthcare workers, high-efficiency masks are essential, but the general U.S. population doesn't need them while the disease remains localized. On the other hand, in Mexico—especially in densely populated areas—school closures and other public health measures have become necessary, with schools staying shut until at least May 6. By early Tuesday, Mexico’s health minister reported 152 suspected swine flu deaths and over 1,600 cases. The WHO escalated its alert to phase 4 out of 6, indicating a significant spread of the virus, though it is not yet a global pandemic. According to the CDC, people should consider wearing a mask if they are ill, live with someone sick, or need to be in crowded places. Caregivers for those with flu-like symptoms should consider respirators like the N95. Nevertheless, the CDC emphasizes the importance of handwashing, covering coughs, and avoiding close physical greetings over universal mask-wearing.

article_content: Every year on World AIDS Day, veterans like me are invited to speak to interested audiences, but the main themes often feel increasingly empty and routine. From 2011 to 2015, the global theme for World AIDS Day designated by UNAIDS is 'Getting to zero'—zero new HIV infections, zero discrimination, and zero AIDS-related deaths. I find this goal unrealistic, as such outcomes are not currently attainable. World AIDS Day is an opportunity for organizations to share recent statistics, but there’s a sense that it becomes an excuse for governments to overlook the issue after the day passes. Effective HIV treatments, available since 1996, have promptly reduced mortality rates worldwide, so fewer people under 30 have witnessed the scale of loss experienced by earlier generations. Yet now, more gay men in many countries, including Britain, are living with HIV than ever before, and rates of new infections remain high. In the UK, 6,364 new cases were reported last year, up from 2,938 in 1998, with infections among gay men reaching a record high. Young people are disproportionately affected—not due to recklessness, but because many lacked access to the early AIDS charities, self-help groups, and targeted education campaigns established by the previous generation. Many older gay men hesitate to share their experiences, so younger men may not learn about the epidemic's complexity. The subject is more taboo than ever, and it is unfair to accuse young gay men of apathy when many lack reliable information. HIV has become less visible in public discourse, as few wish to be identified mainly by a medical diagnosis, which has also contributed to hiding the epidemic. Positive messaging about treatments may reassure those newly diagnosed, but could also unintentionally lead some to underestimate the seriousness of HIV. HIV remains a lifelong condition that cannot be reversed, and diagnosis means ongoing medical appointments and medication, with associated side effects and social stigma. Stigma is still widespread, sometimes even from within the gay community, and stopping treatment can result in serious health consequences. It's unhelpful and dishonest to use fear to promote behavior change, but HIV is still a serious, incurable disease that can profoundly affect relationships. Contemporary issues include the long-term psychological effects for older gay men and the need for better education and support—especially about testing—in communities at higher risk, such as African residents and gay men in the UK. Many gay men grow up with low self-esteem, often focusing more on physical appearance than emotional well-being. Rather than apathy, alliances—especially between different generations—are crucial to addressing ongoing challenges. Unlike overwhelming global issues, specific, achievable goals exist in HIV prevention if addressed with collective effort. Early progress against AIDS was built on grassroots self-help organizations, highlighting the lasting importance of testing campaigns and condom education. Many gay men have avoided infection by consistently practicing safer sex, and while new preventive methods are emerging, using condoms remains vital. If current rates of new infections among gay men occurred in other groups, the response would likely be far more intense. Decades ago I wrote that, until gay men are provided with the resources to address this ongoing health crisis, it may seem as though the community is regarded as disposable. Although progress has been made in some parts of the world, in many areas the struggle continues. The views expressed are solely those of Simon Watney.

article_content: The Super Eagles squad is set to arrive in Kigali, Rwanda—Zimbabwe’s adopted home—early Saturday morning for their second group match against the Warriors, according to PUNCH Sports Extra. Players and officials departed Nigeria’s Victor Attah International Airport Friday night on a chartered flight and are expected to land in Kigali at dawn, ahead of a two-hour road trip to Butare, where the match will take place at Huye Stadium. Huye Stadium seats 20,000 and features an artificial turf, but the Eagles have stated they are focused on getting all three points, not the playing surface. Following a 1-1 draw against Lesotho in Uyo on Thursday, coach Jose Peseiro and his team are determined to approach the remaining nine qualifying matches with a stronger mentality, aiming for victory each time. Given Rwanda’s high-altitude conditions, the team decided to arrive, complete their official training, and play the match before the unfamiliar climate could affect their performance. Zimbabwe, who drew 1-1 with Rwanda in their first fixture, have been training on Huye Stadium’s artificial turf since arriving last weekend. The match between the Super Eagles and Warriors will kick off at 3 pm Rwanda time (1 pm Nigeria time) Sunday. A win will bring the Super Eagles to four points after two group matches. Yohannes Ghirmai Ghebregziabher of Eritrea will serve as referee assessor, and Raphael Lyson Humba of Malawi will be match commissioner.

article_content: At the IIA conference, Ron Miasnik discussed the expanding influence of artificial intelligence, noting its potential to impact everything from infrastructure to technological advancements, including the creation of synthetic speech. He challenged audiences to figure out how to move AI innovations out of labs and scale them through startups. Miasnik, a product manager and entrepreneur who invests in early-stage technology companies, described the rapid growth of the AI market, now at $12 billion this year compared to under $5 billion in each of the previous two years. He pointed out that firms such as Nvidia and Chagg are seeing large AI-related investments. He observed that attention is increasingly focused on AI breakthroughs, particularly from MIT’s CSAIL, with researchers using AI to expand their impact. Miasnik offered four key strategies for startups to succeed in the growing AI space: One, pursue big, transformative ideas, such as developing personalized AI tools or technologies for unstructured data management—areas with potential for major impact. Two, he advised targeting specific, specialized market niches, arguing that innovation often comes from those who take unique approaches rather than copying the mainstream. Three, referencing Jeff Bezos’s idea of 'customer obsession,' Miasnik emphasized putting customers first before product or technology development. Fourth, he spoke about market hype as a valuable tool, suggesting the Gartner hype cycle serves as a useful guide for navigating the ups and downs of AI’s evolving landscape. He noted it will take decades to fully develop the AI industry. Miasnik concluded by commending MIT’s success in turning research into business ventures. He encouraged entrepreneurs to take advantage of the current momentum—assemble strong teams, secure funding, and pursue global impact—saying this is an ideal time to shape the future with AI.

Oliver Benjamin, an American writer and former graphic designer, founded the alternative religion Dudeism in 2005, drawing inspiration from "The Dude,” the laidback character played by Jeff Bridges in the Coen Brothers’ classic, The Big Lebowski. Known as 'The Dudely Lama,' Benjamin created the Church of the Latter-Day Dude, a modern spiritual movement emphasizing relaxation, rationality, and humor over dogma.

Since its inception, more than 250,000 people have become Dudeist priests, with some officiating at ceremonies such as weddings. Though some critics have questioned the religion’s seriousness, Benjamin argues that Dudeism fills a gap left by traditional religions—offering a rational yet lighthearted worldview.

Currently residing in Thailand, Benjamin devotes himself to Dudeism full time, enjoying a relaxed lifestyle in line with the movement’s ethos. He explains that Dudeism is an "open-source" religion designed to suit contemporary sensibilities, free from rigid doctrines and hierarchy.

The Big Lebowski, which inspired the faith, follows Jeffrey ‘The Dude’ Lebowski, who becomes embroiled in a bizarre kidnapping plot due to mistaken identity. The film has become a cult classic, grossing over $40 million worldwide and earning critical acclaim.

Benjamin, who grew up in Los Angeles and studied Psychology at UCLA, admits that his own party-filled student days parallel The Dude’s easygoing approach. He has appeared alongside Jeff Dowd (the real-life inspiration for The Dude) and several actors from the film, becoming a recognizable figure within the community.

The unexpected rise of Dudeism has reportedly surprised both the Coen Brothers and Jeff Bridges, with Bridges describing himself as "flabbergasted" by the movement’s popularity.

After leading the Church of the Latter-Day Dude for nearly a decade, Benjamin is contemplating handing over leadership but says the structure is still evolving. He meets Dudeists around the globe and remains content with the movement’s distinctive approach to life.

For more information about Dudeism, visit its website: www.dudeism.com.

article_content: For many years, Susan Stamberg has upheld the tradition of sharing her late mother-in-law's cranberry relish recipe on the radio every Thanksgiving. This year, she's introducing something new—a cranberry chutney recipe from renowned chef and writer Madhur Jaffrey. Although Stamberg values her family recipe, she reveals her personal favorite is actually Jaffrey's sweet and tangy chutney, crafted with canned cranberries, fresh ginger, garlic, vinegar, and an array of spices. Jaffrey's chutney came about by chance when she accidentally opened a can of cranberries instead of tomatoes. Deciding to improvise, she replaced the tomatoes in her usual chutney recipe with cranberries, and the outcome was wonderful. Here are both recipes featured this year:  Madhur Jaffrey’s Cranberry Chutney - 1-inch piece fresh ginger, thinly sliced into slivers - 3 cloves finely chopped garlic - 1/2 cup apple cider vinegar - 4 tablespoons sugar - 1/8 teaspoon cayenne pepper - 1-pound can cranberry sauce with berries - 1/2 teaspoon salt (or less, to taste) - Ground black pepper Combine ginger, garlic, vinegar, sugar, and cayenne in a small saucepan. Simmer over medium heat for around 15 minutes until about four tablespoons of liquid remain. Stir in cranberry sauce, salt, and pepper. Let it simmer gently for another 10 minutes. Cool and refrigerate. Makes approximately 1 1/2 cups.  Mama Stamberg’s Cranberry Relish - 2 cups whole raw cranberries, washed - 1 small onion - 3/4 cup sour cream - 1/2 cup sugar - 2 tablespoons horseradish from a jar (red is milder) Grind the cranberries and onion together, then mix in the rest of the ingredients. Place in a plastic container and freeze. On Thanksgiving morning, transfer the relish to the refrigerator to thaw, leaving some icy bits. The result is a thick, creamy relish with a uniquely vibrant pink color and a tangy taste that perks up turkey, gravy, leftover sandwiches, and roast beef. Makes 1 1/2 pints.  Stamberg later discovered her family recipe actually traced back to a 1959 New York Times article by Craig Claiborne. When she apologized to Claiborne for not crediting him, he was delighted at the recipe's lasting popularity. Stamberg sends wishes for a joyful Thanksgiving, encouraging everyone to try these cranberry sides—and to welcome their own happy kitchen surprises.

On Monday, the Indian government announced that licensed jewellers are now permitted to import a specified quantity of gold from the United Arab Emirates (UAE) at concessional customs rates through the India International Bullion Exchange (IIBX). According to a notification released by the Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT), these companies can receive physical delivery of gold via vaults registered with the International Financial Services Centres Authority (IFSCA), which are located in special economic zones (SEZs).

This arrangement falls under the India-UAE Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA), which came into effect in May 2022. The agreement grants Indian importers a 1% duty concession on a certain quota of gold imported from the UAE, amounting to up to 200 tonnes per year under the Tariff Rate Quota (TRQ) system. Generally, India imposes a 15% import duty on gold.

The DGFT clarified that valid TRQ holders, as recognized by IFSCA, can import gold through the IIBX and collect physical delivery through IFSCA-registered vaults in SEZs, following the authority's prescribed guidelines. The UAE is a significant gold supplier to India, second only to Switzerland. Additionally, gold dore can be imported by refineries with an import license, provided they meet actual user requirements. Imports are also permitted via agencies nominated by the Reserve Bank of India, DGFT, and IFSCA.

In other economic developments, the government is considering the legal aspects of transferring unclaimed funds from the Sahara-Sebi Refund Account to the Consolidated Fund of India while retaining the possibility for investors to claim their refunds later. Also, Apple aims to manufacture ₹1 lakh crore worth of iPhones in India during the current fiscal year, having already achieved over ₹60,000 crore in production within the first seven months. On the corporate front, Nawaz Modi is seeking three-quarters of industrialist Gautam Singhania’s estimated $1.4 billion net worth for herself and their two daughters as part of a family settlement discussion.

article_content: A series of strong, shallow earthquakes struck a lightly populated island chain in eastern Indonesia on Wednesday. Thankfully, officials report no immediate damage or casualties. According to the U.S. Geological Survey, a 6.9 magnitude tremor was detected 341 kilometers southwest of Tual, Maluku province, at a depth of 10 kilometers. A 7.0 magnitude quake soon followed, along with two 5.1 magnitude aftershocks. Indonesia’s Meteorology and Geophysical Agency stated there was no risk of a tsunami, but advised residents to stay cautious due to potential aftershocks. People living on the Tanimbar Islands, home to about 127,000 residents, recounted feeling intense shaking for a few minutes, but authorities said no panic broke out. The earthquakes originated in the Banda Sea near the Tanimbar Islands. Indonesia frequently experiences seismic activity as it lies within the Pacific ‘Ring of Fire,’ known for earthquakes and volcanic eruptions. The report echoes the memory of the devastating 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami, triggered by a 9.1 magnitude earthquake and resulting in more than 230,000 deaths, most occurring in Indonesia’s Aceh province.

article_content: Police in New Delhi arrested Uber driver Shiv Kumar Yadav on Sunday, accused of raping a female passenger. Yadav was taken into custody in Mathura, about 150 kilometers southeast of Delhi, according to Madhur Verma, Deputy Commissioner of Police for North Delhi. Despite seizing the vehicle, investigators initially struggled to apprehend Yadav, who had been actively evading arrest. Yadav registered with Uber using his real name but provided an incorrect address, and his background was left unverified. He lacked the mandatory security badge that requires police clearance, Verma noted. Previously, Yadav was acquitted in a 2012 rape case. Uber stated it exclusively partners with drivers who are properly licensed and identified by the government. Police have requested further information from Uber regarding the company's driver screening process, as investigations continue. Yadav is scheduled for a court appearance on Monday while police request extended custody for additional questioning. The alleged victim, a 26-year-old finance professional from Gurgaon, booked an Uber after dining at a friend's apartment. She reportedly fell asleep in the car, then awoke on a deserted stretch where she says she was assaulted. Yadav later dropped her near her home, threatening her if she spoke about the attack, according to Indian Home Minister Rajnath Singh. The victim notified police at 1:30 a.m. Saturday, less than an hour after the incident. Uber CEO Travis Kalanick has pledged the company's full cooperation with authorities and called for stricter background checks in India’s commercial transport sector, although Verma asserts that these checks are already in place. Uber denounced the alleged assault as an 'abhorrent crime,' providing officers with Yadav’s information and trip records, and expressed support for the victim, promising to aid the ongoing investigation. The case has revived national debate over women's safety, reminiscent of the 2012 Delhi gang rape. Incidents of sexual violence continue to draw attention throughout India, highlighting the urgent call for better protection for women. Other recent cases—such as the viral video featuring sisters Aarti and Pooja Kumar confronting harassers on a bus—have further fueled the conversation about gender-based violence and women's empowerment in India.

article_content: Mobikwik Systems Ltd., a fintech company headquartered in Gurugram, is preparing for an initial public offering (IPO) in Mumbai that could raise roughly $84 million, according to people familiar with the matter. The company has engaged DAM Capital Advisors Ltd. and SBI Capital Markets Ltd. to help coordinate the IPO. According to sources who prefer not to be named because the plans are private, Mobikwik is expected to file its prospectus as soon as next month, with a potential share sale slated for 2024. Details such as the fundraising goal and listing timeline remain tentative and might change. Representatives from DAM Capital and SBI Capital refrained from commenting. Mobikwik also declined to provide specifics, noting that it continues to explore different growth strategies. Launched in 2009, Mobikwik stands as one of India’s top mobile wallet and buy-now-pay-later platforms, with more than 101 million users and over 3 million e-commerce, retail, and billing partners. Prominent investors in the company include Abu Dhabi Investment Authority, American Express, and Sequoia Capital. Mobikwik became profitable at the end of 2021 but decided to delay its IPO following a downturn in tech stocks after rival Paytm went public in November 2021. Mobikwik’s IPO plans come during a record-breaking year for Indian stock listings—205 companies have gone public in 2023 so far, the most for any full year on record, according to Bloomberg. The enthusiasm is fueled by strong equity markets, which have made India one of the world’s busiest listing markets this year. Other prominent market updates include the Nifty Index closing above 20,000 as investor confidence returns, Byju’s facing regulatory challenges, and HCL Group nearing the launch of a semiconductor plant in Karnataka.

article_content: Wipro has entered into a partnership with Nvidia to advance the use of generative AI within the healthcare industry. By leveraging Nvidia's AI Enterprise software, Wipro intends to expand and enhance its healthcare solutions, notably for the Affordable Care Act (ACA), Medicare, and Medicaid. The collaboration aims to elevate member experiences, simplify enrollment, and improve the efficiency of claims decision-making. Wipro states that this alliance will allow healthcare organizations to more easily utilize large language models supported by Nvidia AI. This is expected to increase productivity, offer deeper insights into member needs, and create more efficient operations. LTTS, or L&T Technology Services, has also revealed a collaboration with Nvidia focused on developing AI-powered architectures for medical devices, particularly in the field of endoscopy to improve imaging and scalability. Additionally, Wipro is establishing an AI Center of Excellence in partnership with Nvidia, where their engineers will receive continuous training on Nvidia frameworks—spanning generative AI, the metaverse, conversational AI, and data analytics—to help accelerate custom solution development. Utilizing Nvidia’s AI platforms for generative, speech, and translation tasks, as well as foundational models like NeMo and Riva and Nvidia DGX hardware, Wipro will be able to design tailored generative AI models for a wide range of healthcare applications. Wipro already integrates Nvidia's AI in several healthcare offerings, including industry-leading billing and enrollment products in Medicare and ACA markets, provider and member services leveraging generative AI, and solutions aimed at enhancing claims processing and provider data accuracy. Executives from Wipro, such as Nagendra Bandaru and Jason Eichenholz, highlighted the significance of the partnership, emphasizing how Wipro’s deep healthcare expertise combined with Nvidia's advanced capabilities will empower major healthcare organizations to embrace new AI-driven solutions. Nvidia’s Manuvir Das noted that organizations are keen to adopt multilingual, voice-enabled generative AI inside business applications, praising Nvidia for delivering high-performance, energy-efficient solutions.

Haskell County, Oklahoma, must pay $199,000 in attorneys’ fees after being required to remove an 8-foot-tall Ten Commandments monument from the courthouse lawn. The county had permitted a resident to fund and place the granite structure in front of the courthouse in Stigler in 2006. This decision led to a lawsuit from the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) of Oklahoma, arguing the monument’s placement on public property was unconstitutional.

Following a series of court rulings, and the U.S. Supreme Court declining to hear the case, the county was ordered to remove the monument. It was taken down in March, with attorneys’ fees settled last week, according to ACLU attorney Micheal Salem. The monument has since been relocated to private property owned by the American Legion, about 150 feet from the courthouse.

ACLU Deputy Director Chuck Thornton explained that displaying the Ten Commandments on public property amounted to a government endorsement of religion. “It’s very unwelcoming for those who do not subscribe to the Judeo-Christian belief system. The government should not endorse religion or show favoritism,” he said. Thornton emphasized the ACLU’s involvement was due solely to the monument’s placement on public land and reaffirmed the organization’s support for free religious expression on private property.

An attorney for the Alliance Defense League, which represented the county, did not respond to a request for comment. Haskell County, home to more than 12,000 residents, is located southeast of Tulsa.

article_content: A significant debate has arisen about how Muslim footballers will manage their preparations for crucial knockout matches now that Ramadan has begun. Many of the tournament's biggest stars, such as France's Karim Benzema and Paul Pogba, Germany's Mesut Ozil, Belgium's Marouane Fellaini, Adnan Januzaj, Eden Hazard, eight Swiss players including Xherdan Shaqiri, and the entire Algeria team, are devout Muslims. During Ramadan, Muslims fast from dawn until sunset, refraining from food and drink. Experts caution that this could affect athletic performance, particularly under the demanding conditions in South America, where players are striving for football's highest honor. Speculation is high—especially in countries like France, Switzerland, and Belgium—over which athletes will observe the fast, since Ramadan started just as the World Cup reached its knockout stage. This is the first overlap of Ramadan and the World Cup in 28 years. The debate is especially intense in Algeria—the only Muslim-majority country remaining in the tournament. Algeria’s Bosnian coach, Vahid Halilhodzic, criticized the media for repeatedly questioning his team’s religious practices, calling such scrutiny disrespectful. He emphasized that every player can choose for themselves whether to fast. Nonetheless, some Algerian clerics have urged players to observe Ramadan during the tournament. Many top Muslim footballers still involved in the competition have not publicly stated whether they will fast. For instance, Karim Benzema, Mamadou Sakho, and Paul Pogba of France, and Belgium's Marouane Fellaini, Adnan Januzaj, and Eden Hazard have not clarified their intentions. Bacary Sagna (France) has said he will not fast, citing professional readiness, while Moussa Sissoko (France) previously said he always fasts during Ramadan. Switzerland, with many Muslim players due to immigration from the Balkans, also faces the fasting question. Philippe Senderos, who converted to Islam in 2012, may fast, while his teammates' intentions remain private. Some players, like Mousa Dembélé (Belgium), have said they will not fast for athletic reasons. In contrast, German Muslims such as Mesut Ozil and Sami Khedira have reportedly chosen not to fast. Nigerians Ramon Azeez and Ahmed Musa are expected to observe Ramadan. Islamic law allows exemptions from fasting when traveling or under certain circumstances, which some players may use. The uncertainty over fasting among these top athletes has drawn considerable attention, with teams and individuals taking varied approaches based on personal conviction, religious guidance, and sporting demands.

article_content: A new management team has been appointed at Silverstone, putting an end to months of internal uncertainty. During the investigation, British Racing Drivers' Club (BRDC) chairman John Grant and director Lawrence Tomlinson served as joint-acting chief executives of Silverstone Circuits Limited (SCL). The BRDC clarified that these suspensions were coincidental, separate from the planned management restructuring. The BRDC has now named Patrick Allen as managing director, citing his experience in sales and marketing. Stuart Pringle has been appointed to the new role of sporting director. Ensuring the future of the British F1 Grand Prix at Silverstone remains a top priority, with Pringle overseeing event management and circuit operations. Patrick Allen stated his ambition to make Silverstone the ultimate entertainment venue, offering a quality experience year-round for a variety of events, including motor racing, music concerts, food festivals, and exhibitions. Phillips, Brookes, and Thompson have now left SCL. John Grant thanked them for their roles in Silverstone’s expansion, including building the Wing and securing the British F1 Grand Prix, and wished them well in their future endeavors.

article_content: Patrick Stewart’s performances as Star Trek’s Jean-Luc Picard and the X-Men’s Charles Xavier have made him a beloved figure for over three decades. His characters are known for their wisdom, compassion, and steadfastness—traits that many see as admirable in a father figure. Now 83, Stewart has published his memoir, 'Making It So', a title nodding to his famous command as Captain Picard. The book traces his journey from a humble upbringing in Yorkshire, where he left school at 15, to his eventual rise in Hollywood. Stewart’s path was not easy. Despite his long tenure at the Royal Shakespeare Company, he had not achieved high-profile roles on stage or screen by his mid-40s. After being noticed during a Shakespeare reading at UCLA, Stewart nearly missed out on Star Trek when Gene Roddenberry reportedly insisted his name not be mentioned again after a poor audition. Facing self-doubt while waiting for news, Stewart even considered retraining as a professional squash player. While the memoir shares Stewart’s introspection, especially about witnessing domestic violence as a child and the breakdown of his first two marriages, these moments are brief. The book also shows Stewart’s respect for other stars, and even those he disagreed with, such as Roddenberry, are treated gently. The writing reveals Stewart’s reserved nature, which some interpret as reluctance to show deep feelings or disappointment about being known mostly for sci-fi roles instead of Shakespearean ones. However, in person, Stewart is warm and open, reflecting the kindness of his most famous characters. His home in Los Angeles is filled with artwork and mementos from friends, including illustrations with his close friend Ian McKellen. Stewart recognizes the limited time he has left but remains enthusiastic about exploring new opportunities and possibly reprising Picard one more time, despite his aging voice.

article_content: Less than a day after former IRS official Lois Lerner was held in criminal contempt of Congress, the IRS agreed to turn over copies of all her emails and correspondence to a Republican-led House committee probing the scandal that led to her retirement. The agency's decision came after a 231-178 contempt vote in the House and a separate resolution calling for a nonpartisan special counsel at the Department of Justice. Lerner has twice refused to answer questions from lawmakers during congressional hearings, even while under subpoena. "This is ALL Lerner documents," a House Ways and Means Committee official confirmed to MailOnline. Chairman Dave Camp, a Michigan Republican, warned the IRS he would issue subpoenas if it did not provide all documents related to Lerner. In response, tea party members have protested at IRS headquarters in Washington, calling for the production of all relevant documents. Lerner was Director of Exempt Organizations at the IRS until her retirement in 2013. She drew criticism from Republicans during a 2013 House hearing for making an opening statement about her role in the tea party targeting issue and then refusing to answer committee members' questions. "While it is good we are finally getting these emails, it should never have taken this long," Camp said in a statement. "The agency is finally doing what is right and hopefully this is the last of the delays." Lerner is accused of impeding tax-exempt status applications from conservative groups, while liberal groups had their applications processed more quickly. The Ways and Means Committee referred her case to the Justice Department on April 9, alleging she used her authority to improperly act against conservative organizations, denying them due process and equal protection under the law. If convicted, Lerner could face a jail term of up to one year and a fine of up to $100,000. During the period around the 2010 midterm elections, many tea party and other conservative groups experienced delays of three years or more, while liberal groups were generally approved more quickly. The House of Representatives voted to hold Lerner in criminal contempt, led by House Oversight Chairman Darrell Issa. Conservative activists have urged Congress to find out who authorized the targeting based on political views. In 2013, tea party activists told MailOnline they believed President Barack Obama was to blame for any IRS corruption uncovered. Committee investigations found that some denied tax-exemption cases were managed in Washington, rather than the Cincinnati office where Lerner worked. Camp warned in a February 24 letter he would begin issuing subpoenas unless all requested documents were produced. Although the IRS began supplying some materials, Thursday's decision includes more Lerner-related documents than previously provided. Meanwhile, the IRS has proposed new regulations for the communications of 'public benefit' organizations such as tea party groups, which are tax-exempt. Republicans have argued this would formalize actions allegedly taken by the Obama administration outside of public scrutiny.

article_content: Since Terrence Malick's fifth film, 'The Tree of Life,' premiered at Cannes earlier this week, the 2½-hour impressionistic work has evoked mixed reactions, including some boos, walkouts, and lengthy standing ovations. When the film won the prestigious Palme d'Or at the close of the festival, discussion intensified. 'The Tree of Life' stars Brad Pitt as a stern but disillusioned father of three boys in 1950s Texas, Jessica Chastain as his luminous wife, and Sean Penn as their grown son years later. The film features little linear narrative or dialogue, relying instead on whispered voiceovers reflecting on existence and faith. It contains extended sequences showing volcanoes erupting, cells dividing, and other impressive natural phenomena reminiscent of programming like 'Nova' and classics like '2001: A Space Odyssey.' Notably, it also includes CGI dinosaurs. While the unusual style might be a hard sell for audiences more interested in familiar sequels like 'The Hangover Part II' or 'Kung Fu Panda 2,' the film compensates with striking visuals and a poetic meditation on family, faith, loss of innocence, and reconciliation. These artistic strengths linger with viewers even after the film’s unconventional story structure ends. Criticisms revolve around the film’s lack of traditional plot development or conflict. While this is true to an extent, the film’s emphasis is on the journey itself. As described by its stars at a Cannes press conference, Malick's approach is to spontaneously capture moments, sometimes shifting focus in the middle of a take to unexpected subjects. Although the film may seem aimless to some, Malick is deliberate in juxtaposing powerful imagery and a soaring score with intimate moments, like sunlight on grass or a baby's first steps, to create the film’s unique atmosphere. Malick was absent from press duties at Cannes, attending briefly only for the premiere. Brad Pitt explained that the director prefers focusing on his work rather than promoting it. Despite raising more questions than providing answers, 'The Tree of Life' is ultimately an experience to be appreciated, not overanalyzed, as its remarkable parts do not always coalesce into a traditional whole. 'The Tree of Life' is currently in limited release in New York and Los Angeles and opens nationwide on July 8.

article_content: Radioactive iodine levels in seawater near the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear power plant dropped significantly even before workers closed a leak believed to come from the damaged No. 2 reactor, according to the plant's operator on Wednesday night. Stopping the flow of highly radioactive water into the Pacific Ocean was a major success for workers, who have been trying to keep the earthquake-damaged plant's reactors from overheating for nearly four weeks. However, Tokyo Electric Power Company (TEPCO) and top Japanese officials warned there are still serious challenges ahead. Iodine-131 concentrations reached up to 7.5 million times the legal standard in water directly behind the plant following the discovery of the leak on Saturday. These levels had fallen to less than 4 percent of that amount in the 24 hours before the leak was stopped Wednesday morning, according to data from TEPCO. While the concentration remained 280,000 times the legal limit, the levels were falling rapidly as water dispersed into the Pacific. Cesium-137, which remains radioactive longer, also dropped but was still 61,000 times above legal standards. Monitoring data 20 kilometers (12.5 miles) southeast of the plant showed iodine-131 levels had decreased to 1.5 times the legal limit, with no measurement for cesium. Japanese authorities believe the leaked water came from the 8 metric tons (2,100 gallons) per hour being pumped into the No. 2 reactor, one of three units that suffered core damage during the massive earthquake and tsunami on March 11. The contaminated water leaked into the basement of the unit's turbine building, carrying radioactive particles. Until Wednesday, the water was flowing into the ocean through a cracked concrete shaft near the water intake for the turbine plant. Workers used a silica-based polymer known as 'liquid glass' to seal the breach Wednesday morning, but government officials said that other issues remain. Chief Cabinet Secretary Yukio Edano questioned whether the leak was completely stopped, expressing concern about possible additional leaks. Hidehiko Nishiyama from Japan's Nuclear and Industrial Safety Agency likewise cautioned that stopping the current leak could cause increased leakage elsewhere. As a precaution, TEPCO began injecting nonflammable nitrogen into the primary containment vessel around reactor No. 1 early Thursday to reduce the risk of hydrogen buildup, which could potentially lead to explosions. TEPCO said the likelihood of a hydrogen explosion was very low, but noted that further hydrogen could develop. Hydrogen accumulation is a sign of overheating fuel rods and caused explosions that damaged the No. 1 and No. 3 reactor buildings after the March 11 earthquake. Despite current precautions, TEPCO does not believe an explosion is imminent. The radioactive cores of reactors No. 1, 2, and 3 were damaged when the tsunami flooded the plant, disabling critical cooling systems. Engineers responded by pumping water into the reactors to prevent a meltdown, but are now faced with large amounts of contaminated water. Since Monday night, TEPCO has been releasing around 10,000 tons of less-radioactive water into the ocean to free up space in waste treatment facilities for the more highly contaminated coolant from reactor No. 2. Michael Friedlander, a former nuclear plant operator, noted that without processing systems in place, dumping the water might continue due to the accumulation of about 400,000 gallons of radioactive water per day. TEPCO had released about three-quarters of this water by Wednesday night and reduced its estimate of how much more was being discharged. Japanese officials describe the release as an emergency step, but it has led to protests from South Korea and anger among Japanese fishermen. Edano said Wednesday that the discharge was unavoidable in order to minimize environmental harm, but acknowledged that authorities could have better informed the public and Japan's neighbors. He explained, 'It was a measure to prevent more serious marine contamination, but we needed to explain the reasoning better.' During a Wednesday meeting, representatives from Japan's fishery association expressed frustration, noting they had not been told in advance about the start of the discharge. Edano stated the government is considering temporary compensation for fishermen, pending a more comprehensive plan. Experts believe the releases are unlikely to cause long-term health risks to people or sea life, partly because iodine-131 decays quickly, losing half its radioactivity every eight days. Timothy Jorgensen, a radiation safety expert from Georgetown University Medical Center, explained that the discharged water represents a small fraction of the vast Pacific Ocean, allowing for rapid dilution. In recent days, officials say conditions in the plant's reactors and spent fuel pools have stabilized, with airborne radiation levels in the surrounding area continuing to decline. However, the presence of large quantities of radioactive water at the site indicates the potential for further leaks and ongoing challenges. Hiroo Saso, Susan Olson, and Tsukushi Ikeda contributed to this report for CNN.

article_content: Punjab Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann is urging the use of cash payments to persuade farmers not to burn paddy stubble after harvesting. He underscored that, even with the government's ongoing discussions and efforts, financial incentives are likely more effective at stopping this practice. Mann explained that the central government wants to motivate farmers, but the core issue remains their economic realities. Punjab proposed that the Centre offer Rs 1,000 and the state add Rs 1,500 per acre—forming a total Rs 2,500 incentive for each acre not burned—but Mann claims the Centre rejected this idea. He also called for a guaranteed Minimum Support Price on crops like maize and pulses, which would encourage crop choice and help reduce dependence on paddy. To support this change, the Punjab government would fill any income gap for farmers who switch to alternative crops, for example, bridging the difference if maize earns less than paddy. Mann pointed out that increasing local pulse production could also help reduce costly imports. He emphasized that taking legal action against farmers is only a last measure, and stressed the need for collective responsibility. A recent case in Bathinda illustrates the difficulties, where some farmers reportedly forced a government official to ignite a pile of stubble.

Botox, widely recognized for smoothing wrinkles, is now showing promise in helping people with severe asthma. In an innovative Australian trial, doctors administered Botox injections directly into the vocal cords of patients who also suffered from vocal cord dysfunction—a condition where muscle spasms make breathing extremely difficult. Botox’s partial paralysis of these muscles brought about a relaxation that eased breathing troubles for about two to three months per treatment.

The study comprised 11 patients, some receiving up to 24 injections. Impressively, 60% of participants reported a significant improvement in their symptoms, with several needing only a few injections for noticeable change. Voice softening appeared as a minor side effect, but swallowing was unaffected.

Professor Phillip Bardin of Monash Health commented that botulinum toxin injections may offer a viable solution for asthma cases complicated by abnormal vocal cord movement. Lyn Dowsey, a 68-year-old patient, described her past experiences as feeling choked and breathless. Following the treatment, she reported greatly improved breathing, even joking about hoping for cosmetic benefits too. The clinical study spanned 18 months and involved 11 researchers.
