Health Secretary Michael Matheson has admitted that an £11,000 data roaming bill on his parliamentary iPad resulted from his sons using the device as a hotspot to stream football matches during a family holiday in Morocco last year. The Scottish Parliament initially paid the bill after Mr Matheson claimed the iPad was used exclusively for work. He has now reimbursed the full amount and referred himself for further investigation.

In an emotional statement to parliament, Mr Matheson revealed that he only learned last Thursday—after media reports—about his family’s use of the iPad's data allowance. He clarified that while the iPad itself was not directly used by his children, its hotspot function provided internet access for other devices to stream football. Matheson admitted he deliberately omitted these details in his earlier public statement, in an attempt to shield his children from political and media attention, a decision for which he expressed deep regret and apologized unreservedly.

He accepted full responsibility for the device and acknowledged his mistake in failing to mention his sons’ involvement. He emphasized that the excessive data charges stemmed from football streaming and reiterated that he did not personally watch the matches. Matheson stated he had been advised that the iPad could be used as a mobile hotspot, and that his son had assisted in setting it up.

Parliamentary records confirm Mr Matheson contacted officials regarding issues with his phone’s functionality in Morocco on 28 December, but no records indicate discussion of the iPad. On Monday, Matheson denied any personal use of the iPad, but on Thursday referred himself for investigation to the Scottish Parliamentary Corporate Body, while maintaining his position as health secretary.

Matheson stated that upon first learning of the high bill in January, he could not immediately explain it. Lacking a clear answer, he initially agreed in March to pay £3,000 from office expenses, with the remainder paid by parliament. The highest charges, including over £7,000 on 2 January during a Celtic vs. Rangers match, resulted from over 6GB of data used between 28 December 2022 and 3 January 2023.

A required SIM card change following a switch in mobile provider from EE to Vodafone in December 2021 was never carried out, despite Mr Matheson being notified well before his holiday, contributing to the excessive charges.

Opposition parties, including Scottish Conservatives and Scottish Labour, have strongly criticized Mr Matheson, calling for his resignation and indicating they will pursue a motion of no confidence. Labour’s Jackie Baillie and Conservative leader Douglas Ross accused him of negligence in managing the device and misleading both parliament and the public. First Minister Humza Yousaf, however, expressed his full confidence in Matheson, describing him as honest and principled.

After receiving the bill, parliamentary IT staff inspected the iPad, but only noted overall data usage, not specific browsing history. Parliament has instituted a review of its mobile device and data roaming policies to prevent future incidents.

RAWALPINDI: On Friday, Pakistan Army chief General Syed Asim Munir asserted that the use of force is solely the prerogative of the state, with no group or entity permitted to use coercive force. He made this statement during a meeting with leading Islamic scholars (Ulema o Mashaikh) from across all Islamic schools of thought at the GHQ in Rawalpindi, according to an army statement.

General Munir emphasized that intolerance and extremist behavior are unacceptable, particularly when directed against minorities and vulnerable segments of society. "Pakistan belongs to all its citizens, irrespective of religious, provincial, tribal, linguistic, ethnic, sectarian or any other differences. The use of force or armed action by any militia, entity, or group other than the State is unacceptable," he said.

The meeting unanimously expressed support for government measures, including the repatriation of illegal foreigners, implementation of the 'One Document Regime' for foreign visitors, efforts to curb smuggling and hoarding, and initiatives to stop power theft.

Additionally, the participants fully acknowledged Pakistan's positions and concerns regarding terrorism originating from Afghan soil, and called for serious action by Afghanistan to address these concerns, the statement added.

Lindsey McNamara, a 24-year-old nursing student from Ashland, Massachusetts, has been reported missing. She was last seen on Valentine’s Day, February 14, having dinner with two acquaintances at PF Chang’s in the Natick Mall. Her family does not recognize these individuals. Police have confirmed her cell phone activity last pinged in the area that evening.

McNamara previously gained notoriety after a December incident where she threw raw bacon and sausages at the Framingham Police Department reception desk while shouting, 'It’s time to feed the pigs.' Surveillance footage of the event went viral, making her an unexpected internet figure. Police said McNamara later stated that God told her to 'feed the pigs.'

McNamara was charged with disorderly conduct and malicious destruction of property under $250. The latter charge was dismissed by a judge, but she was ordered to pay $150 in court costs for disorderly conduct and undergo psychiatric evaluation.

Her family has voiced concern for her mental health and welfare. Her aunt, Denise McNamara Fitzgerald, commented on social media that McNamara believed someone was out to get her. Fitzgerald also said her niece had been doing better on her medication before she went missing. Her mother, Regina McNamara, said Lindsey was experiencing a difficult time during the incident.

Authorities report there is no current evidence of foul play but are continuing to actively investigate McNamara’s disappearance. Police are requesting any information from the public that could help locate her. McNamara is described as having blue eyes and brown hair.

Labour’s political challenges in Scotland deepened as the party admitted it can no longer use David Cameron as a ‘scare tactic’ due to the Prime Minister’s greater popularity compared to Ed Miliband. Scottish Labour leader Jim Murphy revealed the party has dropped the slogan ‘Vote SNP – get Cameron’ in favor of ‘Vote SNP – get Tory’, highlighting the historic negative associations many Scots have with the Conservative Party, especially under Margaret Thatcher.

This strategic shift follows polling by Lord Ashcroft, which found David Cameron is more popular in Scotland than Ed Miliband, including in traditional Labour strongholds. In 15 out of 16 constituencies surveyed, more voters said they were satisfied with Cameron or preferred him as Prime Minister than Miliband.

According to these polls, if results are repeated at the general election, Labour could lose the majority of its 41 Scottish seats to the SNP, boosting Nicola Sturgeon’s influence in a possible left-leaning coalition.

A Scottish Conservatives spokesman stated that many Scots would now rather have Cameron as Prime Minister than Miliband, and criticized Murphy’s strategy for relying on anti-Tory sentiment linked to historic events rather than discussing current leadership.

Meanwhile, Labour’s health spokesman Andy Burnham is emerging as a possible left-wing leadership contender, voicing support for union leader Len McCluskey and distancing himself from the party’s Blairite wing.

New polling also suggests Liberal Democrat leader Nick Clegg is now three points behind Labour in Sheffield Hallam, putting his seat at risk. In Thanet South, the Conservative lead over UKIP leader Nigel Farage has narrowed to one point.

article_content: ATLANTA, Georgia (CNN) – The federal trial of Syed Haris Ahmed, a former Georgia Tech student accused of supporting terrorism, concluded Thursday after Ahmed delivered his own closing argument. The FBI alleges that Ahmed took surveillance video of the Pentagon and discussed possible attacks on the United States. Ahmed, charged with providing material support to terrorism both in the US and abroad, used his closing statement to focus on his Muslim faith instead of directly responding to the prosecution’s evidence. "I just want to convey the message of God," Ahmed said, adding, "Any authority not derived from the authority of God is a state of rebellion. As a Muslim, it's not right for me to use those laws to my benefit." He quoted verses and prayers from the Quran and compared Islam with Christianity, saying, "We worship the same God." Ahmed, a naturalized US citizen born in Pakistan, waived his right to a jury trial to make his statement during closing arguments. US District Judge William Duffey will determine Ahmed's fate. At the close of Ahmed’s remarks, Duffey stated, "Mr. Ahmed, this is somewhat different. This is not a case about your faith, nor my faith. This is about your conduct." The judge said he would decide the case based on US law and evidence. If convicted, Ahmed, 24, faces up to 15 years in prison. Assistant US Attorney Robert McBurney told the court, "The case is not about throwing bombs and shooting soldiers, but providing support for those activities." Prosecutors allege that Ahmed and co-defendant Ehsanul Islam Sadequee traveled from Atlanta to Canada in March 2005, where they discussed potential attacks in the US with three men they met online. Ahmed and Sadequee allegedly recorded 'casing videos' of Washington landmarks during an April 2005 trip. These videos were reportedly emailed to other co-conspirators and found on hard drives of men charged with terrorism in the UK. Prosecutors also claim Ahmed traveled to Pakistan in July 2005 intending to attend a terrorist training camp. "The whole point is to get the terrorist before he gets to flight school and figures out how to fly a commercial airliner," McBurney said. Earlier, Defense Attorney Jack Martin argued for dismissal, stating, "The evidence is very, very thin." During Martin's motion, Ahmed objected, insisting on presenting his own closing argument, which he later delivered. The dismissal motion was denied. Martin had called only two witnesses: Ahmed's older sister and his father. Both testified that Ahmed was searching for his religious identity. Throughout the trial, the defense described Ahmed as a shy, highly emotional young man who moved to suburban Atlanta at age 12 and struggled to find his Muslim identity, turning to the Internet for guidance. Martin argued that no concrete agreement was ever made with co-conspirators and described Ahmed's actions as 'childish fantasies.' Co-defendant Sadequee is scheduled to face similar charges in a separate trial in August.

article_content: The Indian Succession Act, 1925, does not specify a time limit for challenging a will, yet there may be limitations based on certain circumstances. Legal heirs generally challenge a will’s validity if they are dissatisfied with how assets are distributed. The Act outlines specific grounds on which a will can be contested. Ravi Singhania, Managing Partner at Singhania & Partners LLP, states that a valid will must meet legal requirements such as the testator being of sound mind, proper signature, and attestation by witnesses. He notes that around 10 legal grounds exist for challenging wills. In India, succession laws depend on the religion of the person making the will (the testator). Divi Dutta, Partner at Shardul Amarchand Mangaldas & Co., says that for Hindus, Buddhists, Sikhs, Jains, Parsis, and Indian Christians, the Indian Succession Act applies. Other religions like Islam follow their own succession laws. Both registered and unregistered wills can be challenged on the same grounds. However, registering a will makes it more difficult to challenge certain aspects such as execution or authenticity of signatures, even though registration is not legally required. Main grounds for challenging a will under the Indian Succession Act include: 1. Lack of testamentary capacity: Only people of sound mind who are not minors can make a will (Section 59). Illness, intoxication, or other factors affecting decision-making can disqualify someone. However, lucidity at the time of making the will can make it valid. 2. Fraud, coercion, or undue influence: A will made under pressure or manipulation is void (Section 61). Free will of the testator is essential. 3. Improper execution: The will must be signed by the testator and attested by at least two witnesses in the testator’s presence (Section 63). 4. Perpetual transfer: Bequests that try to last forever or indefinitely, beyond the legal heirs, are restricted (Section 114). 5. Uncertainty: If a will is unclear or ambiguous, such as referencing missing attachments, it can be declared void (Section 89). 6. Impossible conditions: If the will’s execution depends on an event that is impossible, it is invalid (Section 126). 7. Illegal or immoral provisions: Any part of the will that breaks the law or is against public policy is void (Section 127). 8. Forgery: If the will or its signature is forged, a legal heir can challenge it, but the challenger must provide proof. 9. Suspicious circumstances: The court may scrutinize the will for suspicious details, such as questionable signatures or unusual distribution of assets. The Supreme Court in Shivakumar v. Sharanabasappa (AIR 2020 SC 3102) highlighted that such features can be grounds to contest a will. There is no statutory time limit to challenge a will in India, but the court may question undue delays. The longer the delay, the stronger the evidence must be to justify both the challenge and the delay. In summary, a will can be challenged at any time, but it is best to act promptly.

article_content: Romania’s President, Traian Basescu, regards emigration as a benefit to his country, saying it helps reduce local unemployment. Basescu claims that numerous unemployed Romanians have left for jobs in the UK, which he believes supports Romania. Responding to concerns in Britain about growing numbers of Romanian immigrants, Basescu suggested many may return once wages in Romania begin to match those in countries like the UK, France, Italy, or Spain. At present, Romanians earn an average of £420 per month, much less than the average UK wage of £2,000. Official statistics show that 28,000 Romanians and Bulgarians moved to Britain in the twelve months before March, more than twice the previous year’s total. This surge follows relaxed border controls that took effect at the start of the year. Presently, about 177,000 Romanians and Bulgarians reside in the UK—more than five times as many as seven years ago. Basescu remarked that Romanians working abroad help keep unemployment down in Romania. He also highlighted the importance of money sent home by migrants, especially during economic crises, for helping to balance Romania’s foreign trade. Speaking to BBC Radio 4, Basescu said most Romanians in the UK are hardworking and do not depend on British welfare. He explained that Romania needs these citizens and will be ready to welcome them back as domestic economic conditions improve. Basescu distinguished today’s situation from the communist era, stating that the government is not responsible for the livelihoods of every individual—and that many Romanians abroad share this belief. Romanian migration attracted public attention when Victor Spirescu arrived at Luton Airport on New Year’s Day after rules eased, and was greeted by MPs Mark Reckless and Keith Vaz. Meanwhile, reports show some Eastern European migrants sleeping rough in parts of central London.
